World.title: Ice Deliveries: How Southern Croatia Coped in Summer Before Air Conditioning
World.content:
August the 7th, 2026 – Ice deliveries through the mountains was how southern Croatia coped during the intense summer heat, long before the advent and comfort of air conditioning.

Long before refrigerators and ice machines, the local people of Dubrovnik developed an incredibly organised ice-supply system. Snow was stored in special pits in winter and kept under straw and brushwood.

Imagine what summers looked like a few hundred years ago. The Dalmatian sun is strong, heating the ancient stone walls and streets; electricity doesn’t even exist, nor do refrigerators, freezers, and definitely not air-conditioners. Putni kofer/Lana Mindoljevic writes that instead of getting a full glass of ice in a few seconds, ice was an extremely precious commodity. Down in Dubrovnik, however, it existed even during the middle of summer.

Mountain snow was stored throughout the winter in special pits in the Konavle hills, kept under straw and brushwood, and in summer lowered by horses down to Cavtat and sent by boat to Dubrovnik. This precious ice was so highly valued that it was given as a gift to distinguished guests, and Dubrovnik even had an Ice Street.

Hundreds of kilograms of ice arrived in the City every summer

How was it possible that something considered a real little miracle during the hot summer days could already be found on the tables of Dubrovnik’s nobility? And not just a few accidentally preserved pieces. In the hottest part of summer, according to surviving accounts, around 260 kilograms of ice arrived in Dubrovnik every day.

Hundreds of kilograms of something that had to be produced months earlier, protected from the spring and summer sun, carried across the mountain, loaded onto horses, brought down to the sea and then transported by boat to the City. Apart from showing the fascinating organisational skill of the former Republic of Dubrovnik, this also reveals how much people already sought ways to refresh themselves in summer.

In winter they stored snow in pits and kept it until summer

Dubrovnik’s main reserve of cold lay far from the hot stone of Stradun, in the Konavle hills, in the Sniježnica area. The Museums and Galleries of Konavle write that in the time of the Republic of Dubrovnik three ice-houses (ledenice) were filled every winter – special natural or adapted pits into which snow was collected. The work was most often done in January or February. The snow was thrown in and compacted, then covered with brushwood and straw, and the ice-houses were closed and locked. The prince (knez) was responsible for their operation and maintenance, and the whole process took place under the supervision of a guard.

The ice-houses were by no means just small holes in the ground. They are located about a two-hour walk from the village of Duba and have been thoroughly explored by speleologists. The Konavle museum blog states that the Great Ice-house is 11 metres deep and 12 metres long, while the Small one is four metres deep and eight metres long.

When summer arrived, the night-time delivery operation began

Although collecting the ice was already interesting, the method of transport when summer arrived was even more fascinating. During the warmer part of the year, ice delivery from the Konavle hills to Dubrovnik was organised almost daily. Ice was taken from the ice-houses in the late afternoon, when the greatest heat had subsided, then loaded onto horses and brought down towards Cavtat.

From Cavtat, the journey continued by sea to the City of Dubrovnik. After the horse journey, the ice would set off by boat from Cavtat in the early morning hours so that it would not melt before reaching its destination.

For the year 1783, there’s concrete data: almost 16 tonnes of ice were brought to dubrovnik

How extensively the whole system was used is best shown by one surviving account. HRT’s programme Gradoplov, referring to Zdravko Šundrica’s book The Secret Box of the Dubrovnik Archive II, gives very precise figures for 1783. From 20 May to 20 August, 12,123 oka of ice arrived in Dubrovnik – that is, 15,759 kilograms. Transport required 146 horse-loads, and the whole operation cost 129 of the prince’s thalers.

in some cases, ice was brought in from herzegovina

On average, around 170 kilograms of ice arrived in the City every day during that period. In June about 110 kilograms were used, in July 170, and in August consumption rose. From 1 to 20 August Dubrovnik needed around 260 kilograms of ice daily. And every one of those kilograms first had to be produced with the help of winter alone, preserved for months and physically delivered to the city. If the winters were weak and did not produce enough snow to fill all three ice-houses, ice was obtained from the Herzegovinian mountains.

dubrovnik’s very own ice street

Over time the trade became so organised that ice had its own place in the City. HRT notes that there was an Ice Street (Ulica od leda) in Dubrovnik where ice could be bought, and interesting equipment for its use was also developed. One of the best examples was the kantiflora, a special glass bottle for cooling drinks. Ice was, of course, available only to the wealthier, so it was often given as a gift to distinguished guests. The Museums and Galleries of Konavle mention another tasty detail: ice cream was already spoken of in Dubrovnik in the 18th century.

Remains of the old ice-houses are still hidden on Sniježnica mountain today

The story does not live only in archival documents today. The Great and Small Ice-houses still exist in the Konavle hills, and in 2016 speleologists explored them and drew up their plans. The Cavtat-Konavle Tourist Board notes that the trail to the Konavle ice-houses is marked and starts in the village of Duba by the Church of St Stephen.

World.title: Iraq oil exports drop 75% amid Hormuz closure
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraqi Oil Minister Hayan Abdul-Ghani announced on Saturday, August 8, 2026, that the nation’s crude oil exports have plummeted by 75% due to the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz and regional military escalations. The severe drop in oil revenues has triggered a liquidity squeeze across the federal government, causing widespread delays in state employee salary disbursements.

Speaking at a press conference in Baghdad, Abdul-Ghani revealed that Iraq is currently exporting only a quarter of its pre-war volumes, which stood at approximately 3.5 million barrels per day (bpd) prior to the outbreak of regional hostilities on February 28. He noted that while Baghdad has engaged in diplomatic talks with Iran to permit the passage of Iraqi oil shipments through the Gulf, no operational agreement has been activated.

Key financial and operational highlights

Export Collapse: Iraq’s crude exports have fallen to ~25% of pre-war capacity, cutting off the primary source of state revenue.

Fiscal Pressure & Salary Delays: Reduced export volumes and below-budget sale prices have caused acute liquidity shortages, delaying public sector payrolls.

Corporate Damage Compensation: Domestic Attacks: Baghdad has agreed to compensate foreign energy companies for damages resulting from attacks originating inside Iraqi territory. External Strikes: The government declared itself legally exempt from compensating firms for damages caused by foreign strikes or broader military actions beyond state control.

Alternative Export Bypasses: Baghdad is fast-tracking pipeline infrastructure projects bypassing the Persian Gulf, including routes south toward Turkey’s Ceyhan port, Syria’s Baniyas terminal, and Jordan’s Aqaba port.

To maintain minimal cash flows, Iraq is currently forced to sell its crude at deep price concessions below the baseline benchmark set in the national budget, compounding treasury deficits.

In response to the prolonged maritime chokehold in the Strait of Hormuz, the Ministry of Oil is accelerating infrastructure development along overland export routes.

Priority has been placed on expanding and constructing pipeline corridors connecting southern production hubs to the Mediterranean via Syria and Turkey, alongside long-term transit planning toward the Red Sea via Jordan.

World.title: Iraq activates Kirkuk oil field development contract with BP
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The Iraqi Ministry of Oil announced on Saturday, August 8, 2026, the official activation of its Kirkuk oilfield development contract with British energy giant BP. The project aims to elevate crude oil production from its current capacity of 320,000 barrels per day (bpd) to a peak target of 420,000 bpd.

Ministry of Oil Spokesperson Salim Al-Rikabi stated that the contract—initially signed in September 2025—focuses on expanding crude extraction while capturing associated natural gas to eliminate routine flaring and feed domestic power generation infrastructure.

Key operational targets & metrics

Crude Oil Output: Increasing current production from 320,000 bpd to a peak target of 420,000 bpd.

Associated Gas Capture: Raising associated gas processing from 255 million standard cubic feet per day (scf/d) to a peak capacity of 400 million scf/d.

Facility Modernization: Upgrading and expanding infrastructure across North Oil Company fields and North Gas Company processing plants.

Power & Social Infrastructure: Constructing a dedicated 400-megawatt (MW) power plant, expanding local employment, funding community development initiatives, and upskilling North Oil and North Gas workforces.

Environmental Impact: Phasing out continuous gas flaring to redirect captured methane directly into national electricity generation.

The activation of the Kirkuk project represents a major component of Iraq’s broader energy strategy to achieve natural gas self-sufficiency and reduce reliance on imported fuel.

By upgrading processing facilities managed by the North Gas Company and constructing a dedicated 400 MW power generation facility, the initiative directly addresses regional electricity shortages while reducing environmental emissions.

The partnership also reinforces BP’s operational footprint in northern Iraq, complementing its long-standing management of the Southern Rumaila field and bolstering state-led efforts to modernize national energy infrastructure.

World.title: India’s Reliance pays record $25 million freight cost for Iraqi crude amid Hormuz crisis
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — India’s Reliance Industries (RELI.NS), operator of the world’s largest refining complex in Gujarat, paid an unprecedented record charter fee of $23 million to $25 million for a Very Large Crude Carrier (VLCC) to transport 2 million barrels of Basrah crude from Iraq, according to shipping sources cited by Reuters on Friday, August 7, 2026.

The extreme freight surge—marking a jump from a pre-war average of $2 million to 12 times the baseline global freight rate—highlights severe shipping chokepoints in the Strait of Hormuz caused by the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict. Daily vessel transits through the strategic waterway have plummeted from a pre-war average of 125–140 ships to a fraction of normal capacity as shipowners avoid military risks.

Key financial & logistics metrics

Soaring Freight Rates: Reliance chartered the VLCC from South Korea’s Sinokor at 1,200 points on the Worldscale freight index—12 times the reference benchmark—up from pre-war levels of 0.8 to 0.9 times ($2 million total).

Deep SOMO Discounts: To offset soaring shipping costs and attract buyers into the Gulf, the State Organization for Marketing of Oil (SOMO) offered steep discounts of $25 to $30 per barrel below Dubai regional benchmarks.

Net Margin Offset: Despite the $25 million freight tag, energy analysts estimate Reliance will still save millions on the overall transaction due to Iraq’s heavy crude price reductions.

Limited Carrier Pool: Sinokor remains one of the few international maritime operators willing to navigate the Strait of Hormuz to load cargo at Iraq’s Basra Oil Terminal.

While Asian refiners—particularly across India and China—are actively seeking chartered tankers to capture Iraq’s discounted crude allocations, shipowner reluctance continues to limit available tonnage entering the Gulf.

By offering deep price concessions, Iraq’s oil marketing arm is successfully maintaining crude flow off the Basra coast despite soaring war-risk insurance premiums and maritime transport bottlenecks.

World.title: Kata’ib Sayyid Al Shuhada clarifies delay in retaliatory strikes against U.S.-Saudi targets
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Abu Ala al-Walai, Secretary-General of Kata’ib Sayyid al-Shuhada, commented on Saturday, August 8, 2026, regarding the decision by the “Islamic Resistance in Iraq” to pause planned military responses to recent joint U.S.-Saudi strikes.

Speaking via a statement on social media platform X, al-Walai confirmed that the delay was granted at the direct request of Coordination Framework leaders, led by Badr Organization chief Hadi al-Amiri, alongside several independent political figures. However, the paramilitary commander emphasized that options for retaliation—including the reassessment of its timing, scale, and nature—remain fully on the table. He urged state officials to utilize this temporary window to secure Iraq’s rights through diplomatic and legal channels.

Key developments in the escalation pause

The Deferred Response: The Islamic Resistance in Iraq announced on Friday, August 7, the postponement of retaliatory operations originally scheduled for the 23rd of Safar targeting Saudi Arabia and U.S. military bases.

Al-Amiri’s Appeal: Badr Organization leader Hadi al-Amiri issued an urgent video address early Friday urging armed factions to delay military action following American-Saudi strikes on Iraqi territory, prioritizing national stability while pursuing accountability for casualties via diplomatic means.

High Security Readiness: The political appeal followed a volatile night across Baghdad and multiple governorates, prompting high-level security alerts and military deployments across the capital.

Command Structure On Site: In response to directives from Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi to elevate combat readiness, senior commanders from Baghdad Operations Command were deployed on the ground to enforce military discipline and secure vital sectors.

The brief pause in military operations provides a critical window for Prime Minister al-Zaidi’s administration to manage state security, navigate delicate diplomatic channels with Washington and Riyadh, and prevent further regional escalation.

World.title: Iraq fish deaths: 7 alarming signs of a deepening water and pollution crisis
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Recurring Iraq fish deaths are becoming an increasingly serious environmental and economic warning, with the Green Iraq Observatory describing the phenomenon as an annual pattern that reflects the accumulation of two interconnected crises: worsening water scarcity and persistent pollution.

Rather than representing isolated incidents caused by temporary changes in river conditions, the repeated deaths of large numbers of fish across Iraq’s rivers, canals and marshlands suggest that the country’s aquatic ecosystems are coming under sustained pressure from declining water flows, untreated wastewater, industrial pollution and weaknesses in water management.

The latest incidents, recorded in April and August 2026, have once again raised concerns about the condition of Iraq’s freshwater resources and the government’s ability to protect them. According to the observatory, more than 1,000 tonnes of fish died in the Tigris and Diyala rivers during April, with particularly heavy losses reported in Wasit province, while a separate incident occurred earlier this month in the Al-Amshan Canal in Maysan.

Although the two incidents were associated with different immediate circumstances, they demonstrate how vulnerable Iraq’s aquatic ecosystems have become when declining water levels interact with pollution and inadequate environmental controls.

Iraq fish deaths are becoming an annual warning sign

The Green Iraq Observatory argues that the recurrence of mass fish deaths should no longer be treated as a series of unrelated environmental emergencies. According to its assessment, similar incidents have occurred repeatedly across different parts of Iraq over the past several years, yet the underlying causes have not been addressed with sufficient consistency to prevent them from returning.

This pattern is particularly concerning because rivers and wetlands are not only ecological assets; they also support fisheries, agriculture and the livelihoods of communities that depend directly on healthy waterways.

The observatory said the April incident involved more than 1,000 tonnes of dead fish in the Tigris and Diyala rivers, with the largest losses concentrated in Wasit. It attributed the event to severe contamination caused by untreated sewage and industrial waste, while also pointing to increased water releases from Hamrin Dam that reportedly moved accumulated pollutants downstream toward the Tigris.

The organization further said that more than 20 people experienced poisoning or skin-related injuries and were taken to hospital, illustrating how deterioration in water quality can potentially extend beyond damage to aquatic life and become a broader public-health concern.

A second incident was reported at the beginning of August in the Al-Amshan Canal in Maysan. According to the observatory, the agriculture and water committee of the Maysan Provincial Council attributed the fish deaths to a sharp decline in the water releases allocated to the canal.

This episode is significant because it demonstrates that pollution is not necessarily the only immediate trigger for fish mortality; inadequate water flows can also create conditions in which fish become increasingly vulnerable to high temperatures, reduced oxygen levels and the concentration of pollutants already present in the water.

Water scarcity Is only part of the problem

Iraq’s water crisis is frequently discussed in terms of declining river flows, prolonged drought and reductions in water arriving from upstream countries. Those factors are undoubtedly important, but the recent fish deaths suggest that the country’s environmental problems cannot be explained simply by saying that Iraq does not have enough water. The quality, distribution and management of the water available can be just as important as its overall volume.

The Green Iraq Observatory highlighted this distinction by noting that the country’s total water storage had reportedly risen to around 34 billion cubic meters at the time of the latest incident.

From the organization’s perspective, the fact that fish mortality continued despite an increase in total reserves indicates that administrative decisions concerning water distribution may be contributing to the problem alongside genuine resource scarcity.

This does not mean that Iraq’s wider water shortage is unimportant. On the contrary, prolonged drought and declining inflows can weaken the natural ability of rivers and wetlands to dilute pollutants and maintain ecological balance. However, when available water is distributed unevenly or when polluted water is allowed to enter already stressed waterways, the consequences can become significantly more severe.

In other words, the crisis is not simply about how much water Iraq has, but also about where the water goes, what quality it has and how effectively it is managed.

Pollution can turn a water shortage into an ecological emergency

Untreated sewage and industrial waste are among the most serious threats facing Iraq’s waterways because they can fundamentally alter the chemical and biological conditions required for aquatic life. When large quantities of organic material enter a river or canal, microorganisms consume oxygen while breaking that material down, potentially reducing dissolved oxygen to levels that fish and other aquatic organisms cannot tolerate.

The situation can become even more complicated when water temperatures rise or when algae proliferate excessively. Some forms of harmful algae can contribute to oxygen depletion, particularly when large quantities of organic matter subsequently decompose.

At the same time, reduced water flows can prevent pollutants from being dispersed naturally, leaving them concentrated in particular sections of a river, canal or wetland.

This combination of factors helps explain why pollution and water scarcity should not be treated as completely separate problems. A waterway with strong flows may have a greater capacity to dilute certain pollutants, whereas a shallow and poorly circulated waterway can become significantly more vulnerable to contamination.

Consequently, environmental protection requires both adequate water releases and strict control over what is discharged into the country’s rivers.

Iraq has experienced similar fish mortality events for years

The latest incidents are not without precedent. The Green Iraq Observatory cited a long record of mass fish mortality events in Iraq, including a major incident in the Euphrates in Babylon in 2018, when tens of thousands of tonnes of fish were reportedly affected.

This was followed by the death of millions of fish at the Hindiya Barrage and another major incident in Al-Dalm Marsh in Diwaniyah in 2020.

Further incidents were reported in the Al-Ezz River in Maysan in 2023, while extensive fish deaths occurred in Ibn Najm Marsh in Najaf last year. Particularly worrying is the recurrence of fish mortality in the Maysan area where a similar incident had already been recorded, because repeated events in the same geographic location can indicate that the environmental conditions responsible for the original problem have not been adequately corrected.

The observatory argues that the repeated nature of these incidents is difficult to reconcile with a system that relies primarily on temporary investigative committees after environmental damage has already occurred. Investigations can establish causes and responsibility, but they cannot substitute for permanent monitoring mechanisms capable of identifying dangerous changes in water quality before they result in large-scale ecological losses.

Iraq’s Marshlands face particular risks

The Iraqi marshlands are especially sensitive to changes in water availability and quality because their ecological health depends on a delicate relationship between water flows, seasonal conditions and the surrounding environment. These wetlands provide habitat for fish and birds while supporting communities whose economic and cultural lives have developed around them over generations.

When water levels fall sharply, sections of the marshes can become isolated or excessively shallow, increasing temperatures and reducing oxygen circulation. If polluted water enters these already stressed environments, the damage can become significantly more difficult to reverse.

Protecting Iraq’s marshlands therefore requires a long-term approach that connects water policy with environmental policy. Maintaining adequate ecological flows, reducing pollution and establishing continuous monitoring systems would be far more effective than treating each fish mortality event as an isolated emergency.

What Iraq can do to prevent future fish deaths

The Green Iraq Observatory has called for several measures aimed at addressing the structural causes behind recurring fish mortality. Among its recommendations is the establishment of fair and sustainable water allocations for provinces and marshlands, rather than relying on short-term decisions that may leave some waterways dangerously depleted.

The observatory has also called for stronger environmental oversight of wastewater treatment facilities and industrial establishments located near rivers. Effective enforcement would require more than regulations on paper; authorities would need regular inspections, reliable water-quality testing and meaningful consequences for facilities that discharge untreated or inadequately treated waste.

Another important proposal is the creation of an early-warning system that monitors dissolved oxygen and pollution levels. Such a system could bring together government agencies, universities and civil-society organizations, allowing scientific data to be collected continuously and shared quickly when dangerous changes are detected.

Finally, rapid compensation for fish farmers affected by major environmental incidents could provide essential economic relief while investigations determine responsibility and long-term solutions.

No. Water scarcity is an important contributing factor, but pollution and poor water management can also play major roles. Even when overall water reserves increase, individual rivers, canals or marshes may experience insufficient flows or deteriorating water quality.

World.title: US Fed sends $500 million cash shipment to Iraq amid financial pressures
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The United States Federal Reserve has sent a new $500 million cash cargo to the Central Bank of Iraq, providing additional dollar liquidity as Baghdad grapples with rising financial pressures and disruptions to its oil-dependent economy.

The shipment was announced by Iraq’s national news agency, citing an official source who claimed the dollars will be used for permitted overseas transfers and transactions involving Iraqi citizens.

Further supplies are planned each month, with a government official estimating annual cash delivery of $8 billion to $10 billion.

These cash payments are part of Iraq’s peculiar financial relationship with the United States.

Proceeds from Iraqi oil exports are mostly placed in an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, with Baghdad obtaining dollars via permitted transfers and cash shipments administered by the Central Bank of Iraq.

The new supply comes at a critical moment for Iraq’s budget.

The disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has increased pressure on a nation that relies significantly on oil exports to support government expenditures and get foreign currency.

Iraq’s enormous public-sector pay bill contributes to this vulnerability.

Millions of Iraqis rely directly or indirectly on government wages, pensions, and social benefits; therefore, stable oil income and liquidity are crucial to the national budget.

Baghdad has lately expressed increased worries about its capacity to fulfill expenditure obligations if oil earnings continue low, strengthening long-standing demands for Iraq to diversify government income and lessen its reliance on petroleum exports.

The most recent dollar cargo should offer further liquidity to Iraq’s banking system, but it also shows the country’s vulnerability to both oil-market shocks and its financial ties with Washington at a time of rising regional tensions.

World.title: Lise Klaveness, the Norwegian thorn in Infantino’s side
World.content:
Oslo – A rare woman in the top echelons of football, the head of Norway’s federation Lise Klaveness has been a thorn in FIFA’s side for years.

Now, some would gladly see her take over the leadership of football’s international governing body from Gianni Infantino.

The 45-year-old lawyer and former footballer who played 73 matches for Norway has been highly vocal about international football’s woes under Infantino.

The Swiss-Italian has been mired in controversy since his plan to open FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, to private investors was swiftly rejected last week.

On Friday she called for him to resign.

When he was elected FIFA president in 2016, “he was a candidate who had been elected on a reform programme focused on good governance,” she told AFP.

“Then things quickly deteriorated: from keeping a distance, we moved to giving up, and even backtracking, all against a backdrop of a lack of independence from heads of state and other influential figures, particularly from World Cup host countries,” she said.

She fired her first salvo at Infantino in 2022, just after she was appointed head of the Norwegian federation, about the conditions under which the World Cup was awarded to Qatar.

From Doha, she publicly lamented that “human rights, equality, democracy, the core interests of football, were not in the starting 11”.

The following year, Norway refused to back Infantino in his re-election bid, signalling its dissatisfaction with his leadership.

Klaveness “was in a way the first standard-bearer for much of this criticism that many others now share when it comes to the way Infantino runs FIFA,” said Mina Finsted Berg, a sports commentator for Norwegian channel TV2.

She “is very committed to ensuring that rules and decisions are respected,” she added.

– Trump, Balogun and investors –

The reasons for her outrage against Infantino have piled up in recent months: FIFA’s decision to award a “Peace Prize” to US President Donald Trump, with whom Infantino has a conspicuously close relationship; the lifting of the suspension of US player Folarin Balogun at the 2026 World Cup following an intervention by Trump; and the aborted plan to open FIFA to private investors.

The Norwegian federation has decided to bring all three issues before the Ethics Committee of the world football governing body.

Klaveness’s voice carries all the more weight after Norway, long absent from major international tournaments, enjoyed a strong run in this year’s World Cup before being knocked out in the quarter-finals by England.

Internationally, commentators have praised her “strong moral compass” and consider her a serious candidate to replace Infantino if he were to step down.

He is standing for re-election for a fourth and final term next March and is currently the only declared candidate.

“She was the only one who always took a clear stand and did not go along with the mainstream. And at FIFA, the time is right for a woman to take the lead,” former FIFA head Sepp Blatter — himself disgraced after a corruption scandal — wrote on social network X.

– Ballot box obstacles –

Klaveness herself has insisted that the crisis in world football should not be reduced to a simple “Game of Thrones” power struggle and has instead called for a renewed focus on good governance.

“For us, it has never been a personal issue against Gianni Infantino,” she told AFP. “The problems go beyond the person of the president.”

And while she “has registered” that her name is being tossed around as a possible successor, she brushed aside questions about whether she was a candidate: “We’re not there yet.”

Many obstacles remain.

“In addition to being seen as extremely radical in many places, especially outside Europe, she is a woman. That is also likely to count against her in many regions of the world,” Mina Finsted Berg said.

Even within Europe’s governing body UEFA, which one could presume would be most favourable to her, Klaveness failed to win election to the Executive Committee in 2023.

She only joined in 2025, when she was the sole candidate for the seat reserved for women.

“If she already has such a hard time getting elected in Europe, how could she convince Africans and South Americans?” asked Erik Thorstvedt, a former goalkeeper for the Norwegian national team turned commentator.

World.title: Clinton compares Trump’s White House to former Iraqi dictator Saddam’s palaces
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Former US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton has compared President Donald Trump’s White House renovations to former Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein’s palaces, remembering her own travels to Baghdad after his ouster.

Clinton, speaking on journalist Kara Swisher’s podcast, compared Trump’s White House decor to meetings she attended in Saddam Hussein’s former palaces while serving as a US senator.

“They were quite reminiscent of what we are seeing in our own White House,” she said.

Her remarks come amid wider criticism of Trump’s renovations and architectural decisions, such as heavy gold décor within the Oval Office, plans for a new White House ballroom, and a projected triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery.

Clinton called the improvements “tacky” and suggested that the president was focusing too much on cosmetic initiatives when the US confronts substantial foreign policy, economic, and technological issues.

She also criticized the process around Trump’s planned ballroom, stating that she was not opposed to the White House having such a facility but was concerned about the architecture and how the project had been handled.

Given Clinton’s past with Iraq, the connection to Saddam was especially relevant.

She was a member of the United States Senate during the 2003 war that deposed Saddam Hussein and subsequently became Secretary of State under President Barack Obama.

During his reign, Saddam was noted for building multiple extravagant presidential palaces around Iraq, many with elaborate interiors and significant use of marble, chandeliers, and gold-colored décor, despite the country’s international sanctions and economic difficulty.

Trump has defended his White House restoration plans, which are part of a larger push to renovate and enhance Washington’s important federal buildings and sites.

Clinton’s parallel brings Iraq and one of Saddam’s most recognizable emblems into the increasingly heated political argument over Trump’s White House moves.

World.title: Captain of turbulence-hit Phuket-Delhi flight may have failed dope test
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The captain operating Air Indiaâs turbulence-hit Phuket-Delhi flight on Tuesday (Aug 4) reportedly tested positive in a psychoactive substances (dope) test conducted on arrival, according to multiple sources.

The airline did not either confirm or deny it, saying while the tests were conducted, the results have not been shared with it.

âWe are aware that a post-flight screening test was conducted on the pilots in accordance with applicable protocols. However, the results of the test have not been shared with Air India, and we are therefore not in a position to comment on any findings,â an AI spokesperson said.

âAir India undertakes regular drug testing of crew members in compliance with civil aviation regulations, independent of any specific flight or operational incident.

We will continue to cooperate with the relevant authorities as required,â the airline added.

The Airbus A320 with 145 people on board had encountered severe turbulence near Odisha and then suddenly dropped 300 feet. On arrival in Delhi, 13 passengers and four crew members were hospitalised. Sources say the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) is probing this case from all angles including whether the handling of this turbulence event was correct; whether the event happened due to weather or some other reason; the likely impact on the aircraft like did it suffer hydraulic failure due to impact and whether it should have flown all the way to Delhi after the episode and not diverted to some nearby airport like Varanasi or Lucknow.





Pending probe, flight crew is taken off flying duty as per protocol. So the pilots of this flight are also not flying currently. DGCA rules stipulate that a pilot testing positive for consumption of psychoactive substances for the first time be referred to for de-addiction and rehabilitation. Such crew member can return for active duties with a negative dope test report.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

But after resuming flying if the same person tests positive for psychoactive substances again, their licence will be suspended for three years.

And if after resuming flying the same person again tests positive for the third time, the flying licence is cancelled.

International Civil Aviation Organisation says that âholders of licences shall not exercise the privileges of their licences and related ratings while under the influence of any psychoactive substance, which might render them unable to safely and properly exercise these privilegesâ.

While the probe in Tuesdayâs event would have focused on pilot handling the situation anyway, the captain reportedly testing positive adds another dimension to the same.

World.title: Proposed MDR for UPI transactions will be nominal, says government
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The government said on Saturday that the proposed merchant discount rate (MDR) for UPI transactions will be nominal and apply only to a limited set of merchants for transactions above a threshold, while seeking to assure users that all person-to-person transactions will remain free and consumers who make the payment will not face any fees.

"A vast majority of the transactions will remain free of charge for merchants on UPI. MDR, if introduced, will only be threshold-based and not levied on a blanket basis to all," the statement said, adding that the UPI and Services Steering Committee, headed by NPCI, will decide on the MDR, if any.

It also dismissed reports of the charges being imposed under pressure from the US, which was seen to be pushing the case of Visa and Mastercard that levy MDR on credit card and debit card transactions, which are up to 2%, and usually not passed on to consumers unless the merchant is keen on a cash transaction.

"If external pressure had been a factor, the government would not have introduced UPI in 2016 or made it free of charge for both merchants as well as citizens since Jan 2020 and ensured that it became the world's largest real-time interoperable payment system.

The amendment should be viewed in the context of the government's broader objective of ensuring that India's digital payment infrastructure remains sustainable, competitive, and capable of serving the country's rapidly expanding digital economy."

World.title: Government spending on education below Unesco's 15% standard
World.content:
NEW DELHI: India remains just above Unesco's minimum GDP benchmark for education, but the sector's share in government spending has slipped below the prescribed threshold. Education accounts for 4.1% of GDP but 14.2% of total public expenditure, down from 15.7% in 2015 and below the 15% benchmark, Unesco's 2026 SDG 4 scorecard has shown.

The funding picture assumes significance because India continues to lag on secondary school completion. Its latest lower secondary (Classes VI-VIII) completion rate is 86% as against its 99% national benchmark for 2025, while upper secondary (Classes IX-XII) completion rate is 51% as against 84%. Unesco classifies progress at both levels as slow.

Under the Education 2030 framework, countries committed to spending 4-6% of GDP and/or 15-20% of public expenditure on education.

The scorecard uses the lower thresholds as minimum benchmarks. India meets one. Its spending on education has remained at 4.1% of GDP since 2015, but its share of public expenditure has declined 1.5 percentage points to 14.2%.

Among major emerging economies, China too meets one benchmark, at 4% of GDP (11.9% of public spending), while figures for Brazil are 5.6% and 12.9%. South Africa meets both, at 6% and 19.1%, while Indonesia, Bangladesh and Pakistan meet neither.





The pattern is common among developed economies too: the US, UK, Germany and France meet the GDP threshold but not the public expenditure benchmark, while Sweden and Switzerland meet both.

Unesco noted that richer countries tend to meet the GDP benchmark but not the public expenditure threshold because they raise more revenue, while education often accounts for a larger share of budgets in poorer countries.

Latest data show 39 of 205 countries, or 19%, meeting both benchmarks, while 72, or 35%, meet neither.

Another 64 countries, including India, spend above 4% of GDP but below 15% of public expenditure. Among high-income countries, 11% meet both benchmarks and 50% follow India's pattern.

India, however, has larger unmet schooling needs. Lower secondary completion has risen from 81% in 2015 to 86% but remains 13 percentage points below its 99% benchmark. Even Unesco's "feasible" 2025 benchmark of 90% is four points above the latest rate.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

This is despite programmes operating at scale. Unesco's India profile says Samagra Shiksha supports about 15.6 crore learners, while PM-Poshan covers around 11.8 crore children in 11.2 lakh government and aided schools. The trend is part of a broader global concern. The scorecard concludes that, on average, countries are "moving away" from the public education expenditure benchmarks of at least 4% of GDP or 15% of total public expenditure.

World.title: News in Frames | The wounds beneath Assam’s deadly flood
World.content:
On July 19, a cloudburst upstream sent a sudden wall of water through Upper Assam. Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat and Golaghat districts are experiencing their worst flooding in decades, with the Dikhow River breaching its extreme flood level. Bihubor, Nepali Khuti, Bihari Basti, and Railwayghat are among the worst-affected areas in Sivasagar district.

Assam has a history of major floods up to five times a year, killing scores of people and animals and damaging crops and assets worth more than ₹1,000 crore annually. The floods this year have killed 98 people so far, most of them in three eastern districts — Sivasagar, Charaideo, and Jorhat.

Experts believe the catastrophe may not have been caused by extreme rainfall alone. Satellite imagery has revealed extensive excavation, deforestation and other human interventions along the river’s upper reaches, particularly in Nagaland, raising concerns that decades of environmental degradation may have intensified the disaster. Coal mining, stone quarrying and shifting (jhum) cultivation have stripped large stretches of hill slopes of vegetation, making them increasingly unstable and vulnerable to erosion and landslides. Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said finding a “national solution” to the State’s annual flooding was more important than declaring it a national problem.

For decades, the All Assam Students’ Union and other organisations have been asking the Centre to declare the State’s flood and erosion crisis as a “national problem”.

“Declaring floods a national problem is not going to work. We need a national solution with scientific interventions. We need concrete schemes on how Assam can protect itself if water comes downhill from Nagaland,” the Chief Minister said on Friday.

The Chief Minister said that Assam has long relied on embankments and geo-bags for flood management, but lacks a scientific mechanism to tackle the issue.

Race to rescue: An aerial view of a rescue operation using rubber boats in flood-hit areas of Sivasagar on August 4, as teams reached people stranded by rising waters. Photo: @himantabiswa X/ANI Photo

Disrupted lives: A view of Nepali Khuti village, one of the worst-affected areas along the Dikhow River in Sivasagar district.

What remains: Moromi Bora Bordoloi searches for her children’s books among the belongings left behind after floodwaters destroyed their home in Majgaon village.

Safe passage: NDRF personnel evacuate villagers from Panbesa village in Sivasagar district as floodwaters continue to isolate homes and communities.

Temporary refuge: Women and children take shelter at a relief camp on the outskirts of Sivasagar town. Altogether, 133 relief camps and relief distribution centres were operational across six districts.

Picking up the pieces: Flood-displaced villagers take shelter in makeshift camps along a railway line in Betbari village, Sivasagar district.

Precious pages: Books salvaged from floodwaters are laid out along a roadside to dry in the Najira area of Sivasagar district.

Lessons continue: Children attend classes at a relief camp in Sivasagar town; with thousands displaced and staying in relief camps, temporary arrangements have been made to keep essential services going.

After the deluge: A car remains stuck in thick layers of mud and silt deposited by receding floodwaters in Nepali Khuti village.

World.title: Vishnu Engineering College transforms into Andhra Pradesh’s first private women’s university
World.content:
Twenty-five years ago, Shri Vishnu Engineering College for Women (SVECW) in Bhimavaram, a semi-urban town in the fertile Godavari delta, began with three undergraduate programmes, 180 students and a larger purpose of making quality technical education accessible to women, particularly those from rural and smaller towns.

A quarter of a century later, that modest beginning has evolved into Vishnu Women’s University, which commenced operations in the current academic year, 2026-27, and has the distinction of being Andhra Pradesh’s first private women’s university.

Over the years, SVECW has steadily expanded its focus from conventional engineering education to research, innovation, entrepreneurship, industry exposure and experiential learning. The numbers reflect this growth. From its initial three programmes, the institution has expanded to nine B.Tech programmes, four M.Tech programmes and an MBA programme, with an approved intake of 1,074 and a student strength of more than 5,000.

“We are trying to carry forward the legacy of my grandfather Bhupathiraju Vissam Raju (B.V. Raju), who believed that education is the most effective instrument for social transformation,” says K.V. Vishnu Raju, Chairman of Shri Vishnu Educational Society. Padma Shri and Padma Bhushan B.V. Raju, an industrialist, educationist and philanthropist, was the founder-Chairman of the Shri Vishnu Educational Society.

Speaking to The Hindu, Mr. Raju says the transition to university status will give the institution greater freedom to introduce new programmes in areas such as law, architecture and journalism.

“Shri Vishnu was among the early institutions to recognise that education had to be closely linked to employability and that students should have access to career opportunities after graduation,” he says. To strengthen its industry connect, the institution established regional offices in Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Chennai and Pune. The initiative, he says, has helped the institution work closely with industry to understand its requirements and groom students accordingly.

Satisfied with the institution’s performance in Andhra Pradesh, Mr. Raju says the next goal is to develop it into a Centre of Excellence with a national footprint.

“We are doing very well in the State. We now aim to make this a Centre of Excellence in the country. Bhimavaram should become the destination for girls aspiring to shine in their careers,” he says.

Highlighting some of the institution’s distinctive facilities, Mr. Raju says the Vishnu Space Application Centre, Radio Vishnu 90.4 community radio, an All-Terrain Vehicle track, an Assistive Technology Lab and a Rural Women Technology Park encourage students to explore ideas beyond conventional classroom learning. An AR/VR laboratory provides exposure to immersive technologies and enables students to work on applications using augmented and virtual reality.

To strengthen the academic foundations required for emerging fields, the institution has collaborated with the Chennai Mathematical Institute, with a focus on application-oriented mathematics. The initiative encourages students to develop analytical and problem-solving skills that can be applied to engineering and real-world situations, he says.

The institution also plans to establish dedicated skilling centres in Bengaluru and Chennai to bring students closer to industry through training, certification, internships and professional interaction.

While the Vishnu Educational Development and Innovation Centre (VEDIC) on the campus focuses on faculty development, pedagogy and educational innovation, the Vishnu Student Success Centre provides mentoring, academic assistance, career guidance and other support to students, Mr. Raju says. Psychological Wellbeing Centres add counselling support to the student ecosystem.

As a university, the institution’s next phase is expected to place greater emphasis on emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence and Data Science, besides research, innovation and entrepreneurship. Stronger industry and international collaborations will also be a key focus, Mr. Raju says.

World.title: Natyarangam to host its annual dance festival themed on Pancha Bhootham
World.content:
Thematic festivals have, over the years, found a special place among rasikas and artistes since it offers newer ways to view and explore familiar subjects. It is from this perspective that Natyarangam has been, for the past 27 years, curating the annual Bharatham festival. It gives dancers the freedom to work around a chosen theme and present an entire performance. Most often their efforts are supported by research scholar and professional musicians.

This year, Natyarangam will focus on Pancha Bhootham, which will bring together Bharatanatyam dancers, Carnatic musicians and research scholar Dr. Sudha Seshayyan to present choreographic pieces on the five elements — Prithvi (Earth), Apah (Water), Agni (Fire), Vayu (Air) and Akasa (Sky).

Talking about working on Apah (water) dancer Shweta Prachande says, “The Thales philosophy helps me understand how water, which is crucial for sustenance, assumes different forms as solid, liquid and vapour. While I did a deep dive into this element, I realised how closely it connects to our life’s journey”.

Carnatic musician Rithvik Raja, who is working with wife Shweta on the concept says, “More than simply representing water through sound, it was fascinating to see how music and movement seamlessly come together.”

Dancer K. Sarveshan, who presents Prithivi, shares that the creative process helped him reimagine the Pancha Boothas for the contemporary audience. “Collaborating with senior vocalist Amritha Murali has been an incredibly enriching and rewarding journey.”

Dancer Navia Natarajan, describes it as an introspective journey. Through her performance she will highlight how Agni (fire) revealed itself though its many layers, making her understand better its significance.

The festival will reiterate the interconnectedness between art and Nature.

World.title: Two killed as car crashes into bridge pillar on ORR service road in Hyderabad
World.content:
Two migrant workers from Rajasthan were killed after the car they were travelling in crashed into a pillar of the Neopolis Bridge on the Outer Ring Road service road in Hyderabad early on Saturday (August 8, 2026).

The accident occurred around 12.25 a.m. when Kanaiyalal, 25, and his colleague Deram, 24 — both tile workers residing at Indra Reddy Nagar in Kollur — were travelling from their locality to Satva in Nanakramguda.

Police said Kanaiyalal was driving the vehicle at high speed when he allegedly lost control and rammed into the bridge pillar. Both men died on the spot.

Police said no other vehicle was involved in the accident. Further investigation is underway.

World.title: 347 police recruits pass out at Muttikulangara
World.content:
As many as 347 recruits from the Kerala Armed Police (KAP) First and Second Battalions and the India Reserve Battalion took part in a passing out parade at Muttikulangara on Saturday. The recruits included 127 from KAP First Battalion, 110 from KAP Second Battalion and 110 police drivers from the India Reserve Battalion.

Home Minister Ramesh Chennithala, who received the parade salute, said police officers must protect the lives and property of people while upholding constitutional values. He said the entry of educated young people into the force would improve its performance and urged every officer to be a role model.

The recruits underwent training in physical fitness, weapons, firing, karate, yoga, swimming and self-defence. Indoor training covered topics including the Constitution, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Motor Vehicles Act, VIP security, telecommunications, social media and cybercrime. They also received training in forensic science, forensic medicine, penology, victimology and cyber forensics.

Ajith K.R. was named the best indoor cadet from KAP First Battalion, while Shinu Robin R.J. was the best outdoor cadet and all-rounder. Vishnu P.S. was the best shooter. From KAP Second Battalion, Sreehari N. Anand was adjudged the best indoor cadet, Vineeth P. the best outdoor cadet, Sajith C.B. the best shooter and Harshad V. the best all-rounder.

From the India Reserve Battalion, Rahul R.S. was named the best indoor cadet, Arjun K.A. the best outdoor cadet, Bijin Raj V.S. the best shooter and Ubaith M. the best all-rounder. The parade was led by Vineeth P., with Hashim Aliyar as second-in-command. Senior police officers, people’s representatives and relatives of the recruits attended the ceremony.

World.title: VACB in Kerala books former TDB officials over ₹2.27 crore Sabarimala ghee scam
World.content:
The Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau (VACB) has registered a First Information Report (FIR) against key former officials of the Travancore Devaswom Board (TDB) over alleged corruption and irregularities in procuring ghee for the Sabarimala temple during the 2025–2026 Mandala-Makaravilakku pilgrimage season.

According to the FIR filed on August 6, 2026, by the VACB Southern Range, Trivandrum, the named accused include former TDB president Prasanth P.S., board member Aji Kumar, and late former Executive Officer Murari Babu, along with unidentified others.

The case was registered following directions from the High Court of Kerala after a preliminary TDB Vigilance inquiry revealed severe procedural violations that allegedly caused a financial loss of ₹2,27,76,435 to the Devaswom Board.

The investigation revealed that the accused bypassed mandatory tender procedures and food safety norms to award the supply contract to Milma at an inflated rate of ₹510 per liter. Qualified lower bidders were systematically excluded despite Milma not participating in the original tender process.

To justify selecting Milma, the former executive officer submitted an unscientific report claiming that seven litres of Milma ghee could replace the standard 10 litres required per batch of Aravana prasadam, overruling explicit objections raised by the Devaswom Commissioner.

Over 1.61 lakh litres of ghee were purchased from Milma and utilized for Aravana production without proper quality testing by food safety officers or adequate documentation. The report further noted that ghee offered by devotees was mixed into production, raising suspicions of misappropriation.

The VACB has booked the accused under Sections 7, 13(1)(a), and 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act, along with criminal conspiracy and breach of trust provisions under Sections 61(2) and 316(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023.

World.title: Kerala Police intensify search as Arjun Ayanki traced to Edappal in Malappuram
World.content:
Arjun Ayanki, an accused in several criminal cases who is currently absconding, reportedly reached Edappal in the district while the police were conducting a search for him. He visited a private Ayurveda hospital at Edappal, the police said.

Surveillance camera footage showing Mr. Ayanki at the hospital has led the police to intensify the search for him at different parts of Malappuram. The footage also shows four men from Vattamkulam in the district accompanying him.

The police took the four persons into custody and questioned them. The police said they were later released.

The four reportedly came into contact with Mr. Ayanki through social media. Their accounts had earlier featured photos and reels with him. The police also suspect that Mr. Ayanki had visited Edappal with them previously.

The police have also reportedly received information that Mr. Ayanki travelled through Kuttippuram, Edappal and Changaramkulam in recent days. Searches have intensified in these areas.

World.title: Long-pending Ulakkai Aruvi dam project gets fresh push from farmers to meet future water demands
World.content:
Farmers from Kanniyakumari district have called for the implementation of the long-pending Ulakkai Aruvi dam project, which they said would ensure uninterrupted drinking water supply for Nagercoil Corporation and address irrigation water shortages in Thovalai region.

They said that project was essential as releasing water from Kodhayar irrigation system to Nagercoil Corporation to meet the city’s summer demands would affect irrigation of thousands of hectares of agricultural land in the district. They also pointed out that Pechiparai and other Kodhayar irrigation dams could eventually be used primarily as reservoirs to store water to meet the drinking water needs of the district.

Chenbagasekara Pillai, a farmer from Thuvarankadu said, Ulakkai aruvi, located at the foothills of Injikadavu and Mahendragiri in the western ghats, receives substantial water, especially between June and January. However, he said a large quantity of water currently flows through Thoovachi, Kesavanputhoor before joining the Pazhayar river near the upper portion of Pallikondan check dam near Gnalam.

Mr. Chenbagasekara Pillai stated that a proposal for the project was submitted in 2006 at an estimated cost of ₹82 crore. A few years later, PWD officials were again directed to prepare an estimate, he added.

“At that time, 25 acres of forest department land was required for the project, and a land near Marungoor was also identified as compensation. However, no concrete measures were taken to implement the project,” he noted.

Highlighting that Mukkadal dam was constructed during Travancore reign to cater an estimated population of 50,000 in Nagercoil, Mr. Chenbagasekara Pillai said that the population had increased considerably since then and the city had also expanded significantly in recent years.

“The government must consider constructing a dam at Ulakkai aruvi, keeping the future requirements in mind. The Kodhayar irrigation dams, including Pechiparai and Perunchani are the backbone of agriculture in the district and their water should not be diverted for drinking water requirements at the cost of irrigation,” he said.

Arun, a resident of Vadalivilai in Nagercoil Corporation said that the drinking water shortage during summer had become a recurring issue. He added that the district, which receives two monsoon rainfall, should plan its water resources effectively to meet the drinking water requirements of its growing population.

Meanwhile official sources in Kanniyakumari district said a Detailed Project Report (DPR) for the project estimated at ₹2,200 crore, was prepared last year.

Speaking on this Kanniyakumari District Collector M. Prathap said that a DPR had been prepared by the Water Resource Department (WRD) last year and has been submitted to the government for approval.

World.title: Goods, oil transporters’ strike threatens industry, exports
World.content:
KARACHI: Goods carriers remain parked in Mauripur on Saturday, disrupting cargo movement to and from the city’s ports.—Online

• Movement of over 400,000 goods-carrying vehicles suspended

• Transporters refuse to end strike before talks with govt

KARACHI: A countrywide strike by goods transporters and oil tankers started affecting industrial and export supply chains on Saturday, with operators vowing to continue the protest until the outcome of talks with the government on Monday, while manufacturers warned that prolonged disruption could halt production and jeopardise export commitments.

Pakistan Goods Transporters Alliance Chairman Nisar Hussain Jafry told Dawn that “our countrywide strike will continue as our leadership intends to meet the ministers concerned with petroleum, transport and ports on Monday”.

He said the movement of more than 400,000 goods-carrying vehicles, ranging from small to large, had been suspended from Saturday until the outcome of Monday’s meeting. “We have already unloaded our containers at the ports,” he said.

Mr Jafry said goods transporters were striking over multiple issues, including the government’s recently introduced daily fuel price mechanism.

“We are dissatisfied with the daily fuel price fixation introduced by the government, which is only creating problems,” he said.

Since intercity movement of vehicles takes between one and three days, transporters and industries cannot make firm commitments on transportation charges because of daily changes in fuel prices, he said.

Mr Jafry urged the government to restore the monthly fuel price mechanism and reduce withholding tax on transporters to 2pc from 7pc, noting that oil carriers were paying 2pc withholding tax on services.

He said the government and goods transporters had signed a charter of demands in December 2025, but the commitments made under it had yet to be fulfilled.

Mr Jafry also complained about the number of toll plazas, saying they had been established at intervals of around 30km and that transporters were perturbed over high toll rates.

Transporters were also facing issues related to parking of heavy vehicles in areas surrounding the ports and driving licences, he added.

Supply-chain disruption

Already struggling with high production costs, industrialists warned that the nationwide strike by goods transporters could further disrupt industrial activity if supplies of raw materials remained suspended.

They cautioned that prolonged disruption in cargo movement could paralyse factories, derail production schedules and jeopardise export commitments, ultimately affecting employment and the overall economy.

SITE Association of Industry President Abdul Rehman Fudda said the strike had created an alarming situation for manufacturers.

“The entire production system depends on timely supply of raw materials and delivery of finished goods. If factories fail to receive essential inputs, production will stall, while delays in dispatching finished products will worsen financial stress for industries,” he said.

The export sector was already grappling with multiple challenges, Mr Fudda said, warning that if export consignments failed to reach buyers on time because of the transporters’ strike, industries could face penalties, price cuts or claims for damages.

He urged the government to intervene urgently and resolve the dispute through negotiations with goods transporters.

“Authorities must act before the situation escalates to the point where the country’s industry and supply chain collapse entirely. If the strike prolongs, the damage will extend beyond manufacturers — affecting exports, jobs and overall economic activity,” he said.

Mr Fudda also called for immediate relief measures for the industrial sector, warning that rising production costs, expensive energy and policy uncertainty were putting the survival of industries at serious risk.

He said escalating electricity and gas tariffs, rising production costs, high financing expenses and the absence of consistent economic policies had significantly undermined industrial activity.

Despite these challenges, he said, the business community continued to keep the wheels of the economy moving, adding that further neglect of the industrial sector would be against the country’s economic interests.

He called on the government to ensure energy supplies at competitive tariffs, simplify the tax regime, expedite payment of pending refunds, improve the ease of doing business and introduce investor-friendly policies.

World.title: Fuel cost hits Lahore Metro service
World.content:
• Private firm says bus operations to be suspended from 11th as talks with authorities fail

• Punjab Mass Transit Authority calls move ‘blackmail’, vows to challenge court order against it

LAHORE: A private firm operating the Lahore Metro Bus on the 27km Gajjumata-Shahdra route has decided to suspend its operations from Aug 11 after talks with the Punjab Mass Transit Authority (PMA) over rising fuel costs and other issues failed to yield a solution.

As the company has served a final notice on the PMA, the authority has termed the move an attempt to blackmail and pressure the government into accepting its demands. It said it would challenge the court verdict against it and invoke a clause in the contract that provides for the appointment of arbitrators by both parties to settle any dispute.

According to the final notice, the company referred to its letters of July 31 and Aug 4, which had yet to be responded to by the PMA, and a meeting held on Aug 6 between company representatives and authority officials regarding implementation of the court’s July 29 orders directing the PMA to provide fuel from its own sources.

The company further said that during the meeting, it reiterated that it had exhausted its financial resources and was no longer in a position to continue operations.

On the occasion, the PMA stated that it was unable to take any decision without directions from the government.

The meeting concluded with an understanding that the PMA would propose a solution. However, the company said no solution or arrangement was communicated by the PMA.

It said that unless the PMA immediately commenced the uninterrupted supply of fuel from its own sources in compliance with the court orders, the metro bus operation could not be continued and would stand suspended from Aug 11.

“Any such suspension shall solely arise from PMA’s failure to implement the court order and shall not constitute any fault, default or unwillingness on the part of the company. All resulting operational, financial and legal consequences shall rest entirely with PMA,” the letter warned.

Talking to Dawn, a senior official of the company said the situation had worsened following frequent increases in fuel prices.

“When we took over, the diesel price was around Rs105 per litre or so. Later, the prices continued to rise from time to time, making it difficult for the company to meet its fuel costs,” the official added.

“In fact, the formula regarding calculation of fuel cost never reimbursed the company’s full fuel bill, as it covered only a fixed portion of the cost and the gap widened as soon as prices rose. When diesel prices increased sharply, the PMA’s payment increased slightly, but the company’s actual fuel expense increased much more,” the official, requesting anonymity, explained.

“A new formula was devised that reduced this gap but did not eliminate it, forcing the company to pay the remaining fuel costs from its own funds and borrowings, resulting in continuous losses and additional costs.”

To a question, he said the court in its orders of June 8, 2023 had directed the PMA to provide from its own sources. However, the PMA claimed the orders were already set aside by the respective court.

“For this, we sought clarification from the court as to whether or not the June 8, 2023 order had been cancelled. To this, the court issued a clarification on July 29, stating that the order had not been set aside and, therefore, the PMA should implement it, failing which action may be taken,” he maintained.

When contacted, a senior PMA official confirmed the court verdict against the authority.

“But we have already challenged this order in the relevant court. We are also invoking the contractual provision for appointing an arbitrator to decide the case,” he said, claiming that under the contract the company was being paid on a per-kilometre basis.

“We also raised the price. But the company is insisting on a further increase, which we cannot make without getting the government’s nod,” he added.

To a query, the official admitted that the PMA was not in a position to implement the court orders until it received approval from the government.

“We admit that fuel prices have increased. But we are unable to provide fuel to the company from our own sources as directed by the court. For this, the government [transport department] is the authority to do something,” the official added.

He said the PMA had some options to continue the metro bus service even if the company walked out of the system. “Though there could be some issues from Aug 11 onwards, we have managed to arrange some buses from outside in a bid to continue the service,” he added.

It is pertinent to mention that the Lahore Metro Bus Service, the country’s first modern mass transit project, was officially inaugurated and opened to the public on Feb 10-11, 2013, running on a 27-km route from Gajjumata to Shahdara.

World.title: IHC seeks govt reply over withholding tax hike on goods transportation
World.content:
• Petitioners term concessional treatment of oil tanker contractors ‘discriminatory’

• Argue distinction based merely on nature of goods being transported

ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) has sought responses from the federal government, the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) and other respondents on a petition challenging the increase in withholding tax (WHT) on goods transportation from 6pc to 7pc through the Finance Act, 2026.

A division bench comprising Justices Khadim Hussain Soomro and Muhammad Asif also issued a notice to the attorney general for Pakistan (AGP) after the petitioners challenged the vires of relevant provisions of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.

The court fixed the matter for further hearing on Sept 17.

The petition was filed by Advocate Kashif Ali Malik on behalf of I.S. Enterprises and Shaheen Freight Services.

During the hearing, the counsel argued that the enhanced WHT was discriminatory, particularly in view of the concessional tax regime available to oil tanker contractors under the Second Schedule of the Income Tax Ordinance.

He contended that the same prime movers and transport infrastructure were being used for carrying petroleum products and other goods of similar capacity.

However, an oil tanker carrying petroleum products was subjected to withholding tax at 2pc, while the same vehicle, when used to transport other goods, attracted 7pc WHT.

According to the counsel, the distinction was based merely on the nature of goods being transported and had no rational basis. He argued that the differential treatment violated Articles 4 and 25 of the Constitution, which guaranteed protection of law and equality before law.

‘No justification’

The counsel further questioned the basis for increasing the withholding tax from 6pc to 7pc, submitting that no publicly available economic impact assessment or empirical study had been conducted to justify the additional tax burden on goods transporters.

He argued that oil tanker operators had historically been given concessional tax treatment because any strike by them could disrupt fuel supplies across the country.

On the other hand, goods transport operators, despite providing the same basic transportation service and not resorting to such measures, were subjected to a substantially higher withholding tax.

The petitioners maintained that the impugned amendment created an unreasonable and discriminatory classification betwe­­en transport operators performing essentially the same service.

After hearing the preliminary arguments, the IHC bench issued notices to the federal government, the FBR and other respondents.

As the petition also challenged the constitutional validity of statutory provisions, the court directed issuance of a notice to the AGP. The respondents have been asked to respond to the petition before the matter is taken up on Sept 17.

Through the Finance Act, 2026, the federal government revised the withholding tax regime on services, with rates increased from 6pc to 7pc for services such as courier, logistics, hotel, transport, air cargo, car rental, human resource outsourcing and oil drilling.

World.title: Unregulated placer gold mining raises concerns in GB
World.content:
A recently sealed placer gold extraction site in Hunza. —Photo by Gilgit-Baltistan Environmental Protection Agency

• Authorities warn of risks to Diamer-Bhasha Dam, roads, bridges and settlements

• Untreated wash water, debris and oil from machinery areas of concern

GILGIT: Increasing placer gold mining activities in stre­ams and rivers are threatening the fragile ecosystem of Gilgit-Baltistan (GB), with au­­thorities describing them as a serious risk to dams, including the Diamer-Bhasha Dam, as well as roads, bridges, important infrastructure and human settlements along riverbanks.

Currently, a large number of local companies, in joint ventures with national and multinational companies, are enga­ged in extracting gold from rivers and streams across GB.

Sources said placer gold mining activities in rivers and streams had increased across the region in violation of environmental laws, causing environmental degradation and putting roads, bridges, government and private infrastructure, human settlements and agricultural land at risk of river erosion. The activities were also causing water, air and land pollution.

Speaking to Dawn, Gilgit-Baltistan Environmental Protection Agency (GBEPA) Director Khadim Hussain said the issue had become more serious in recent years as placer gold mining companies were not complying with environmental laws.

According to the GBEPA, it had been observed that heavy machinery was being used for gold extraction from riverbeds and streams, mostly near brid­ges, roads, government and pri­­vate infrastructure, human settlements and agricultural land.

Oil and other materials lea­king from generators and other machinery used in the extraction process were also mixing with river and stream water.

It had also been observed that untreated wash water generated from gold-washing activities, along with debris, was being discharged into rivers without any sedimentation or settling mechanism.

The polluted river water was being used by people in many areas for drinking and other daily needs.

The GBEPA said the construction of protection walls along riverbanks for gold extraction and the use of excavated material altered the natural flow of rivers and streams, diverting water towards roads, bridges, human settlements, infrastructure and agricultural land.

The diversion of natural watercourses posed a serious risk of erosion and destabilisation of steep slopes adjoining roads, bridges, infrastructure, human settlements and agricultural land situated near riverbanks and streams. Such damage could be particularly severe during periods of high river discharge.

Furthermore, the dumping of excavated material could cause serious and irreversible damage to sensitive infrastructure.

No proper campsites had been established at the project sites, while no appropriate mechanisms had been provided for the safe collection and disposal of solid waste. Adequate sanitation and restroom facilities had also not been provided for workers at the sites, resulting in improper waste management.

“These actions constitute a breach of the environmental conditions of approval and endanger public health and safety,” the GBEPA said, adding that they had also caused environmental degradation.

Operations suspended

According to a notification issued after a visit by GBEPA officials, a fine of Rs1 million had been imposed on a placer gold mining company and its operations suspended for allegedly violating environmental protection laws in Nasirabad, Hunza.

The notification ordered that all project operations cease with immediate effect. The project premises had already been sealed by the competent authority. The notification also direc­ted the company to immediate­­ly comply with environmental laws.

Mr Hussain said the GBEPA and the minerals department lacked sufficient human resources to monitor mining activities and enforce environmental protection laws at gold extraction sites across GB.

In a recent letter to the Dire­ctor General of the GBEPA, the general manager of the Water and Power Development Authority (Wapda) Diamer-Bhasha Dam Project requested measures to control sediment erosion caused by mining activities in the dam project area.

The letter said extensive gold extraction from the Indus River bed was being carried out inside the proposed Diamer-Bhasha Dam project reservoir area, from Basri to Raikot near Chilas in Diamer.

In another letter sent to the Astore deputy commissioner, the executive engineer of the Communication and Works De­­partment in Astore reques­ted a ban on excavation activities near bridges over the Indus River.

World.title: Pakistan bags three medals at Nuclear Science Olympiad
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: A Pakis­tan team has won one gold and two silver medals at the 3rd International Nuclear Science Olympiad (INSO-2026), held in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia from Aug 2 to 8.

Supported by the Inter­national Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the competition brought together around 120 students and experts from 19 countries, including China, Japan, Russia, Turkiye, Malaysia, Indonesia, and Saudi Arabia.

The team was selected and trained by the Pakis­tan Institute of Engi­neer­ing and Applied Sciences (PIEAS), under the auspi­ces of the Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission (PAEC).

Muhammad Ali from Govt College University, Lahore, won a gold medal, while Muhammad Usman from F.G. Sir Syed College, The Mall, Rawalpindi, and Seerat Fatima from Nixor College, Karachi, secured silver medals. Syed Shuja Haider from Sundar STEM School, Lahore, also represented Pakistan at the Olympiad.

The students were selec­­ted through the Pakis­tan Nuclear Science Olymp­ia­­­d, an initiative of PAEC ai­­m­ed at identifying and nurturing young scientific talent for participation in the International Nuclear Science Olympiad.

In another developme­­nt, Pakistan was annou­n­ced as the host of the 4th In­­ternational Nuclear Sci­ence Olympiad in 2027.

On the occasion, Dr Mu­­hammad Maqsood from the PAEC Directorate of Edu­cation and Dr Sajjad Tahir from PIEAS received a commemorative memento.
