World.title: A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018850/A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.content:
A Chinese city has launched a new residential cooling program using water from abandoned coal mines, a low-carbon initiative that could replace traditional air conditioners.

The initiative in the eastern Jiangsu province’s city of Xuzhou routes water from the now-defunct Woniushan Coal Mine to apartments in a nearby neighborhood, domestic media reported this week. The water maintains a consistent temperature of 19 degrees Celsius year-round.

Disused mines often fill with water via rainwater accumulation and groundwater seepage — water that can then be used to heat or cool nearby homes.

Xuzhou, a former coal-producing center with a decades-long mining history, has previously used abandoned mine water for clean heating, including a system installed last winter at its former Hanqiao Coal Mine. With annual average temperatures climbing and China’s “dual carbon” initiative — where the country aims to peak its carbon emissions by 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060 — a national priority, the cooling initiative, which began June 1, has been a focus for the city.

“After heat exchange (with the homes), the water returns to the mine, without having consumed any energy or produced any carbon emissions,” Zhang Tao, leader of the cooling project and a worker at Xukuang Heating Company, told state media outlet CCTV. Compared with traditional air conditioning, he said, this technology lowers carbon emissions and aligns more closely with China’s energy conservation and emission reduction policy.

According to domestic media, such closed-loop geothermal systems reduce energy consumption by approximately 50% compared with traditional methods. It is also estimated to reduce carbon dioxide emissions for the 100 homes in the pilot program by about 50 tons annually.

The city offered residents in the pilot program two free months of cooling, after which they’ll be charged quarterly at 4 yuan ($0.60) per square meter.

Wang, a resident in the pilot area, said that in previous summers her monthly electricity bill often exceeded 400 yuan due to air conditioner usage. In contrast, the pilot program has allowed her to cool her home for four months this summer for only 410 yuan. She said her home now maintains a constant temperature 24 hours a day, and the system is quiet, unlike air conditioners.

Zhang, the heating company researcher, noted the great potential of the pilot program. “This year we only used a part of Woniushan Coal Mine’s capacity, and since the mine has significant potential, in the future we plan on using it to capacity, extending it to more neighborhoods.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.title: [Two Pronged] Getting an ‘old person’ smell from my husband
World.content:
Our letter sender is complaining of a smell emanating from her husband. How should she, and her husband, deal or adapt to the situation at hand?

Rappler’s People section runs an advice column by couple Jeremy Baer and clinical psychologist Dr. Margarita Holmes.

Jeremy has a master’s degree in law from Oxford University. A banker of 37 years who worked in three continents, he has been training with Dr. Holmes for the last 10 years as co-lecturer and, occasionally, as co-therapist, especially with clients whose financial concerns intrude into their daily lives.

Together, they have written two books: Love Triangles: Understanding the Macho-Mistress Mentality and Imported Love: Filipino-Foreign Liaisons.

Dear Dr. Holmes and Mr. Baer,

Writing this letter is very hard for me. I hope I am just imagining things.

This is what my husband insists I am doing: Creating problems where none exist. I tried to convince myself it was merely my imagination, but this is something I started to notice almost a year ago, and it has not stopped.

In addition, when I shared this to my group of girlfriends (50-70 years old) they all laughed but one friend came up to me afterward and confessed that she was also smelling something “strange” about her husband.

Is it possible that this is not just a basis of our imagination?

For the first time in my life, I have asked my husband to use a deodorant, because, frankly, I cannot stand to be near him. But often the deodorants don’t even work!

It is so sad for me that this smell thing has happened. Being in his arms used to be one of my greatest joys. Now I just suffer through it and calm myself knowing that his putting his arms around me will end soon.

Please help me and my 55-year old girlfriend with the same problem.

– Mia

Dear Mia,

Thank you for your message.

There are studies, such as this one, which indicate that body odor changes as people age.

Babies often have a particular smell, as do teenagers, adults, and the elderly. These changes are normal and not associated with poor personal hygiene.

Researchers have also isolated a chemical compound, 2-nonenal, in people aged 40 and older that increases with age and changes the body’s natural musk.

None of this, Mia, will be of much comfort if you dislike your husband’s smell, so what can you do to remedy the situation?

There are products that are persimmon-based, especially Japanese skin products such as soaps, shampoos, deodorants, that purport to tackle this problem but their effect is contested. It is, however possible, that one or more of these might be efficacious in your case.

The fact that your husband is in denial is, however, a worry. He needs to understand the reality of the situation if any sort of intimacy is going to continue.

Of course, this presupposes that he values being in your arms as much as you do, which isn’t a given. Hopefully, he is as invested as you in maintaining the closeness of your relationship, or otherwise, you run the danger of drifting into being companionate rather than intimate which would be a loss for both of you.

Finally, be mindful that as you age your body too may start to change its smell, an irony which may not escape you!

Best wishes,

JAF Baer

Dear Mia,

Thank you very much for your letter.

Mr. Baer has given you both the facts about ”old people smell” and also the practical ways in which you can deal with it. Perhaps the best thing I can do is share some emotional ways to also deal with it?

Especially in the light that, while old man smell might be stronger than old lady smell, the latter still exists… this is a good reminder not to squeeze your husband’s neck when he starts smelling “old” (unless — ULP! — I’m the only one who has such strong reactions to my husband’s “misbehaviors”).

But that’s just it, isn’t it? This has nothing to do with what he does, and thus is not your husband’s fault in any way!

As Mr. Baer mentioned, the 2-nonenal natural chemical compound can only be detected in people 40 and above. This compound forms because of changes in skin oil composition and in sweat patterns, and there is nothing people can do about all this!

Perhaps realizing this will help you be more tactful with him, because these things — tact, kindness, gentleness, an understanding that none of this is his fault — often make it easier to get the message across.

Not all the messages you share need be about the smell per se; they can also be about some of the fears and anxieties you each have. Mia, you might be afraid/worried that you, too, will get this old people smell. Your husband might fear his smell will get worse. Not only is a “grief shared half a grief,” but then neither you nor he will feel like isolated ice floes trying to hard not to sink in the middle of a dark, over-expansive ocean. You will have someone to talk to, someone with whom you feel seen (again) and that will take a lot of the pressure off — believe me.

Then you can not only learn about “nose blindness” (NB); you can also have fun experimenting with it! For example, at what distance does nose blindness happen most quickly?

The scientific term is called olfactory adaptation, which is the process that happens when you stay in a smelly room and your scent receptors slow down their signals.

This does not only make both you and he feel better, but it makes evolutionary sense. Once your brain can ignore constant background scents, it can then have the bandwidth to focus on new, sudden dangers.

Finally, dearest Mia, when your husband complains of your “creating problems where none exist, he is not being defensive or deliberately obtuse. A 2009 review by Drs. Doty and Cameron clearly stated that “women generally outperform men in various olfactory tests.”

In other words, you and your gf, Mia, are generally more sensitive to odors than men are.

I know, I know, this will not change the way your husband literally smells, but it may make your perception of it somehow less judgmental and “blame-ie” of him.

I cannot help thinking that at this time in our lives, knowing as much as we can about the inevitable changes that might happen to some or all of us as we age, will help us be kinder to ourselves and to each other.

Isn’t that part of what it has always been about?

My very best wishes,

MG Holmes

– Rappler.com

Life got complicated? Write to our Two Pronged duo at twopronged@rappler.com.

World.title: Iran says deal on Strait of Hormuz is close but not enough to open the waterway
World.content:
STRAIT OF HORMUZ. Vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, August 6, 2026.

Agreement between Iran and Oman over the strait, which separates the two countries, is seen as vital to a wider deal to end the war

Iran said on Saturday, August 8 (August 9, Philippine time), that a deal with Oman on control of the Strait of Hormuz was close but would not be enough to free up the waterway, and the United Arab Emirates said Iran had hit another ship there.

Agreement between Iran and Oman over the strait, which separates the two countries, is seen as vital to a wider deal to end the war, which began with US and Israeli attacks on Iran on February 28 and led to Tehran establishing a chokehold over the major energy export route.

A US official, who declined to be identified, said on Friday that Washington anticipated an agreement soon between Iran and Oman, so normal oil traffic could resume.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said Iran and Oman were “very close” to an agreement on a new shipping route through the strait, but reopening it would depend on other conditions, including US compensation to Iran.

The secretary of Iran’s top national security body, Mohammad Baqer Zolqadr, listed other demands including ending US threats against Iran, stopping aggression against Iran and its Lebanese, Palestinian, Yemeni and Iraqi allies, lifting a blockade and sanctions on Iran and freeing Iranian assets.

Oman reports positive negotiations, condemns ship attacks

Oman condemned what it described as repeated attacks on vessels while transiting the strait, without assigning blame, and said that negotiations with Iran on arrangements for shipping through Hormuz were “positive and constructive”.

“Oman stresses the importance of avoiding any actions that could affect these negotiations and the progress achieved in a manner that takes into account the interests of all parties,” the foreign ministry said.

Araqchi said the previous shipping traffic separation scheme through the strait was no longer acceptable to Tehran and Iran was discussing a temporary route with Oman while technical and legal issues surrounding a permanent route were resolved.

Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian, a relative moderate, said he believed now was the best time for an agreement.

“There is cohesion, strength, and unity in the country, and as far as I know, Iran is considered victorious and powerful in this war,” Iranian news agencies quoted him as saying.

Iran has reacted to the US attacks by targeting US bases in Gulf states and Jordan as well as striking shipping in the narrow strait, which carried a fifth of the world’s oil and gas shipments before the war.

The UAE said on Saturday that Iran had attacked a carrier affiliated with the UAE’s state oil company with a missile as it transited the Strait of Hormuz. No injuries were reported in the latest attacks on shipping there.

The UK maritime trade monitor UKMTO said a vessel had caught fire after being hit by an unknown projectile but the fire was put out and there was no reported environmental impact.

There was no immediate comment from Iranian authorities.

In recent weeks, the Trump administration has repeatedly signaled that a deal to open the strait could be close, only to have Iran deny that talks are under way. It was unclear whether the latest flurry of negotiations would yield a more lasting arrangement.

“Once the deal is announced to restore commercial shipping without impediments, the United States will lift the blockade of Iranian ports,” the US official told Reuters on Friday. US actions would be tied to Iran’s implementation of its commitments, he said.

US Central Command said on Saturday it had allowed more than 30 ships through for humanitarian aid since the current blockade started. US forces have turned away 53 ships, disabled two vessels and boarded two others, Central Command said in a statement on social media.

Prices of food and other necessities have increased rapidly in Iran since the conflict began in February. At a news conference on Saturday, Pezeshkian blamed the US for causing difficulties in importing basic goods.

He did not mention any blockade exceptions for humanitarian aid.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, who have targeted the ships, also said on Saturday that reopening the strait depended on Washington accepting Iran’s conditions and was not related to the Iran-Oman negotiations.

“Whenever the United States accepts Iran’s conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will certainly be reopened,” said Guards spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi, according to Iran’s Tasnim news agency.

Sources said this week a deal would give Iran some control

A proposed deal between Iran and Oman to help end five months of war between Iran and the US would give Tehran control over ships entering the Gulf through the strait, a senior Iranian source and two regional officials told Reuters on Wednesday, one of the biggest concessions yet to Iran.

US officials have repeatedly said they would never agree to Iran controlling access to the world’s most important trade route for energy supplies. It was not clear whether they had sought to change the parameters of the deal.

Iran has used the hostilities to justify charging a toll on oil tankers. That, and the firing on ships that attempt to cross the strait without its permission, has badly disrupted global shipments, causing energy prices to surge and fueling inflation. – Rappler.com

World.title: [The Wide Shot] Tips for faith communities when Sara Duterte attacks truth and Truth
World.content:
I hope that people of faith will realize how such attacks on the press erode our capacity to distinguish fact from fiction and, ultimately, right from wrong

Even if classic journalism books have sought to define our profession, my favorite definition of journalism comes from a non-journalist.

The late Pope Francis, in awarding two Vatican journalists in November 2021, offered a definition of journalism that I have since required my students to read and imbibe.

“Journalism does not come about by choosing a profession, but by embarking on a mission, a little like a doctor, who studies and works so that the evil in the world may be healed,” Francis said in his 2021 speech.

He continued: “Your mission is to explain the world, to make it less obscure, to make those who live in it less afraid of it and look at others with greater awareness, and also with more confidence. It is not an easy mission.”

How did Francis get it right?

It is all about truth.

A bedrock of faith

I believe that Francis understood the heart of journalism because it hews closely to the heart of every faith community’s mission: “to explain the world,” to ferret out the truth in a world of chaos.

Truth is a bedrock of major religious traditions, including Christianity, Buddhism, and Islam. When referring to it in a religious sense, we even capitalize the word “Truth” to emphasize that it is sacred, ultimate, and even divine — another name for God, at least in monotheistic traditions.

In the Bible, Jesus declares, “I am the Way and the Truth and the Life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). Buddhists also hold truth in high regard, with the “Four Noble Truths” forming the core of the Buddha’s teachings. The same is the case in Islam, where one of the names of Allah is Al-Haqq, which means “The Truth.”

This means that journalistic truth-telling is not only a distant cousin of faith; it is one of its offspring.

An attack on truth is an attack on faith.

So I hope religious leaders were listening when Vice President Sara Duterte, speaking to her family’s supporters in The Hague, launched yet another attack on the country’s truth-tellers. Duterte claimed the quality of Philippine journalism falls below international standards and that “social media” is doing a better job than Filipino journalists.

The National Union of Journalists of the Philippines called out the comment as an attack on a free press. “By denigrating Philippine media, Sara is unleashing one of the tactics straight out of a dictator’s playbook: controlling information by demonizing the independent press and weaponizing social media for her propaganda,” said the NUJP in a statement on August 2.

Discernment of spirits

Much has been said about how populist attacks on the press can weaken democracy, as we have seen in the Philippines and the United States.

I hope, however, that people of faith will also realize how such attacks erode our capacity to distinguish fact from fiction and, ultimately, right from wrong.

The Jesuits, following their founder Saint Ignatius of Loyola, have a practice called the “discernment of spirits.” In this spiritual practice, a person examines his or her feelings — what brings consolation or desolation, or what comes from “good spirits” or “evil spirits” — to more clearly understand God’s will.

It is, in a theological sense, a way of approaching the Truth who is Christ.

This skill of discernment does not come about by beholding a glorious apparition from heaven, but by exercising logic and emotional mastery on a day-to-day basis. Developing this skill is like bodybuilding; we do it block by block, muscle by muscle, in all things grand and mundane.

What happens to this spiritual skill if we impair our ability to discern the things of the earth?

If one easily falls for a fake Senate statement, how can one be an expert in interpreting biblical texts? If one subscribes to AI-generated health tips that go viral on Facebook, how can one recognize a vaccine as life-saving science rather than “the mark of the beast”? If one gives full assent to just any influencer, how can one avoid falling for a “Son of God” like Apollo Quiboloy?

In our context as Asia’s biggest Christian-majority nation, how can one claim to seek Jesus, “the Way and the Truth and the Life,” while choosing peddlers of lies over journalistic truth-tellers?

Tips for faith communities

Following Duterte’s new tirade against journalists, I asked veteran journalist Inday Espina-Varona about her thoughts on the role of the Catholic Church in countering attacks against the press.

She pointed to the need for media literacy, especially among the youth, at the parish level.

I did my own reflection and listed tips that faith-based groups can consider:

1. Religious leaders, first of all, should be more discerning about their media diet. It will help if they fast from social media for a time and reexamine their sources of information. If people can be picky about clothing brands, why not about the news we consume? It will also help if they bring the matter to prayer.

2. Faith communities can hold media literacy sessions for their members, especially the youth. They can organize briefings with journalists or subscribe to structured media literacy programs offered by media groups such as Rappler. The media landscape can be confusing even for industry veterans. We need the help of experts in our parishes, mosques, and congregations.

3. Churches can consider turning fact-checking into a full-fledged ministry, in the same way that parishes have volunteers focusing on the environment or social justice. Or they can add fact-checking to the job description for social communications teams, in addition to their usual tasks of taking photos and videos of church events.

4. Faith communities can leverage the strengths of members to build what Lesmore Ezekiel, a Lutheran minister in Nigeria, calls “communities of meaning” — similar to #FactsFirstPH in the Philippines. Ezekiel said in a webinar in 2023: “All the expertise and competencies are within the church. How are we using them to fact check and all of those things?”

People of faith should realize that media literacy, in this age of disinformation, is not merely an aid to a more informed politics. It is, more than this, a part of our moral responsibility.

In the face of populists building kingdoms of falsehood, journalists and religious groups share the heart of the fight for truth. – Rappler.com

Paterno R. Esmaquel II is a journalist specializing in religion and public life. A former Rappler reporter and news editor, he now writes for international Catholic news outlets, teaches journalism at the University of Santo Tomas, and runs a YouTube channel called The Religion Reporter.

World.title: [Inside the Newsroom] Alex Eala frenzy: When tennis feels like basketball
World.content:
Like the Ginebra diehards, Alex Eala fans can be loud, wildly cheering not just the Filipino’s every point, but also her opponent’s errors — defying some of tennis’ unwritten rules

When Alex Eala started hitting international headlines, the raucous Filipino fans became as much a part of the spectacle as her giant-slaying ways.

Just days after Eala captured her first WTA Tour title before a capacity crowd in Washington, the 21-year-old Filipina ace packed the stands again in Toronto, with tournament organizers noting how tickets in her opening match sold out in 30 minutes, and how they had to move it from the Grandstand to the bigger Centre Court of the Sobeys Stadium.

“Our Grandstand court is 2,800 seats. We can’t put her on there because she probably sold upwards of 5,000 tickets,” tournament director Karl Hale said.

Come match day, the fans made Toronto feel like a home court, with Philippine flags all around and the boisterous cheers making it less like a tennis event and more like a basketball game.

“Parang Ginebra lang (It’s just like a Ginebra game),” someone joked online, alluding to how the pro basketball team has long been Philippine sport’s crowd darling.

Like the Ginebra diehards, Eala fans can be loud, wildly cheering not just the Filipino’s every point, but also her opponent’s errors.

This defies, though, one of tennis’ unwritten rules: fans can’t distract the players, hence the sport’s polite cheers and decorous silence during rallies.

And here lies the split among the media, as well as longtime tennis aficionados. While some feel embarrassed by Filipino supporters’ lack of tennis etiquette in international matches, others relish the atmosphere and rumble of the arena filled with fans discovering the excitement of the sport for the first time.

For Eala, however, it’s just all love. After winning her first match in Toronto, she even made sure to address them in the vernacular.

“Linggo-lingo ko kayong nakikita, sinusuporta ako. Linggo-linggo kong nakikita kung gaano ’nyo kamahal ang kapwa ’nyong Pinoy, kaya proud na proud akong maging Pinoy. Salamat, mga kababayan.”

(I see you supporting me week after week. And, week after week, I see how much you love your fellow Filipino, and that makes me incredibly proud to be Filipino. Thank you, my fellow Filipinos.)

“Thank you to everyone who’s here supporting tennis and creating atmospheres like this,” Eala added. “It’s really the pleasure of my life to experience these things.”

The New York Times once wrote how some elite players hope tennis will be more like “every other sport, in which self-expression, celebration and trash talk are welcomed,” as some fans really do not understand “why they have to behave like they are at a funeral.”

The Eala on-and-off-court frenzy may not make sense to a tennis purist, and, as one Chinese sports fan puts it, even the Filipina player herself “makes no scientific sense.”

“She isn’t tall, isn’t fast, lacks power, and comes from an obscure Asian island nation,” the Chinese social media post said in a report by the South China Morning Post after Eala’s unbelievable title run in Washington, where she stunned Olympic and Asian Games champion Zheng Qinwen, defending champion Leylah Fernandez, world No. 10 Elina Svitolina, four-time Grand Slam champion Naomi Osaka, and world No. 3 Jessica Pegula.

The Chinese comment may have triggered some, but as Eala rises, so do the Filipino global fans — whether one likes them or not.

During Eala’s brief visit to Manila last July — just right after her historic Wimbledon run, where she became the first Filipino to reach the fourth round of a Grand Slam singles tournament — reporter Delfin Dioquino recounted how fans of all ages “patiently waited for hours just to get an up-close look” of the tennis star in a packed mall event.

He described Eala’s homecoming as “proof that she is no longer just an ordinary athlete but a cultural figure in her own right.“

Buoyed by her fervent fans, Eala changed the game in many ways over the past months — a true disruptor, just like other sports greats. – Rappler.com

World.title: Rappler trains 2026 Aries Rufo Fellows in public interest journalism
World.content:
2026 FELLOWS. Campus journalists from different provinces during the final day of their onsite training at the Rappler newsroom in Pasig City on Saturday, August 8.

The Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship, now on its sixth cycle since its launch in 2021, is a four-month collaborative initiative between Rappler and the Journalism for Nation Building Foundation.

MANILA, Philippines – Seven campus journalists selected for this year’s Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship completed an intensive onsite training program at the Rappler newsroom from August 5 to 8, 2026.

The onsite training, which is an essential component of the program, aims to strengthen the fellows’ knowledge and skills in public interest reporting, with a particular emphasis on spotting corruption and local-level accountability.

For this year’s cohort, the training sessions covered critical areas such as local community reporting, the budget process, spotting corruption red flags, and digital security, alongside technical skills in data journalism, responsible and efficient use of AI for research, liveable cities and community engagement, vertical video creation, and long-form writing.

During the training, the transition from reporting within campus borders to tackling complex public-interest issues marked a fundamental shift for the fellows.

“We are usually branded as campus journalists and known to only write stories on campus. But with the training, I realized that we are student journalists capable of writing about the plight of the people. We can do so much more,” said Ahyenne Estancio of Pampanga, who reported about Angeles City’s recurring water woes under PrimeWater during her first month as a fellow.

After the training sessions, she gained a deeper understanding of the budget process and spotting red flags in public documents, among others.

For Lance Bustos of Laguna, who wrote about Santa Rosa City’s heritage preservation efforts, learning more about the “Rappler treatment” of reporting became his highlight.

“I was used to the traditional approach to reporting. In this training, we were introduced to Rappler’s approach or treatment to journalism — learning not only to serve as watchdogs, but also to connect with the community,” Bustos said.

He also appreciated the training’s approach to AI, noting that while many institutions restrict its use, the technology can still be valuable for tasks such as data visualization and vibe coding, provided that the information remains accurate.

REPORTING LOCAL GOVERNMENTS. Rappler Managing Editor Miriam Grace Go leads a discussion with the fellows on the first day of the four-day onsite training on August 5 in Pasig City.

Storytelling and community engagement

The training also emphasized the intersection of rigorous research and human-centered storytelling.

Axel John Cainglet of Cavite had already been digging into complex provincial issues, including a reclamation project impacting Bacoor’s “tahong” (mussel) harvests, Noveleta’s traditional salt-making industry, and ₱5 billion in DPWH contracts linked to the Revilla family.

“Before the fellowship, tingin ko sobrang tapang ko na, but in this weeklong training, I realized puwede pang tapangan ‘yung pagsulat (I thought I was already very bold, but during this weeklong training, I realized that I could be even bolder in my writing),” Cainglet shared.

Cainglet also stressed the importance of community engagement in his stories. “It shouldn’t be just a one-way process. After the stories are written, they should create an impact for the people they are written for. The community we write about is also relevant to us.”

This deep community connection was echoed by Mark David Silencio of Bulacan, who wrote about the kangkong farmers struggling alongside rising floodwalls during his first month in the program.

“In times like this, our communities need us most. We are not meant to be extractive, but to connect and engage with them even after the story is published,” Silencio said.

Finding support and purpose

Meanwhile, for Caloocan City-based fellow Eunicito Barreno, the training reframed his perspective about his hometown. Initially discouraged by Caloocan’s troubled reputation and association with political dynasties, extrajudicial killings, and the drug war — for which the city has become for him, the “worst of the worst” — Barreno realized these challenges informed his purpose.

“I have both love and hate for Caloocan because of its issues but the training and my fellowship experience so far taught me that I have a role in telling the stories of Caloocan,” Barreno said.

During his first month, Barreno leveraged his local ties, reporting about local grievances over what Caloocan residents describe as a “useless” drainage project. He also amplified the story of the Caloocan furniture makers striving to sustain their craft.

The onsite training provided vital space for camaraderie and support among fellows, too.

“Since the very first night, I realized that hearing my co-fellows share stories about their work [as journalists] made me feel like I wasn’t out of place. From the moment I arrived from the island, in a place I wasn’t familiar with, I felt at home,” Vic Bagaan, a fellow who traveled from Palawan, said in a mix of English and Filipino. During his first month, Bagaan wrote about the students still displaced by the 2024 Quito fire.

For Jennifer Jezreel Kaye Pading of Eastern Visayas, the fellowship was an opportunity not only to strengthen her journalism skills, but also a chance to extend the support she received to her sphere of influence.

Inspired by two former campus journalists from her school who previously joined the fellowship, Pading is committed to sustaining this cycle of mentorship and learning.

FELLOWSHIP NIGHT. The 2026 Aries Rufo fellows with alumni fellows, Rappler reporters, editors, and staff during fellowship night, building connections and sharing experiences in public-interest journalism.

Challenge as they continue

During the four-day training, Rappler also hosted a fellowship night where the 2026 Fellows had the opportunity to network with Rappler reporters, editors, and alumni fellows.

Amid the challenges facing journalism today, Rappler CEO and Nobel laureate Maria Ressa spoke to the fellows about the future of the profession and encouraged them to continue on the journey.

“While there’s a lot of opportunity, there are also a lot of challenges in the media industry and we will not take it against you if you take a different path, but we would appreciate it so much if you continue to pursue journalism,” she told the fellows.

Meanwhile, Rappler’s executive editor Glenda Gloria challenged the fellows as they continue their fellowship program when they head home.

“Because you are Aries Rufo Journalism Fellows, you carry the name of Aries, who, as a journalist, preferred to listen, ask, and never assume. You also carry the name of Rappler. Take pride in it but be responsible,” Gloria said.

“You are going back to the field…Remember that you are not only a storyteller, but more importantly a truth teller,” she added.

Gloria concluded with a definition of the craft that will guide the fellows: “Journalism, as we know it is the discipline of verification but journalism is also finding joy in discovery. What do you discover when you do journalism? You don’t just discover the wrongdoings of others, you discover skills, courage, and character you never thought you had.”

As a final requirement, fellows will produce a long-form story, either investigative or in-depth, focused on accountability and the use — or misuse — of public resources in their communities. Online sessions before and after the onsite training covered journalism foundations, the media landscape, basic research, ethical standards of journalism, fact-checking methodology, and story distribution.

The Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship, now on its sixth cycle since its launch in 2021, is a four-month collaborative initiative between Rappler and the Journalism for Nation Building Foundation (JNBF). The current cycle, supported by the Friedrich Naumann Foundation for Freedom (FNF) Philippines, runs until November 2026. – Rappler.com

World.title: Rappler Talk: Reintroducing Leanne with the single ‘Babaero’

LIVE

The multitalented artist talks about her decision to step into her new persona as Leanne, her work as an actress, and what else she has in store for her fans

MANILA, Philippines – Most people first encounter Leanne Mamonong as one-half of the duo Leanne and Naara, as the soloist barb., or even as Mihan from the film Open Endings.
