World.title: Armed officers to bolster security at Melbourne hospitals under opposition proposal
World.content:
Victoria's opposition has pledged to deploy dozens of armed law enforcement officers in major hospitals around the state in a bid to curb violent incidents if it wins government later this year.

The Liberal-National Coalition plan, announced ahead of the November election, would see 70 Protective Services Officers (PSOs) work across seven hospitals as part of a two-year pilot.

The role of the armed officers working in shifts across 24 hours would be to provide additional security presence, respond to serious incidents, assist with the guarding of prisoners and escort hospital staff to their vehicles.

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said the trial would help those in power understand "how we can best protect our hospitals".

"PSOs will provide that security presence, working alongside existing security, integrating with them, and providing a visible deterrence around these hospitals to ensure that patients feel safe and clinicians feel safe," she said.

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson announced the policy outside the Alfred Hospital. (ABC News)

She said it was not a "radical" idea.

"PSOs are on our train stations. They work on government buildings. These people are trained, they know how to de-escalate, they know how to work in an operational sense.

"Every single day in Victorian hospitals, Victoria Police are in our ED (emergency department)," she said.

"They are responding to incidents.

"This frees up our police force to ensure that our PSOs are there, they can respond quickly ... to provide that sense of security to our clinicians and our patients."

According to reports tabled in the Victorian parliament at the end of 2025, in the 2024-2025 financial year there were close to 24,000 violent incidents recorded across dozens of public health services.

PSOs were introduced in 2011 under the Liberal-National government led by Ted Bailleu, with the armed officers' roles centred on bolstering safety at railway stations.

The armed, uniformed officers have the power to apprehend, arrest, search and fine people, but only in designated areas related to public transport.

In April, the opposition also vowed to recruit 200 additional PSOs to patrol train stations across the city if elected.

That proposal, which had the support of the Police Association Victoria, was announced a month after Mernda man Aidan Becker was fatally stabbed at the railway station while trying to protect a 14-year-old boy from an alleged group robbery.

On Sunday, Minister for Medical Research Anthony Carbines announced $2 million for mRNA research under the mRNA Pipeline Victoria grant program.

On the opposition's PSO proposal, Mr Carbines accused the opposition of being "sort of obsessed" with law and order in healthcare.

"It's fascinating that the opposition are more focused about law and order in our health services than investment in nurses, investment in health workers, investment in health practitioners," he said

"That's the sort of conversation I want to have about how we invest in the people that make change in our health services that save lives, that change lives."

"That's where the investment has to go."

World.title: New attempt to revive manganese smelter in Tasmania
World.content:
The union representing workers at Australia's last manganese smelter says there are parties interested in taking over the site.

Creditors on Monday voted to liquidate Liberty Bell Bay, leaving about 200 workers without a job.

Manganese is a critical component to make steel, meaning Australia no longer has sovereign steelmaking capability.

The Australian Workers' Union (AWU) said a consortium involving White Oak and OM Holdings was conditionally interested in buying the site and eventually restarting the smelter.

"The consortium has been involved in a range of discussions with private investors and they believe that they have enough private investors to recapitalise the plant," assistant branch secretary Richard Flanagan said.

" Obviously the plant has now been idle for some time and there'll be work which will need to be done for the smelter to be ready to resume production. "

Workers at the Liberty Bell Bay smelter have faced a long period of uncertainty about their futures. (ABC News)

Liberty Bell Bay stopped operations in May last year, originally citing ore supply challenges and global market volatility.

The company's owner, GFG Alliance, has been accused of moving about $200 million out of Liberty Bell Bay via inter-company loans.

Liquidator EY Parthenon believes Liberty Bell Bay was trading while insolvent for more than a year, including when the Tasmanian government granted the company a $20 million loan.

Of that, $14.5 million was used to purchase ore — which the government has since repossessed due to the failure of the company to resume operations.

New company 'TEMCO Bell Bay' established

The union said the consortium had established a new company to bid to take over the site.

"From the union's perspective, this is a real phoenix opportunity and we would urge the Tasmanian government to embrace the proposal with some enthusiasm," Mr Flanagan said.

Two of the parties involved in a previous bid are said to be involved in the latest proposal. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Corporate records show a company called TEMCO Bell Bay was registered in late June.

White Oak is listed as a shareholder, and the company director is White Oak's Kenneth Pereira.

Before the manganese smelter was bought by GFG Alliance, it was known as the Tasmanian Electro Metallurgical Company (TEMCO).

The ABC understands the consortium is not the only party interested in the site, and liquidator EY Parthenon would need to consider any proposals.

Consortium seeks exemption from pre-existing environmental liabilities

Mr Flanagan said he understood the consortium's interest was conditional on the state government waiving the pre-existing environmental liabilities at the site.

"So, the new owner would work and be responsible for any environmental impact that they have going forward, but the pre-existing environmental liabilities would not be their responsibility," he said.

" When you have ongoing operations at a site of this nature, you wouldn't expect that there would be too much remediation which would need to be done. "

On top of that, Mr Flanagan said the consortium wanted the existing power deal between Hydro Tasmania and Liberty Bell Bay transferred to them.

"So they would pay the power prices which were contracted by Liberty Bell Bay," he said.

Robert Flanagan described the proposal, from his union's perspective, as "a real phoenix opportunity". (ABC News: Emily Smith)

Resources Minister Felix Ellis said the government would have a conversation with any parties interested in the site.

He did not indicate if the government would accept the consortium's requests, but said any deal had to be in the interests of Tasmanian taxpayers.

"The government has received indication from White Oak that it is considering putting forward a proposal to EY," he said.

"We welcome [the AWU] supporting the 10-year power agreement, which was offered to White Oak as part of the administration process."

A consortium involving Adroit Capital, White Oak and OM Holdings had previously been interested in purchasing the site, until Adroit Capital pulled out of the process in June.

OM Holdings is a manganese ore and ferroalloy company operating in Australia, Malaysia, Singapore and China.

White Oak is a United States-based investment advisor and private credit firm.

Mr Flanagan said OM Holdings was interested in purchasing the ore from the Tasmanian government.

Labor calls on government to do 'everything possible' to see smelter restarted

Deputy Labor leader Janie Finlay said the best outcome for workers and the Tasmanian economy would be a restart of the smelter.

"If there is an opportunity to recapitalise that site and get it back up and running again to protect those major industrials in Tasmania and to support those jobs, this government should be doing everything possible to make that happen," she said.

Janie Finlay called on the Rockliff state government to do everything in its power to see the manganese smelter restarted. (ABC News: Emily JB Smith)

Mr Flanagan said many of the smelter's workers, who are now out of a job, would like to remain in the area.

"We believe that a lot of the workers would return if that was available to them," he said.

" But the longer it's left, the more likely it is workers will find alternative employment. "

EY Parthenon and White Oak have been approached for comment.

World.title: Inside this street food market are signs of a crashing currency
World.content:
Over the past six months, the world has been glued to charts, gripped by the high price of oil.

But in Indonesia, there's another chart that's been causing fear and anxiety.

Indonesia's currency, the rupiah, has fallen to historic lows against the US dollar.

From September 2024, it went from about 15,000 rupiah per $US1, passing a psychological threshold of 17,000 rupiah in April this year.

It worsened through June to more than 18,000, and has stubbornly remained around that low ever since.

The rate is worse than it was during the 1998 Asian financial crisis, which sparked such severe unrest and protests that it led to the downfall of Indonesia's former authoritarian president Suharto.

And despite the war in the Middle East causing pain across Asia, some Indonesian economists say it is mostly domestic factors that have made the rupiah one of the worst-performing currencies in the region.

"The damage in most of the economy is quite severe," economist Dipo Satria Ramli said.

"Everyone is quite affected."

Street food sellers have had to raise their prices to deal with rising production costs. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

The nation's central bank, Bank Indonesia, has issued four rate rises in quick succession to try and wrangle the slide in the rupiah.

But further fears have been raised after the sudden resignation of the bank's governor, well before the end of his second term.

While the government scrambles to stabilise the currency, the crisis is inflicting a serious toll on Indonesians.

'A lot of businesses could go bankrupt'

The drop in currency has been acutely felt by the nation's Tempeh makers.

Tempeh is an iconic Indonesian food made from soybeans, which are mostly imported from the United States.

It is a major source of affordable protein, but the declining rupiah has been pushing up the price of soybeans.

Ahmad Saikhu says the poor currency could lead to wide unemployment. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

Ahmad Saikhu, a long-time tempeh maker and secretary-general of a 4,000-strong producers association, said he and the members were in "total disarray".

"If this keeps going on, our family finances will become total chaos," he said.

"The government isn't really managing to control these prices, leaving grassroots producers at the bottom with their livelihoods in total disarray."

Tempeh, usually made with imported US soybeans, is becoming more expensive to produce. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

Ahmad said he and other producers have had to cut down the size of their packages, because they cannot increase the prices they sell at.

"We have to survive so we can continue supplying the protein needs of low-income people," he said.

" If this keeps up, I estimate within three to six months, a lot of businesses could go bankrupt, leading to widespread unemployment. "

At a street food market in Central Jakarta, the increasing cost of imports has been squeezing already low-income sellers.

Chilies, broths, and sambal, a type of spicy sauce, are commonly packaged in plastic for customers here.

But the cost of naphtha, a key petrochemical used to make plastics, has soared because supplies have been choked off with the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

The sinking currency has acted as a double-whammy, further causing the price of plastic products to surge.

"The main increase is definitely plastic," Andri, a satay seller, told the ABC.

"It's well over 50 per cent higher."

Andri has been seeing fewer customers in the markets recently. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

Andri has also noticed the market getting quieter, driven by less demand and tighter economic conditions.

"This current situation is getting pretty concerning … every one of us is taking home less money, and as for customers, there are fewer of them coming by," he said.

Another seller in the market, Syamsul, has had to raise prices at his noodle cart.

"Every day more and more goods are going up in price, while everyone's spending less," he said.

"The impact on me is pretty substantial … what choice do you have? Sometimes you just have to look for loans here and there."

Syamsul says customers have been spending less, putting a strain on vendors. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

Tens of millions of Indonesians are taking out online loans, known locally as pinjol, to help cover basic costs.

The growth in potentially risky pinjol loans has been rapid, with the amount of money borrowed growing by 25 per cent from the middle of 2025 to the middle of this year.

According to the government's financial services regulator, more than $8 trillion has been borrowed in these types of loans by tens of millions of Indonesians, mostly people aged under 35.

Rising inflation and stagnant wages

Economist Dipo Satria Ramli estimated "50 to 60 per cent" of the decline in the rupiah was because of domestic factors and not because of shocks from the war in the Middle East.

He said three issues were contributing to the decline: "unpredictable policies", concern over transparency and accountability, and fiscal policy.

"[Inflation] is across all different goods," Dipo said.

"At a consumer's perspective, it's eating up purchasing power."

The government says it's working to try and contain the currency drop. (Reuters: Ajeng Dinar Ulfiana)

Most people in Indonesia work in what's known as the "informal sector", which covers unregulated work, such as markets and manual labour, and typically pays low wages.

But Dipo said workers in the "formal sector" — which includes corporations and government — were feeling the pain too.

"The real wage hasn't really gone up in the past few years, so it's quite a challenge for most Indonesians," he said.

In a statement, Indonesia's Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa said: "The depreciation of the rupiah is considered to be driven more by market sentiment than by changes in national economic fundamentals.

"The government, together with relevant authorities, continues to maintain financial system stability through coordination within the Financial System Stability Committee (KSSK).

"The government is ensuring that inflation remains within a controlled range."

The pain has not been localised to just the currency, with Indonesia's stock market losing almost 30 per cent this year.

The Jakarta Composite Index ranks as one of the worst-performing major equity markets in the world.

Major index provider MSCI has flagged it could downgrade Indonesia's equity market status, saying it was concerned about transparency.

Earlier this year, ratings agencies Moody's and Fitch lowered Indonesia's credit rating to negative.

Fitch Ratings said this was because of an "increasing policy uncertainty and erosion of Indonesia's policy mix consistency and credibility amid growing centralisation of policymaking authority".

On Wednesday, Indonesia's economic growth slowed to 5.3 per cent, down from 5.6 per cent earlier in the year, although it outperformed earlier predictions.

And even though the currency rate is worse than during the 1998 crisis, economists say that institutions are stronger now and the decline in the rupiah has been much more gradual this time around, allaying fears of economic-related unrest.

Across Indonesia, people are appealing for greater support.

"If things reach a complete dead end, we might have to go on a production strike," Ahmad said.

"That's all we can do … we don't have any other way to voice our struggle.

"We're appealing to the president and the government to resolve this issue."

World.title: Wildfire forces more than 20,000 people evacuate homes in western Canada
World.content:
Thousands of people in western Canada have been ordered to flee a fast-moving wildfire that nearly doubled in size overnight.

A state of emergency was declared in British Columbia (BC) on Saturday, local time, after the Bald Range wildfire was burning out of control and grew rapidly to about 9,510 hectares.

Climate scientist caught up in Europe's 'dystopian' summer Stefan Rahmstorf was holidaying in southern France when he came face to face with the climate future he has tried to fight.

Evacuation orders were in place for Summerland, Peachland and other districts west of Okanagan Lake in the province's southern interior.

The region produces most of BC's wine and is Canada's second-largest wine-producing area.

Premier David Eby told a news conference on Saturday that one fire official had likened the fire to "a bomb going off".

"He described flames on 100-foot tree, flames going 200 feet above that, and the fire creating its own weather system, which creates lightning, which then feeds on itself," Mr Eby said.

"Homes have been lost, and properties have been destroyed. Some people became trapped as conditions changed very quickly, and needed to be rescued," the premier said, adding it remained a very dynamic and threatening situation.

Summerland has a population of about 12,000 people, according to the 2021 census, and Peachland is home to about 6,500 residents.

The fire painted the skies with orange hues. (Reuters: Paige Taylor White)

A state of emergency grants the provincial government immediate access to special powers including travel restrictions and supply protections to prevent price gouging, and specific tools to coordinate rescue work.

Officials said the Bald Range wildfire triggered the largest evacuation event so far this summer and more than 20,000 people across BC have been forced to evacuate their homes.

"A lot of farms have been affected. We don't know how many structures have been lost. They're still busy fighting the fire," Summerland Mayor Doug Holmes said in a phone interview from Penticton.

"We have to brace ourselves for the worst."

Overnight evacuation

Many residents left overnight, driving south to Penticton or north to Kelowna before highways began to close.

Trees burn in the Bald Range wildfire on Friday. (Reuters: BC Wildfire Service/handout)

Terry Fries of Summerland was watching a football game on Friday night when a neighbour advised him to get a bag ready as the fire grew.

"At the time, it was still farther back, and you could see it behind the hills," he said.

When BC authorities issued the evacuation order around midnight, he and his family drove about 45 kilometres north to the city of Kelowna.

By Saturday afternoon, ashes began to settle on cars and houses in nearby areas as the fire painted the skies with orange hues.

Danube dries up Europe's second-longest river is carrying less water than it has in decades, revealing shipwrecks and shutting down nuclear reactors.

Several Canadian provinces, including Ontario and Quebec, have battled blazes this year as hot, dry weather fuelled wildfires in dense forest areas. Firefighters from Mexico, Australia, France and New Zealand have helped combat the fires.

In BC, where hot and dry conditions have increased the risk of more fires spreading, about 1,500 firefighting personnel were battling more than 100 fires.

Fires have burned through 9.9 million acres in Canada this year, according to the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Centre.

Europe's heatwave rages on

The fires in Canada follow what has also been a record-breaking summer so far across western Europe, with scorching temperatures and destructive wildfires.

France and Spain have been particularly hard hit in recent weeks.

A wildfire in Niebla, Huelva, Spain, burning on August 8. (Reuters: Mikel Konate)

The extreme weather across Europe has pushed temperatures above 40 degrees Celsius in many countries, prompting health warnings for millions of people. Scientists and officials warn that such events are becoming more frequent and intense as the climate warms.

In Central Europe, Slovakia and Austria both recorded all-time high temperatures this week, at 42.2C and 41.2C.

In Italy, officials placed all its major cities under the highest heat alert on Thursday, signalling a health risk for the entire population, not only vulnerable groups.

The UK government has declared half of England, and all of Wales, as officially being in drought.

England saw its warmest June on record and the UK its second warmest, while England and Wales experienced their driest July on record, according to Met Office data.

Reuters/AP

World.title: Love story: Supporting your soulmate through voluntary assisted dying
World.content:
Hilda Quiroga says she was "struck" by Steve Mayer from the moment they first met in Naarm/Melbourne in 2007. Hilda, who works in social services, and Steve, a barista and musician, went on to have an 18-year partnership and travel the world together, until his death at 53 through voluntary assisted dying (VAD).

Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us.

The funny thing is I met him at a gym.

I hate gyms. He hated gyms with a passion.

But, he was the barista at a cafe in the gym and I was there signing up a client.

I noticed how kind and respectful he was towards her.

I knew nothing about him. He could have been married or gay for all I knew. But, I emailed my friend and said to him, "I have just met a man that is going to change my life."

Not long after I was off overseas by myself, but I took him with me in my mind. I wanted to tell him that day, "We're going to be travelling together mate, so get ready, get your passport ready."

We got together in February 2008 and three months later we moved in.

I was in my 30s. He was in his 30s. There's no point in wasting time.

I had been married before, but it was short. Steve just made me feel like he saw me.

I was 100 per cent sure that I'd met my soulmate. I cringe at that word, but I just knew, and we were together, inseparable from that day to the very last.

An 'unstoppable force'

He knew all about the places that I'd been to and all the places that I wanted to go — like all the Inca ruins — because he was so well read.

He'd never had the opportunity to travel, but then when we got together, we were like this unstoppable force.

He got his passport and found his travelling legs and because we had no children, we were free to just travel, work, travel. That was us.

He wanted to go to see Machu Picchu and the Amazon and take ayahuasca and we did.

Hilda Quiroga says the couple had "incredible adventures", which included travelling to Samoa, Guatemala and Peru. (Supplied: Hilda Quiroga)

A diagnosis

Everything changed in June 2023.

He had the results of a CT scan come back and they found a mass in his lung.

His only symptoms were that he was fatigued — which was not like Steve, who normally had the energy of a kid — and he was also sweating a lot.

A couple of days later tumours were found in his brain and elsewhere. It had already metastasised.

In September I quit my job. I had taken time off in those first months but was going to back work a little bit and it didn't feel right.

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

I successfully applied for carer's allowance and disability support.

It was tricky, but I'm good at paperwork.

In our relationship, Steve usually took care of cooking and cleaning (mostly because I'm not great), and I took care of social engagements, finances, and personal administration.

He taught me a lot about myself, and I didn't think I could do the things that I did when he got sick.

You're a partner, but you also become a "carer".

I've never been comfortable with that word because I'm his partner, of course I'm going to do this.

But everything changes, like intimacy.

We were still very close and intimate, but that was a big deal for him because we'd always had a lovely sex life.

We still had our lovely little rituals in the morning — even at [the hospital], I'd get him the coffee, I'd get him the papers, he could do the sudoku. He would do the "diabolical" sudoku without even using a pencil.

And while he was in the worst possible place, he was still trying to look after me too.

When he vomited at home, he'd never let me clean it up. I would be dry-reaching because that's the one bodily fluid I can't handle.

Friends who would come and see him told me afterwards, that he would whisper, "take care of her."

Their last trip to Wye River, on Victoria's Great Ocean Road, in November 2024. (Supplied: Hilda Quiroga)

Together at the pointy end

Steve mentioned voluntary assisted dying to his specialist about four months after being diagnosed.

It's a very legal process and then a pharmacist comes to your house with the medication.

That box of medication was here in the apartment for months.

Steve was then moved into palliative care and two weeks later during a terrible night, he said to me, "I think we're at the pointy end."

The next morning when the doctors were doing their rounds, he looked at me, I looked at him and he said to the doctor, "I've decided I want to use voluntary assisted dying today."

Right at the end it was just me, Steve's nephew, his partner and the VAD nurse.

He took his medication, swallowed it all in one go, and then had a bit of Coke because it's so vile.

Within about 20 minutes, he started to fall into unconsciousness.

I didn't cry. I just held Steve in my arms and just whispered in his ears as he passed away, because I thought he doesn't need to hear me sobbing, not now.

All I wanted him to hear was my voice saying, "It's all right, love. It's time. You're tired. It's time to rest."

He took his last breath. I listened to his heart. I loved falling asleep on his chest to hear that beautiful steady beat and it was gone.

Then I lost it.

Hilda Quiroga says Steve Mayer was a completely selfless, glorious and funny human. (Supplied: Hilda Quiroga)

18 months without Steve

I'm 18 months down the track and I still cry every day. I shed tears all over Melbourne.

[But] there's comfort in knowing he decided when he had had enough. Our apartment is just full of him. He's everywhere.

I've still got like his death T-shirt and I sleep with it every night and I haven't washed it. It's probably very unhygienic. My friend also nicked the pillow he died on and I sleep with that too.

We would hold hands when we fell asleep every night. He would tell me that he loved me every night and not just, "Love you, babe." He would turn around, face me and look me intently in the eyes and tell me how much he loved me.

Even though I've lost him and he's gone, I still feel obviously blessed and fortunate that I had that big love.

I think we all want that love and I'm a better person for meeting him. So, where there's grief, there's love.

World.title: Two planes involved in second recent near-miss at Sydney Airport
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWAirports Two planes involved in second recent near-miss at Sydney Airport Amber Schultz Updated August 9, 2026 — 1:57pm ,first published August 9, 2026 — 9:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two planes have been involved in a near-miss while taxiing on the runway at Sydney Airport, forcing one plane to brake suddenly and injuring a crew member, in the second such incident at the airport in a fortnight. A Qatar Airways and Jetstar aircraft were photographed on the runway metres from each other just after 7am on Sunday. A Jetstar plane and a Qatar Airways plane on the runway at Sydney Airport on Sunday morning. Nine News There were 180 passengers on board Jetstar flight JQ402, which was heading to the Gold Coast, when the pilot spotted the Qatar Boeing 777 to his right, Nine News reported. The Qatar plane had no passengers on board and was being towed at the time, according to the report. The pilot applied the brakes on the Airbus A320, causing one flight attendant who was moving throughout the cabin to fall. The attendant was treated by paramedics for minor injuries. No passengers were injured.



The Jetstar pilot, captured on videos by passengers, told them a cabin crew member had been injured. “We need a safety car due to the proximity of the [plane] to the right,” he said. “We were focusing on crossing a runway so only by chance … we were able to stop.” Loading A Jetstar spokesperson said the aircraft was following air traffic control instructions. “The pilots were forced to brake firmly after another aircraft came in close proximity,” the spokesperson said.



An investigation into the incident has been launched. A spokesperson for Airservices Australia, which manages air traffic movement, said departures had been spaced at longer intervals after the incident. “We are working with airlines to reduce delays and the impact on passenger travel as much as possible,” the spokesperson said. The company will review the incident and assist with safety investigations. The return Jetstar flight from the Gold Coast has been cancelled, with customers to be rebooked on later services.



The Australian Transport Safety Bureau said it would collect available data from both aircraft and air traffic control, with investigators to interview the involved flight crew, tug operators and air traffic controllers, plus other witnesses and involved parties, and collect relevant recorded information including CCTV footage. Related Article Aviation Dozens of flights out of Sydney delayed up to 80 minutes The bureau confirmed there was damage to the Qatar plane’s nose gear and the aircraft tug. Premier Chris Minns said he was concerned about the incident. “We want to make sure that the airport’s operating at full capacity. That’s hugely important for our economy,” he said.



“We don’t want to see people disrupted if they go to the airport and services are cancelled because there’s not enough air traffic controllers … We can’t have massive delays or near misses.” An investigation into a second near miss at the airport on Wednesday is also underway, after a Qantas flight was cleared to cross a runway in front of another of the airline’s flights that had just come in to land. Both parties had been cleared to proceed by air traffic control, a Qantas spokesperson said. Sydney airport experienced lengthy delays across Friday and Saturday with more than 150 flights affected amid staff shortages at air traffic control. Chief executive of airline peak body A4ANZ Stephen Beckett previously told the Herald workers calling in sick or for carer duties were causing the network to “grind to a halt,” and calling for Airservices Australia to improve its capabilities. Airservices Australia said it was investing in training and recruitment. Ground delays attributable to the company fell by 13% year-on-year to less than 0.1% of total network delays, according to its latest financial report.



Qatar Airways has been contacted for comment. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Alleged Sydney gun-runner sexually tortured an unconscious teen for more than 10 hours, police say
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWCrime Alleged Sydney gun-runner sexually tortured an unconscious teen for more than 10 hours, police say Perry Duffin August 9, 2026 — 1:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: Graphic content An alleged Sydney gun-runner has been charged with filming the prolonged drugging and sexual torture of a teenage girl. Ararat Damirdjian, 55, was arrested in April this year after the Australian Federal Police followed a digital trail of a man importing a pistol to a home on Cunningham Street, Telopea, in the city’s west. Ararat Damirdjian has been charged with filming the prolonged drugging and sexual torture of a teenage girl. Fairfax Media The weapon, a $29 Chinese pistol that folds down into the size of a wallet, was imported under Damirdjian’s name but seized at the border, according to a police document released by the NSW Supreme Court.



Inside his home, police allegedly found 85 grams of cocaine, 32 firearms, four crossbows, a silencer, methamphetamine and “The Great Big Narcotics Cookbook”. Detectives, who pulled Damirdjian’s criminal history, realised he had an extensive criminal history for drugs and weapons and was subject to a firearms prohibition order. “Damirdjian is a long-term, high-risk offender with entrenched involvement in organised crime, large-scale drug manufacture and supply, and he has links to weapons trafficking, drug distribution, and the storage of firearms, ammunition, and explosive materials,” the court document claims. Detectives went through Damirdjian’s phone and found “highly sensitive and distressing” recordings of a young woman with a distinctive tattoo, the document says. The woman, aged 18, was unconscious but appeared completely lifeless on Damirdjian’s bed, police allege.



What Damidjian allegedly did to the woman, while recording, is too confronting to print. He allegedly administered GHB, a date-rape drug known as liquid ecstasy, through a syringe, until she passed out. Then methamphetamine was exhaled into her body, police say, on multiple occasions. ‘It is difficult to contemplate a more serious example of taking advantage of a complainant who is unable to consent in any capacity over a prolonged period of time.’ Police document released by the NSW Supreme Court “The accused repeatedly sexually assaulted the victim over a period exceeding 10 hours,” the police document says in an unusually emotive plea to the court. “It is difficult to contemplate a more serious example of taking advantage of a complainant who is unable to consent in any capacity over a prolonged period of time.”



Damidjian allegedly sent the recording to another woman, named Chantelle in court documents, telling her “girls want me to invite them back because they love partying” with him. “You know that? I was about to call the ambulance. I was f---ing scared shitless. I thought you were gonna die,” Damidjian allegedly said in one recording to the unconscious teenager. The court heard that Damidjian, who also goes by Darius Khachigian and other aliases, has spent years in prison going back to 2001, when police found firearms including military rifles, drugs and cash in his Fairfield West bedroom. Among them were a Steyr military assault rifle with laser sight, a silenced .22 pump-action rifle, detonators, explosive cord, a snake and $87,100 cash, court documents state. While in prison he linked up with a drug cook who specialised in the “Nazi-method” of manufacturing ice, and the pair ran a drug operation while on parole until Damirdjian was re-arrested in 2006.



Editor's pick Exclusive

Crime Serious sexual offenders are walking free on community orders Damirdjian asked the court to release him so he could care for his elderly mother. Police noted Damirdjian’s brother lives with their mother, but he does not. Damirdjian’s nephew offered to surrender $20,000 if his uncle skipped court. His 82-year-old mother offered to let him live with her. “I am aware of the serious charges against the applicant… (we) continue to hold a very close relationship,” she wrote in a statement. Rick Kumar and Marc Gorin, who own and operate Star Car Wash, penned letters of support for Damirdjian saying he was “vital” to the operation of the Summer Hill, Leichhardt, Blacktown, Penrith and Casula businesses.



“The site safety is of utmost importance to our staff and customers, which he managers (sic) and overseas (sic) as well (sic),” Gorin’s letter says. Damirdjian, who was refused bail, is facing drug supply, weapons and multiple counts of sexual intercourse and touching without consent. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: What Kiss’ approach to attack will mean for million-dollar man Suaalii
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionWallabies What Kiss’ approach to attack will mean for million-dollar man Suaalii Paul Cully August 9, 2026 — 1:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii finished the 35-32 win against Japan on the wing - and that was a preview of where he will end up under new coach Les Kiss. A number of push and pull factors are at play - including the value that Hunter Paisami offers in the way Kiss likes to attack - but ultimately Suaalii’s strengths and weaknesses are better suited to the outside backs. Wallabies outside back Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii looks set for a positional change. Getty Images The 23-year-old is a sight to behold with ball in hand - and showed it in Osaka - but his distribution isn’t good enough for an elite Test midfielder, and his defensive issues persist. Interestingly, the Wallabies picked an out-and-out midfielder on the bench for the first time this year, so Kiss might have always had a plan to have a look at Suaalii on the edge.



Paisami was a massive part of how the Reds played under Kiss, and his strong game against Japan means that a Paisami-Len Ikitau combination is likely once Ikitau returns from injury. Amatosero red card was a fair call There was a scramble to find mitigating factors after Miles Amatosero put a shoulder to the head of Japan captain Warner Dearns in the first half, but it always looked like red-card material. Loading All Blacks flanker Luke Jacobson was lucky to avoid a red card in similar circumstances for a clean-out against Ireland last month, but Amatosero can’t have real complaints.



While late changes of direction and dips in height might be relevant to tackle situations, when the tackler is caught out by a ball carrier’s dynamic movement, Amatosero has lined up Dearns from metres away and has his eyes locked on him until turning his shoulder to hit him with force. His selection was always a risky one. Perhaps the Wallabies expected Harry Hockings to start and wanted to counter his size, but as it turned out Jack Cornelsen was selected for the Brave Blossoms, and he used his greater mobility to produce a strong performance. It’s easy to understand Amatosero’s appeals to coaches, given his size, but at the moment there is a big gap between what coaches want him to be and where he actually is with his rugby. Declan Meredith gestures to a teammate during the Wallabies’ win over Japan. Getty Images Declan Meredith struggles at No.10



The Brumbies five-eighth showed great mental courage to turn around an uncertain first half and put the Wallabies in some great attacking positions with a few great touch finders. Brumbies fans will remember all too well how Meredith completely lost his way against the Hurricanes during Super Round in Christchurch. But the cold, hard reality is that Meredith won’t get away with repeats of his performance in Osaka against the Rugby Championship sides or the Six Nations teams in November. Carter Gordon ran the water in Japan and is presumably close to a return, but Ben Donaldson must be wondering what he needs to do to earn a crack at the jersey. On the flipside, there was a big positive in Tom Wright’s return to top speed and form, Harry Potter was excellent, and Josh Canham outpointed Dearns in a high-quality duel in the second row. He would have relished nicking one lineout off the giant Dearns in the first half. As far as the Kiss imprint goes, it is too early to say. However, some of the Wallabies’ ball movement and ambition was the best they have produced since the opening segment of the loss to the All Blacks in Perth last October.



Interestingly, Kiss told the Stan coverage after the Test the Wallabies had “overplayed” at times in Osaka. However, the key to unlocking this particular group of Wallabies is not to pull the reins too tightly. Billy Proctor and the All Blacks were given a stern test by their South African opposition. AP Photo/Halden Krog Stormers show what Super Rugby is missing Everyone understands the economic difficulties of putting 30 massive humans on a plane and flying them from Sydney to Cape Town or Johannesburg for two games of rugby played in the middle of the night, Australian time, and viewed only by insomniacs or tragics. Imagine trying to do that in the current climate: it’s a fast-track to bankruptcy. But watching the Stormers bully the All Blacks’ set-piece on Saturday night was a stark reminder of the high-performance cost of not having South African teams in Super Rugby.



Even though the Stormers are in preseason mode, they did a number on the All Blacks’ scrum and maul defence and exposed them under the high ball. Related Article Opinion

Wallabies There were plenty of mistakes, but the Wallabies’ win also brought plenty of satisfaction Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author The All Blacks said they knew what was coming, but the reality of playing in South Africa hit them hard, and they will have to be very fast learners to succeed on their tour of South Africa. Super Rugby Pacific has its merits, but Australian players are missing out on an education that only the South Africans can provide. The great Kolisi might not face the All Blacks



The Springboks were pushed to the last second in their 17-10 win against Los Pumas in Argentina, with Argentina replacement Matias Moroni dropping the ball with the tryline in sight. South Africa’s depth is impressive, but it is not bottomless. They will likely view the Test as perfect preparation for the All Blacks, but there will be concern after captain Siya Kolisi limped off the field after just 24 minutes. Kolisi has been struggling with a calf injury, and it looks like his participation in the first Test against the All Blacks is in real doubt. Kolisi’s ability as a rugby player, rather than a leader and talismanic figure, has always been underrated. He is a destructive force at the breakdown and a great ball carrier, so the Springboks will lose something on the field if he can’t play. Rassie Erasmus also has a big call to make at No.10. Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, also returning from injury, was very much rocks or diamonds against Argentina.

World.title: Back before Christmas: Fremantle bridge return on budget and ahead of schedule
World.content:
NationalWARoads Back before Christmas: Fremantle bridge return on budget and ahead of schedule Michael Philipps August 9, 2026 — 1:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The long-awaited return of the Fremantle traffic bridge is set to be complete before the end of the year, with the state government confirming the build is ahead of schedule and also within budget. The new Fremantle Traffic Bridge is progressing ahead of schedule, with the project on track to fully open to road users this year. The bridge was closed for the build in February and was set to be completed in the first half of 2027. However, the WA government has now stated that traffic will be back on the new build before the end of the year. “We’re happy to announce that the new bridge will be opening before Christmas,” Transport Minister Rita Saffioti said.



“There’ll be two lanes each way and works will be underway to finish the ramps in and out the bridge. “There’s also going to be a lot of terracing and landscaping done around this area too, so it’s going to be a place where people can sit and enjoy their beautiful view.” The cost of the project was updated in the recent state budget, coming in at $596 million in a 50-50 split between the WA and federal governments. Saffioti added that the closure of the bridge had seen a surge in public transport from the Fremantle area. “Weekly boardings at Fremantle Station have been up 20 per cent and parking up 30 per cent which show there’s been more people catching public transport, which has helped ease some of those traffic pressures,” she said.



“The overall river crossings have been down by one fifth, so again, it shows that people have modified their behaviour. “We’ve seen everyone really play their part in making sure that this bridge closure has gone probably smoother than anyone would have expected. “So thank you to everyone across the community for playing their part in delivering this project.” Fremantle MLA Simone McGurk acknowledged the impact the project has had on local business and thanked the community for their patience and support. “It has been hard, particularly around North Fremantle and George Street in East Fremantle,” she said.



“I thank them for their patience and also thank the community who has tried to get behind local Fremantle businesses to ensure that they can keep the doors open and keep thriving, “It’ll be so good to see the bridge now open for the summer trading period.”

World.title: ‘Punched, slapped, groped’: How the manosphere is putting teachers and students at risk
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaEducation ‘Punched, slapped, groped’: How the manosphere is putting teachers and students at risk Nicole Precel August 9, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s 11am, bleak and eight degrees outside. A classroom packed with year 9 boys is asked what their biggest fear is. “Women,” one student volunteers, “because they are mean.” The Man Cave facilitator Leeson Timms is working to tackle the rise of misogyny in classrooms and support male students’ mental health. Chris Hopkins The answer lands in The Man Cave session, a male-focused mental health charity, with awkward laughter, but the subtext is heavy. Australian schools are facing a “crisis due to rampant misogyny and sexism” fuelled by online influencers, with educators struggling to tackle it, experts say.





“I was punched [in the crotch], slapped, groped, told sexual fantasies about what I did to them in their dreams; some said they could smell fish when I walked past,” she said. Ruby, who is fighting a WorkCover claim, said she believes some of the behaviour was due to students consuming “manosphere” content, but that students’ home environments also played a role. Misogyny in schools has become so widespread, Australian Education Union deputy federal president Matt Jarman said, it has become a key reason that some female teachers are leaving the profession. “Education departments need to address this growing issue with clear policies, adequate resources and strong leadership to confront misogyny and ensure schools are safe and respectful places to work and learn.”



Data compiled exclusively for The Age by the Crime Statistics Agency found that in the past 10 years, at least 35 allegations of rape were reported and 198 alleged indecent assaults at school or reported by schools where the alleged offender was between 10 and 17 years old. Related Article Lunch with Daniel wishes the rest of the world could witness what he sees in Australia’s high schools A Victoria Police spokesperson said the data included schools reporting sex offences whether they occurred on its grounds or elsewhere. Police proactively visit schools to provide advice on the law and safety, including consent. While the data doesn’t show the gender breakdown of alleged offenders, Monash University lecturer Stephanie Wescott says research shows that males perpetrate the most sexual harm. “We have a cultural issue in schools, and I think schools are the best place to do this work because that is where young people spend most of their time,” she said.



Wescott also said teachers found that anecdotally, the schools’ “crisis due to rampant misogyny and sexism” was causing a decline in girls’ attitudes to school. “If you are a girl student sitting in a classroom, and you are seeing a [female teacher] ... and see how they are degraded, that sets up an expectation for you in how you might be treated in your lifetime.” Youth advocate and educator Daniel Principe says male students need a holistic approach to tackling the manosphere. Picture: Supplied Though the federal government’s social media ban is well-intentioned, Leeson Timms, a facilitator for The Man Cave, calls it a “band-aid over an open wound”. Timms himself was lured into the manosphere when he was in year 11, at the height of the pandemic.



Related Article Listen

Social media Who are ‘looksmaxxers’? And why are they calling other men ‘sub-human’? “It snuck in without me realising it,” he said. Timms said that before his partner helped him realise how harmful the content he was watching was, it resulted in destructive behaviour towards people in his life. For children, he says the combination of manosphere content and boys observing how “dad talks about mum” can have dire results, he said. “Boys are swimming in a pool, looking for something to hold them afloat.” Since becoming a facilitator, Timms has run almost 250 school workshops, and says about two out of every three elicit a disclosure of suicidal ideation from a male student.



At a recent full-day relationship session, facilitators worked quickly to suss out the dynamics of the group of 27 teenage boys. Initially, there was jostling and cackles, but by the end of the day, the year 9 boys had connected and opened up. One talked about how they were struggling since their dad had died, while another boy shared for the first time he wanted to kill himself. Loading Timms said boys needed direction, positive male role models, counterarguments, education about healthy masculinity, and ideally, changes to social media. “If there’s a world where there’s a possibility to change algorithms, that should be the step,” he said.



This is something the advocacy group Teach Us Consent is calling on the Australian government to investigate, saying that algorithms – which largely dictate the content we are exposed to online – are creating a “pipeline for extreme misogynistic content”. They want laws that will “fix our feeds” by introducing an opt-in feature for algorithms. “This has real consequences offline, both for victim-survivors of sexual violence and for the boys being fed this material,” a Teach Us Consent spokesperson said. If you think your son is engaging with manosphere content Youth advocate and educator Daniel Principe recommends: Stay curious, not confrontational: Ask about what he’s watching and ask him to show you. Ask him what he finds interesting about it rather than criticising it straight away.

Ask about what he’s watching and ask him to show you. Ask him what he finds interesting about it rather than criticising it straight away. Don’t shame or ridicule him: If he feels judged, he’s more likely to retreat further into the online communities reinforcing the beliefs you may be hoping to counter.

If he feels judged, he’s more likely to retreat further into the online communities reinforcing the beliefs you may be hoping to counter. Listen for the underlying need: Most boys aren’t chasing misogynistic ideas. They’re chasing confidence, belonging, success or advice on relationships they might not be getting.

Most boys aren’t chasing misogynistic ideas. They’re chasing confidence, belonging, success or advice on relationships they might not be getting. Talk about healthy masculinity and being a good human: Help him see that strength, decency and respect for others aren’t opposites, but that they can all coexist.

Help him see that strength, decency and respect for others aren’t opposites, but that they can all coexist. Make critical thinking a conversation, not a lecture: Ask what a mate would actually say about the content, or how we can know if someone online is helping or manipulating us.

Ask what a mate would actually say about the content, or how we can know if someone online is helping or manipulating us. Make sure he’s got other people to look up to: Coaches, mentors, older siblings. People who model respect and accountability in real life, not just online.

Coaches, mentors, older siblings. People who model respect and accountability in real life, not just online. Keep the conversation going: One calm chat beats one big argument every time. Most of this is curiosity, but if you’re seeing escalating anger, isolation, content for women or rigid “us vs them” thinking, don’t ignore it.

One calm chat beats one big argument every time. Most of this is curiosity, but if you’re seeing escalating anger, isolation, content for women or rigid “us vs them” thinking, don’t ignore it. Get support early from someone your son already trusts: Curiosity and connection are key. Cyber safety expert Susan McLean says Respectful Relationships, a whole-of-school program aimed at preventing gender-based violence, needs to be updated at least yearly due to the rapidly changing nature of online culture. “People can argue it’s [just] a parent’s job,” McLean said. “Everyone has to work together.”



In Victoria, the state government has invested $129 million to deliver the whole-of-school Respectful Relationships program in schools, while a further $10.4 million allocated in the most recent budget will expand the program to over 400 schools. More independent and Catholic schools have been signing up, but Wescott says there were very few “who have been willing” to implement the whole-of-school approach, which is what evidence says is the most transformative. Loading For change to happen, she said, schools needed to admit there was a problem with misogyny. “We are afraid of saying that because it implicates boys.” Tintern Grammar head of junior school principal Adam Kenny uses a whole-of-school approach and says gender equality isn’t a box to tick at the Ringwood East school, but rather something that is embedded in every element.



“It’s living and breathing it, and guiding and supporting and mentoring and rectifying immediately when mistakes are made,” he said. UNSW lecturer Alex Fleck says Australia could learn from Brazil, where an anti-misogyny bill that could send people to jail is being considered. Tintern Grammar Head of Junior School Adam Kenny says a holistic approach to tackling the manosphere and promoting gender equality are important. Picture: Supplied Modelled on existing anti-racism legislation, the proposed bill would make engaging in violence, inciting violence, or restricting a woman’s rights or dignity could result in a two- to five-year prison sentence, and rise to a sentence of three to 10 years if posted online for profit or by someone with a large following. “I don’t think that it is a stretch to say that the latter circumstance of the offence is aimed at combating manosphere online influencers,” Fleck said.

World.title: ‘Give me a freaking break’: Greens senator spells out terms on Albanese’s gambling bill
World.content:
PoliticsFederalGambling ‘Give me a freaking break’: Greens senator spells out terms on Albanese’s gambling bill Michelle Griffin August 9, 2026 — 1:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Online betting s and inducements such as free bets should be banned if Labor wants its gambling bill passed into law, Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young says, but she is prepared to negotiate on advertising in streaming services. Hanson-Young spelt out the terms the Greens want the government to meet to get their gambling bill passed in the Senate in an interview on ABC’s Insiders. “If you are not prepared to do what’s needed here, well, we’ll take this out of your hands and we’ll do it in the Senate ourselves”, Hanson-Young said in the wake of a parliamentary inquiry where sports betting companies were grilled about claims they had offered lavish free bets, sex workers and drugs to VIP clients. Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young. Alex Ellinghausen Communications Minister Anika Wells said last week she was in talks with both the Coalition and the Greens about finding a deal. Liberal Senator Sarah Henderson said on Wednesday the bill was “riddled with deficiencies and must be significantly amended”.



“Unless there is real move online, this whole thing is set up to fail. We need proper bans on online advertising,” Hanson-Young told the ABC. Opposition, cross-bench and Greens MPs joined campaigners in condemning a carve-out for streaming services in Labor’s gambling laws that allows online services to show unlimited gambling ads in breaks during matches unless subscribers explicitly opt out. Hanson-Young said she could consider a switch to a model where adults could register to get the ads during sports on streaming services. “You know, some people are suggesting an opt-in rather than an opt-out,” Hanson-Young said. “Well, I want to hear what the government has to say about that. Well, I’m prepared to entertain that.” Loading



Resolving the stalemate over this bill is a top priority when Prime Minister Anthony Albanese returns on Monday from a week’s leave. The Albanese government took more than 1000 days to respond to the bipartisan 2023 report led by the late Labor MP Peta Murphy, which recommended a national regulator, banning inducements, and a total advertising blackout. None of these recommendations were in the government’s response, which was tabled on Budget Day, Tuesday 12 May. Labor’s scaled-back proposal restricts television ads to three an hour between 6am and 8.30pm, with no cap overnight, bans the use of sports stars and other celebrities to promote gambling, bans ads on sports jerseys and limits commercials on radio during school pick-up times. Both the Greens and the Coalition have raised concerns about inducements offered by sports betting companies, such as free bets, bonus bets and other direct incentives to clients.



Gambling companies last week denied the evidence tendered by anti-gambling campaigner Tim Costello and reformed addict and ex-NRL player Luke Bateman that they lured serious addicts to VIP events with drugs, escorts and five-figure bonus bets. Related Article Gambling Coalition will force Albanese to cede ground on gambling reforms Kai Cantwell, the chief executive of industry peak body Responsible Wagering Australia, said some “pretty egregious claims have been levelled against some of my members and non-members”. Hanson-Young dismissed the argument of the corporations that special offers were not inducements but legitimate products better described as “generosities”. “Give me a freaking break,” she said. “I think they use every trick in the book to promote and it’s a real predatory nature, whether it’s special deals, whether it’s extra credits, whether it’s favours to events. Inducements need to be off the table.”



While Henderson last Monday told the inquiry she thought further action was required to regulate inducements, opposition shadow treasurer Tim Wilson told News24 (formerly Sky News) there was a diversity of views within the Coalition on the bill. He said he was chiefly concerned with protecting children from too much exposure to gambling ads, and that online ads were examined. “There are a lot of other platforms people watch sports these days and receive gambling advertising as well,” he said. Labor frontbencher Jenny McAllister refused to say on News24 if the government was looking to change inducements, but noted: “We think we’ve broadly got the legislation right, but if there are sensible amendments that could improve the bill, of course we’re open to discussion across the parliament.”

World.title: How to spot if something has been written by AI
World.content:
TechnologyAI How to spot if something has been written by AI The Economist August 9, 2026 — 1:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ghost writer is haunting the English language. The linguistic spectre can turn its hand to prose, poetry, journalese and corporate jargon. It is frightfully versatile: you can get it to mimic Shakespeare’s sonnets or a schlocky beach read; Ernest Hemingway’s taut prose or the office-printer manual. It is frightfully fast, churning out thousands of words a minute. (Hemingway rarely produced as many in a day, and required much more booze.) Wordsmiths are spooked. AI prose is distinguishable by word and punctuation choice as well as sentence and paragraph structure. But its hallmarks are not what you might expect, partly because its writing style has changed with software updates. Bloomberg AI writing is everywhere. It is in your inbox and on your LinkedIn feed. It is all over the internet, drafting more than a third of new websites by one count. Large language models (LLMs) are helping students write essays and probably helping scientists write papers. Some allege AI-generated prose won the Commonwealth Short Story prize this year, with judges praising its “quiet authority”. (The Commonwealth Foundation denied the claim.) LLMs have stylistic quirks. They are thought to maximise the use of long em-dashes—and the use of words like “maximise”. They like to “deep dive” (and, better yet, “delve”) into the “rich tapestry” of the world. AI writing is not about a single word or phrase, but a rich tapestry of things. Spotting AI texts can be tricky. This is in part because you need evidence beyond a few words or dashes: claiming that a text is by an LLM because it uses the word “delve” is like claiming one is by Jane Austen because it uses “imprudence”. Bots also write in slightly different ways. There is no single style of AI writing, explains Karolina Rudnicka, a linguist at the University of Gdansk in Poland, just as there is no single style of human writing. Writers have idiosyncrasies—Emily Dickinson, for instance, loved em-dashes—and bots may do, too.



But there are a few ways to identify LLM-generated text. One is to use detection algorithms that are trained to spot the texture of human or AI prose. Pangram, a leading firm, claims to have 99.98 per cent accuracy. (It has partnered with Substack, a blogging platform, on such a tool.) Detectors, however, are black-box algorithms that can give false positives. They do not give reasons for why they reach their conclusions. Related Article Opinion

Tripologist Is AI better at travel advice than me? I put it to the test Michael Gebicki The Tripologist Researchers have also tried scouring texts for suspicious words or comparing papers from before and after LLMs were made available to the public. But these approaches have drawbacks too, not least because it is hard to disentangle AI quirks from other language trends. You can discover AI’s hallmarks by comparing the writing of man and machine. To do this you need a baseline that is distinctive and familiar. The Economist turned to prose that we’re sure is human and that readers will recognise: our own. We designed a study to ask top LLMs—OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, Google’s Gemini and xAI’s Grok—to write versions of our articles without consulting the web. (As a prompt, we gave them the AI-generated summaries that we have experimentally added to some of our articles.) This gave us a corpus of human and AI creations and we compared them across 55,940 sentences and 1.2 million words. To make sure we were detecting AI quirks rather than our own, we also checked the AI texts against journalism from CNN, the New York Times and the Washington Post. Excerpts from hit novels published between 1950 and 2022 offered another test.



Our findings are surprising. AI prose is distinguishable by word and punctuation choice as well as sentence and paragraph structure. But its hallmarks are not what you might expect, partly because its writing style has changed with software updates. That does not mean that LLMs are great writers: their prose lacks lucidity and elegance and is often formulaic. So those aspiring to be impressive (human) storytellers should avoid the following peculiarities in their own prose. Loading First, consider words. The vocabulary that bots overuse has changed: they no longer “delve” and there are not as many “tapestries”. Instead they offer a significant number of polysyllables like “significant”, “increasingly” and “consequences”. They use more rare words (“interdependence”, “reindustrialisation”) and scientific lingo (“parameter”, “methodology”) than humans, and are fond of nominalisations (making nouns from verbs, such as “expansion” from “expand”). All the LLMs in our study use such words, but particularly Gemini and Claude. Much of this language could be described as what George Orwell called “pretentious diction”. He railed against writers who “dress up simple statements” with complicated words and jargon to sound clever. Such pontificating penmen, Orwell observed, also believe that “Latin or Greek words are grander than Saxon ones”. (Bots agree: more Latinate suffixes crop up in their writing than in human texts.) Then look at punctuation. Many believe LLMs stuff their prose with em-dashes, but that is not true after the most recent updates. Today only Claude uses more em-dashes than human writers, with ChatGPT using markedly fewer than any other writer in our study. Humans rejoice—and start using dashes again.



A better way to spot AI-generated writing would be to look for texts without much punctuation at all. LLMs are very Joycean about it: they use fewer commas and semicolons than humans (and hardly any parentheses). They use less punctuation in part because they write longer sentences—“and” is their most overused word—and in part because they do not quote experts. Related Article AI AI used to create new viruses in the lab Finally, study the sentence. Bots’ sentences tend to be long; paragraphs are rarely interrupted with short, punchy statements. How dull. When LLMs want to make their sentences more lively, they often reach for a rhetorical device. Their favourites include: “not X but Y”, “not only but also” and the “rule of three”. (Grouping ideas in threes makes them more engaging, as we did just then.) ChatGPT and Claude use more of these constructions per 1,000 sentences than other LLMs and humans. So if you want to spot AI writing, look for bland, pretentious prose lavished with Latinate words—at least for now. With every update, our study shows, AI writing is becoming more similar to human prose. Pangram successfully detected AI-generated copy, but may struggle in future. LLMs are trained on human writing and learn from human feedback, notes Tommie Juzek of Florida State University, picking up things people find impressive and dropping things they do not. Bots learn fast, too. Take ChatGPT: until very recently it used an em-dash in almost every sentence. When your correspondent asked an older model whether it thought AI overused the dash, it said: “Ha—great question!” Ask the bot the same thing today and it soberly says “they’re best used sparingly.” Only a ghost could shapeshift so quickly.

World.title: It’s Gang of Youths - but not how you remember them
World.content:
Concert Hall, Sydney Opera House, August 8

“Thanks for letting us play the show we want to play,” says Gang of Youths frontman David Le’aupepe as the evening draws to a close.

The show they wanted to play eschews the bluster, adrenaline, and stadium-filling affectations that have long been the Sydney-born, London-based band’s trademark. Instead, we get something more thoughtful, restrained and effortlessly confident.

Gang of Youths got to play the show they wanted to play. Jess Gleeson

It’s in the way Le’aupepe begins the performance – the group’s first in Australia in three years – sitting solo at the piano, teasing the opening chords of goal of the century.

While on record the song is a string-soaked epic with peaks and valleys and lavish production flourishes, here it is naked, fragile and breathtakingly delicate.

It sets the tone for an evening in which the band – now an eight-piece in the live setting – bypass many of their hits, and deconstruct those they do play to breathe new life into the material.

By performing the normally rousing Magnolia solo on guitar, Le’aupepe lends even more desperation to the song’s cry for help.

The Deepest Sighs, the Frankest Shadows is slowed to half time, surging with a newfound power complemented by the harmonies of singer-songwriter Gretta Ray, who provides backing vocals.

Do Not Let Your Spirit Wane starts smaller than its recorded form, the band teasing it to a powerful and majestic climax; Let Me Down Easy adds more nuance to its motorik strut, and is sexier for it.

A handful of new songs are debuted, hinting at an evolution in the outfit’s forthcoming fourth album.

Things Take Time is soulful and quietly joyous, with trumpet lines lending it a Burt Bacharach-esque lightness; in another, country-leaning song “about tarot cards” the horn adds a more desolate touch.

Peppering the set with moments of levity and humour adds to the sense that this is a group comfortable in their own skin – witness the cover of Jimmy Buffett’s A Pirate Looks at Forty, complete with onstage margaritas and dedicated to Le’aupepe’s wife, who turned 39 days earlier.

That it all looks so effortless is a trick only the truly great acts can pull off.

World.title: Two planes involved in second recent near-miss at Sydney Airport
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWAirports Two planes involved in second recent near-miss at Sydney Airport Amber Schultz Updated August 9, 2026 — 1:57pm ,first published August 9, 2026 — 9:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two planes have been involved in a near-miss while taxiing on the runway at Sydney Airport, forcing one plane to brake suddenly and injuring a crew member, in the second such incident at the airport in a fortnight. A Qatar Airways and Jetstar aircraft were photographed on the runway metres from each other just after 7am on Sunday. A Jetstar plane and a Qatar Airways plane on the runway at Sydney Airport on Sunday morning. Nine News There were 180 passengers on board Jetstar flight JQ402, which was heading to the Gold Coast, when the pilot spotted the Qatar Boeing 777 to his right, Nine News reported. The Qatar plane had no passengers on board and was being towed at the time, according to the report. The pilot applied the brakes on the Airbus A320, causing one flight attendant who was moving throughout the cabin to fall. The attendant was treated by paramedics for minor injuries. No passengers were injured.



The Jetstar pilot, captured on videos by passengers, told them a cabin crew member had been injured. “We need a safety car due to the proximity of the [plane] to the right,” he said. “We were focusing on crossing a runway so only by chance … we were able to stop.” Loading A Jetstar spokesperson said the aircraft was following air traffic control instructions. “The pilots were forced to brake firmly after another aircraft came in close proximity,” the spokesperson said.



An investigation into the incident has been launched. A spokesperson for Airservices Australia, which manages air traffic movement, said departures had been spaced at longer intervals after the incident. “We are working with airlines to reduce delays and the impact on passenger travel as much as possible,” the spokesperson said. The company will review the incident and assist with safety investigations. The return Jetstar flight from the Gold Coast has been cancelled, with customers to be rebooked on later services.



The Australian Transport Safety Bureau said it would collect available data from both aircraft and air traffic control, with investigators to interview the involved flight crew, tug operators and air traffic controllers, plus other witnesses and involved parties, and collect relevant recorded information including CCTV footage. Related Article Aviation Dozens of flights out of Sydney delayed up to 80 minutes The bureau confirmed there was damage to the Qatar plane’s nose gear and the aircraft tug. Premier Chris Minns said he was concerned about the incident. “We want to make sure that the airport’s operating at full capacity. That’s hugely important for our economy,” he said.



“We don’t want to see people disrupted if they go to the airport and services are cancelled because there’s not enough air traffic controllers … We can’t have massive delays or near misses.” An investigation into a second near miss at the airport on Wednesday is also underway, after a Qantas flight was cleared to cross a runway in front of another of the airline’s flights that had just come in to land. Both parties had been cleared to proceed by air traffic control, a Qantas spokesperson said. Sydney airport experienced lengthy delays across Friday and Saturday with more than 150 flights affected amid staff shortages at air traffic control. Chief executive of airline peak body A4ANZ Stephen Beckett previously told the Herald workers calling in sick or for carer duties were causing the network to “grind to a halt,” and calling for Airservices Australia to improve its capabilities. Airservices Australia said it was investing in training and recruitment. Ground delays attributable to the company fell by 13% year-on-year to less than 0.1% of total network delays, according to its latest financial report.



Qatar Airways has been contacted for comment. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Alleged Sydney gun-runner sexually tortured an unconscious teen for more than 10 hours, police say
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWCrime Alleged Sydney gun-runner sexually tortured an unconscious teen for more than 10 hours, police say Perry Duffin August 9, 2026 — 1:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: Graphic content An alleged Sydney gun-runner has been charged with filming the prolonged drugging and sexual torture of a teenage girl. Ararat Damirdjian, 55, was arrested in April this year after the Australian Federal Police followed a digital trail of a man importing a pistol to a home on Cunningham Street, Telopea, in the city’s west. Ararat Damirdjian has been charged with filming the prolonged drugging and sexual torture of a teenage girl. Fairfax Media The weapon, a $29 Chinese pistol that folds down into the size of a wallet, was imported under Damirdjian’s name but seized at the border, according to a police document released by the NSW Supreme Court.



Inside his home, police allegedly found 85 grams of cocaine, 32 firearms, four crossbows, a silencer, methamphetamine and “The Great Big Narcotics Cookbook”. Detectives, who pulled Damirdjian’s criminal history, realised he had an extensive criminal history for drugs and weapons and was subject to a firearms prohibition order. “Damirdjian is a long-term, high-risk offender with entrenched involvement in organised crime, large-scale drug manufacture and supply, and he has links to weapons trafficking, drug distribution, and the storage of firearms, ammunition, and explosive materials,” the court document claims. Detectives went through Damirdjian’s phone and found “highly sensitive and distressing” recordings of a young woman with a distinctive tattoo, the document says. The woman, aged 18, was unconscious but appeared completely lifeless on Damirdjian’s bed, police allege.



What Damidjian allegedly did to the woman, while recording, is too confronting to print. He allegedly administered GHB, a date-rape drug known as liquid ecstasy, through a syringe, until she passed out. Then methamphetamine was exhaled into her body, police say, on multiple occasions. ‘It is difficult to contemplate a more serious example of taking advantage of a complainant who is unable to consent in any capacity over a prolonged period of time.’ Police document released by the NSW Supreme Court “The accused repeatedly sexually assaulted the victim over a period exceeding 10 hours,” the police document says in an unusually emotive plea to the court. “It is difficult to contemplate a more serious example of taking advantage of a complainant who is unable to consent in any capacity over a prolonged period of time.”



Damidjian allegedly sent the recording to another woman, named Chantelle in court documents, telling her “girls want me to invite them back because they love partying” with him. “You know that? I was about to call the ambulance. I was f---ing scared shitless. I thought you were gonna die,” Damidjian allegedly said in one recording to the unconscious teenager. The court heard that Damidjian, who also goes by Darius Khachigian and other aliases, has spent years in prison going back to 2001, when police found firearms including military rifles, drugs and cash in his Fairfield West bedroom. Among them were a Steyr military assault rifle with laser sight, a silenced .22 pump-action rifle, detonators, explosive cord, a snake and $87,100 cash, court documents state. While in prison he linked up with a drug cook who specialised in the “Nazi-method” of manufacturing ice, and the pair ran a drug operation while on parole until Damirdjian was re-arrested in 2006.



Editor's pick Exclusive

Crime Serious sexual offenders are walking free on community orders Damirdjian asked the court to release him so he could care for his elderly mother. Police noted Damirdjian’s brother lives with their mother, but he does not. Damirdjian’s nephew offered to surrender $20,000 if his uncle skipped court. His 82-year-old mother offered to let him live with her. “I am aware of the serious charges against the applicant… (we) continue to hold a very close relationship,” she wrote in a statement. Rick Kumar and Marc Gorin, who own and operate Star Car Wash, penned letters of support for Damirdjian saying he was “vital” to the operation of the Summer Hill, Leichhardt, Blacktown, Penrith and Casula businesses.



“The site safety is of utmost importance to our staff and customers, which he managers (sic) and overseas (sic) as well (sic),” Gorin’s letter says. Damirdjian, who was refused bail, is facing drug supply, weapons and multiple counts of sexual intercourse and touching without consent. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.
