World.title: What Kiss’ approach to attack will mean for million-dollar man Suaalii
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionWallabies What Kiss’ approach to attack will mean for million-dollar man Suaalii Paul Cully August 9, 2026 — 1:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii finished the 35-32 win against Japan on the wing - and that was a preview of where he will end up under new coach Les Kiss. A number of push and pull factors are at play - including the value that Hunter Paisami offers in the way Kiss likes to attack - but ultimately Suaalii’s strengths and weaknesses are better suited to the outside backs. Wallabies outside back Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii looks set for a positional change. Getty Images The 23-year-old is a sight to behold with ball in hand - and showed it in Osaka - but his distribution isn’t good enough for an elite Test midfielder, and his defensive issues persist. Interestingly, the Wallabies picked an out-and-out midfielder on the bench for the first time this year, so Kiss might have always had a plan to have a look at Suaalii on the edge.



Paisami was a massive part of how the Reds played under Kiss, and his strong game against Japan means that a Paisami-Len Ikitau combination is likely once Ikitau returns from injury. Amatosero red card was a fair call There was a scramble to find mitigating factors after Miles Amatosero put a shoulder to the head of Japan captain Warner Dearns in the first half, but it always looked like red-card material. Loading All Blacks flanker Luke Jacobson was lucky to avoid a red card in similar circumstances for a clean-out against Ireland last month, but Amatosero can’t have real complaints.



While late changes of direction and dips in height might be relevant to tackle situations, when the tackler is caught out by a ball carrier’s dynamic movement, Amatosero has lined up Dearns from metres away and has his eyes locked on him until turning his shoulder to hit him with force. His selection was always a risky one. Perhaps the Wallabies expected Harry Hockings to start and wanted to counter his size, but as it turned out Jack Cornelsen was selected for the Brave Blossoms, and he used his greater mobility to produce a strong performance. It’s easy to understand Amatosero’s appeals to coaches, given his size, but at the moment there is a big gap between what coaches want him to be and where he actually is with his rugby. Declan Meredith gestures to a teammate during the Wallabies’ win over Japan. Getty Images Declan Meredith struggles at No.10



The Brumbies five-eighth showed great mental courage to turn around an uncertain first half and put the Wallabies in some great attacking positions with a few great touch finders. Brumbies fans will remember all too well how Meredith completely lost his way against the Hurricanes during Super Round in Christchurch. But the cold, hard reality is that Meredith won’t get away with repeats of his performance in Osaka against the Rugby Championship sides or the Six Nations teams in November. Carter Gordon ran the water in Japan and is presumably close to a return, but Ben Donaldson must be wondering what he needs to do to earn a crack at the jersey. On the flipside, there was a big positive in Tom Wright’s return to top speed and form, Harry Potter was excellent, and Josh Canham outpointed Dearns in a high-quality duel in the second row. He would have relished nicking one lineout off the giant Dearns in the first half. As far as the Kiss imprint goes, it is too early to say. However, some of the Wallabies’ ball movement and ambition was the best they have produced since the opening segment of the loss to the All Blacks in Perth last October.



Interestingly, Kiss told the Stan coverage after the Test the Wallabies had “overplayed” at times in Osaka. However, the key to unlocking this particular group of Wallabies is not to pull the reins too tightly. Billy Proctor and the All Blacks were given a stern test by their South African opposition. AP Photo/Halden Krog Stormers show what Super Rugby is missing Everyone understands the economic difficulties of putting 30 massive humans on a plane and flying them from Sydney to Cape Town or Johannesburg for two games of rugby played in the middle of the night, Australian time, and viewed only by insomniacs or tragics. Imagine trying to do that in the current climate: it’s a fast-track to bankruptcy. But watching the Stormers bully the All Blacks’ set-piece on Saturday night was a stark reminder of the high-performance cost of not having South African teams in Super Rugby.



Even though the Stormers are in preseason mode, they did a number on the All Blacks’ scrum and maul defence and exposed them under the high ball. Related Article Opinion

Wallabies There were plenty of mistakes, but the Wallabies’ win also brought plenty of satisfaction Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author The All Blacks said they knew what was coming, but the reality of playing in South Africa hit them hard, and they will have to be very fast learners to succeed on their tour of South Africa. Super Rugby Pacific has its merits, but Australian players are missing out on an education that only the South Africans can provide. The great Kolisi might not face the All Blacks



The Springboks were pushed to the last second in their 17-10 win against Los Pumas in Argentina, with Argentina replacement Matias Moroni dropping the ball with the tryline in sight. South Africa’s depth is impressive, but it is not bottomless. They will likely view the Test as perfect preparation for the All Blacks, but there will be concern after captain Siya Kolisi limped off the field after just 24 minutes. Kolisi has been struggling with a calf injury, and it looks like his participation in the first Test against the All Blacks is in real doubt. Kolisi’s ability as a rugby player, rather than a leader and talismanic figure, has always been underrated. He is a destructive force at the breakdown and a great ball carrier, so the Springboks will lose something on the field if he can’t play. Rassie Erasmus also has a big call to make at No.10. Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, also returning from injury, was very much rocks or diamonds against Argentina.

World.title: Back before Christmas: Fremantle bridge return on budget and ahead of schedule
World.content:
NationalWARoads Back before Christmas: Fremantle bridge return on budget and ahead of schedule Michael Philipps August 9, 2026 — 1:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The long-awaited return of the Fremantle traffic bridge is set to be complete before the end of the year, with the state government confirming the build is ahead of schedule and also within budget. The new Fremantle Traffic Bridge is progressing ahead of schedule, with the project on track to fully open to road users this year. The bridge was closed for the build in February and was set to be completed in the first half of 2027. However, the WA government has now stated that traffic will be back on the new build before the end of the year. “We’re happy to announce that the new bridge will be opening before Christmas,” Transport Minister Rita Saffioti said.



“There’ll be two lanes each way and works will be underway to finish the ramps in and out the bridge. “There’s also going to be a lot of terracing and landscaping done around this area too, so it’s going to be a place where people can sit and enjoy their beautiful view.” The cost of the project was updated in the recent state budget, coming in at $596 million in a 50-50 split between the WA and federal governments. Saffioti added that the closure of the bridge had seen a surge in public transport from the Fremantle area. “Weekly boardings at Fremantle Station have been up 20 per cent and parking up 30 per cent which show there’s been more people catching public transport, which has helped ease some of those traffic pressures,” she said.



“The overall river crossings have been down by one fifth, so again, it shows that people have modified their behaviour. “We’ve seen everyone really play their part in making sure that this bridge closure has gone probably smoother than anyone would have expected. “So thank you to everyone across the community for playing their part in delivering this project.” Fremantle MLA Simone McGurk acknowledged the impact the project has had on local business and thanked the community for their patience and support. “It has been hard, particularly around North Fremantle and George Street in East Fremantle,” she said.



“I thank them for their patience and also thank the community who has tried to get behind local Fremantle businesses to ensure that they can keep the doors open and keep thriving, “It’ll be so good to see the bridge now open for the summer trading period.”

World.title: ‘Punched, slapped, groped’: How the manosphere is putting teachers and students at risk
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaEducation ‘Punched, slapped, groped’: How the manosphere is putting teachers and students at risk Nicole Precel August 9, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s 11am, bleak and eight degrees outside. A classroom packed with year 9 boys is asked what their biggest fear is. “Women,” one student volunteers, “because they are mean.” The Man Cave facilitator Leeson Timms is working to tackle the rise of misogyny in classrooms and support male students’ mental health. Chris Hopkins The answer lands in The Man Cave session, a male-focused mental health charity, with awkward laughter, but the subtext is heavy. Australian schools are facing a “crisis due to rampant misogyny and sexism” fuelled by online influencers, with educators struggling to tackle it, experts say.





“I was punched [in the crotch], slapped, groped, told sexual fantasies about what I did to them in their dreams; some said they could smell fish when I walked past,” she said. Ruby, who is fighting a WorkCover claim, said she believes some of the behaviour was due to students consuming “manosphere” content, but that students’ home environments also played a role. Misogyny in schools has become so widespread, Australian Education Union deputy federal president Matt Jarman said, it has become a key reason that some female teachers are leaving the profession. “Education departments need to address this growing issue with clear policies, adequate resources and strong leadership to confront misogyny and ensure schools are safe and respectful places to work and learn.”



Data compiled exclusively for The Age by the Crime Statistics Agency found that in the past 10 years, at least 35 allegations of rape were reported and 198 alleged indecent assaults at school or reported by schools where the alleged offender was between 10 and 17 years old. Related Article Lunch with Daniel wishes the rest of the world could witness what he sees in Australia’s high schools A Victoria Police spokesperson said the data included schools reporting sex offences whether they occurred on its grounds or elsewhere. Police proactively visit schools to provide advice on the law and safety, including consent. While the data doesn’t show the gender breakdown of alleged offenders, Monash University lecturer Stephanie Wescott says research shows that males perpetrate the most sexual harm. “We have a cultural issue in schools, and I think schools are the best place to do this work because that is where young people spend most of their time,” she said.



Wescott also said teachers found that anecdotally, the schools’ “crisis due to rampant misogyny and sexism” was causing a decline in girls’ attitudes to school. “If you are a girl student sitting in a classroom, and you are seeing a [female teacher] ... and see how they are degraded, that sets up an expectation for you in how you might be treated in your lifetime.” Youth advocate and educator Daniel Principe says male students need a holistic approach to tackling the manosphere. Picture: Supplied Though the federal government’s social media ban is well-intentioned, Leeson Timms, a facilitator for The Man Cave, calls it a “band-aid over an open wound”. Timms himself was lured into the manosphere when he was in year 11, at the height of the pandemic.



Related Article Listen

Social media Who are ‘looksmaxxers’? And why are they calling other men ‘sub-human’? “It snuck in without me realising it,” he said. Timms said that before his partner helped him realise how harmful the content he was watching was, it resulted in destructive behaviour towards people in his life. For children, he says the combination of manosphere content and boys observing how “dad talks about mum” can have dire results, he said. “Boys are swimming in a pool, looking for something to hold them afloat.” Since becoming a facilitator, Timms has run almost 250 school workshops, and says about two out of every three elicit a disclosure of suicidal ideation from a male student.



At a recent full-day relationship session, facilitators worked quickly to suss out the dynamics of the group of 27 teenage boys. Initially, there was jostling and cackles, but by the end of the day, the year 9 boys had connected and opened up. One talked about how they were struggling since their dad had died, while another boy shared for the first time he wanted to kill himself. Loading Timms said boys needed direction, positive male role models, counterarguments, education about healthy masculinity, and ideally, changes to social media. “If there’s a world where there’s a possibility to change algorithms, that should be the step,” he said.



This is something the advocacy group Teach Us Consent is calling on the Australian government to investigate, saying that algorithms – which largely dictate the content we are exposed to online – are creating a “pipeline for extreme misogynistic content”. They want laws that will “fix our feeds” by introducing an opt-in feature for algorithms. “This has real consequences offline, both for victim-survivors of sexual violence and for the boys being fed this material,” a Teach Us Consent spokesperson said. If you think your son is engaging with manosphere content Youth advocate and educator Daniel Principe recommends: Stay curious, not confrontational: Ask about what he’s watching and ask him to show you. Ask him what he finds interesting about it rather than criticising it straight away.

Ask about what he’s watching and ask him to show you. Ask him what he finds interesting about it rather than criticising it straight away. Don’t shame or ridicule him: If he feels judged, he’s more likely to retreat further into the online communities reinforcing the beliefs you may be hoping to counter.

If he feels judged, he’s more likely to retreat further into the online communities reinforcing the beliefs you may be hoping to counter. Listen for the underlying need: Most boys aren’t chasing misogynistic ideas. They’re chasing confidence, belonging, success or advice on relationships they might not be getting.

Most boys aren’t chasing misogynistic ideas. They’re chasing confidence, belonging, success or advice on relationships they might not be getting. Talk about healthy masculinity and being a good human: Help him see that strength, decency and respect for others aren’t opposites, but that they can all coexist.

Help him see that strength, decency and respect for others aren’t opposites, but that they can all coexist. Make critical thinking a conversation, not a lecture: Ask what a mate would actually say about the content, or how we can know if someone online is helping or manipulating us.

Ask what a mate would actually say about the content, or how we can know if someone online is helping or manipulating us. Make sure he’s got other people to look up to: Coaches, mentors, older siblings. People who model respect and accountability in real life, not just online.

Coaches, mentors, older siblings. People who model respect and accountability in real life, not just online. Keep the conversation going: One calm chat beats one big argument every time. Most of this is curiosity, but if you’re seeing escalating anger, isolation, content for women or rigid “us vs them” thinking, don’t ignore it.

One calm chat beats one big argument every time. Most of this is curiosity, but if you’re seeing escalating anger, isolation, content for women or rigid “us vs them” thinking, don’t ignore it. Get support early from someone your son already trusts: Curiosity and connection are key. Cyber safety expert Susan McLean says Respectful Relationships, a whole-of-school program aimed at preventing gender-based violence, needs to be updated at least yearly due to the rapidly changing nature of online culture. “People can argue it’s [just] a parent’s job,” McLean said. “Everyone has to work together.”



In Victoria, the state government has invested $129 million to deliver the whole-of-school Respectful Relationships program in schools, while a further $10.4 million allocated in the most recent budget will expand the program to over 400 schools. More independent and Catholic schools have been signing up, but Wescott says there were very few “who have been willing” to implement the whole-of-school approach, which is what evidence says is the most transformative. Loading For change to happen, she said, schools needed to admit there was a problem with misogyny. “We are afraid of saying that because it implicates boys.” Tintern Grammar head of junior school principal Adam Kenny uses a whole-of-school approach and says gender equality isn’t a box to tick at the Ringwood East school, but rather something that is embedded in every element.



“It’s living and breathing it, and guiding and supporting and mentoring and rectifying immediately when mistakes are made,” he said. UNSW lecturer Alex Fleck says Australia could learn from Brazil, where an anti-misogyny bill that could send people to jail is being considered. Tintern Grammar Head of Junior School Adam Kenny says a holistic approach to tackling the manosphere and promoting gender equality are important. Picture: Supplied Modelled on existing anti-racism legislation, the proposed bill would make engaging in violence, inciting violence, or restricting a woman’s rights or dignity could result in a two- to five-year prison sentence, and rise to a sentence of three to 10 years if posted online for profit or by someone with a large following. “I don’t think that it is a stretch to say that the latter circumstance of the offence is aimed at combating manosphere online influencers,” Fleck said.

World.title: ‘Give me a freaking break’: Greens senator spells out terms on Albanese’s gambling bill
World.content:
PoliticsFederalGambling ‘Give me a freaking break’: Greens senator spells out terms on Albanese’s gambling bill Michelle Griffin August 9, 2026 — 1:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Online betting s and inducements such as free bets should be banned if Labor wants its gambling bill passed into law, Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young says, but she is prepared to negotiate on advertising in streaming services. Hanson-Young spelt out the terms the Greens want the government to meet to get their gambling bill passed in the Senate in an interview on ABC’s Insiders. “If you are not prepared to do what’s needed here, well, we’ll take this out of your hands and we’ll do it in the Senate ourselves”, Hanson-Young said in the wake of a parliamentary inquiry where sports betting companies were grilled about claims they had offered lavish free bets, sex workers and drugs to VIP clients. Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young. Alex Ellinghausen Communications Minister Anika Wells said last week she was in talks with both the Coalition and the Greens about finding a deal. Liberal Senator Sarah Henderson said on Wednesday the bill was “riddled with deficiencies and must be significantly amended”.



“Unless there is real move online, this whole thing is set up to fail. We need proper bans on online advertising,” Hanson-Young told the ABC. Opposition, cross-bench and Greens MPs joined campaigners in condemning a carve-out for streaming services in Labor’s gambling laws that allows online services to show unlimited gambling ads in breaks during matches unless subscribers explicitly opt out. Hanson-Young said she could consider a switch to a model where adults could register to get the ads during sports on streaming services. “You know, some people are suggesting an opt-in rather than an opt-out,” Hanson-Young said. “Well, I want to hear what the government has to say about that. Well, I’m prepared to entertain that.” Loading



Resolving the stalemate over this bill is a top priority when Prime Minister Anthony Albanese returns on Monday from a week’s leave. The Albanese government took more than 1000 days to respond to the bipartisan 2023 report led by the late Labor MP Peta Murphy, which recommended a national regulator, banning inducements, and a total advertising blackout. None of these recommendations were in the government’s response, which was tabled on Budget Day, Tuesday 12 May. Labor’s scaled-back proposal restricts television ads to three an hour between 6am and 8.30pm, with no cap overnight, bans the use of sports stars and other celebrities to promote gambling, bans ads on sports jerseys and limits commercials on radio during school pick-up times. Both the Greens and the Coalition have raised concerns about inducements offered by sports betting companies, such as free bets, bonus bets and other direct incentives to clients.



Gambling companies last week denied the evidence tendered by anti-gambling campaigner Tim Costello and reformed addict and ex-NRL player Luke Bateman that they lured serious addicts to VIP events with drugs, escorts and five-figure bonus bets. Related Article Gambling Coalition will force Albanese to cede ground on gambling reforms Kai Cantwell, the chief executive of industry peak body Responsible Wagering Australia, said some “pretty egregious claims have been levelled against some of my members and non-members”. Hanson-Young dismissed the argument of the corporations that special offers were not inducements but legitimate products better described as “generosities”. “Give me a freaking break,” she said. “I think they use every trick in the book to promote and it’s a real predatory nature, whether it’s special deals, whether it’s extra credits, whether it’s favours to events. Inducements need to be off the table.”



While Henderson last Monday told the inquiry she thought further action was required to regulate inducements, opposition shadow treasurer Tim Wilson told News24 (formerly Sky News) there was a diversity of views within the Coalition on the bill. He said he was chiefly concerned with protecting children from too much exposure to gambling ads, and that online ads were examined. “There are a lot of other platforms people watch sports these days and receive gambling advertising as well,” he said. Labor frontbencher Jenny McAllister refused to say on News24 if the government was looking to change inducements, but noted: “We think we’ve broadly got the legislation right, but if there are sensible amendments that could improve the bill, of course we’re open to discussion across the parliament.”

World.title: How to spot if something has been written by AI
World.content:
TechnologyAI How to spot if something has been written by AI The Economist August 9, 2026 — 1:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ghost writer is haunting the English language. The linguistic spectre can turn its hand to prose, poetry, journalese and corporate jargon. It is frightfully versatile: you can get it to mimic Shakespeare’s sonnets or a schlocky beach read; Ernest Hemingway’s taut prose or the office-printer manual. It is frightfully fast, churning out thousands of words a minute. (Hemingway rarely produced as many in a day, and required much more booze.) Wordsmiths are spooked. AI prose is distinguishable by word and punctuation choice as well as sentence and paragraph structure. But its hallmarks are not what you might expect, partly because its writing style has changed with software updates. Bloomberg AI writing is everywhere. It is in your inbox and on your LinkedIn feed. It is all over the internet, drafting more than a third of new websites by one count. Large language models (LLMs) are helping students write essays and probably helping scientists write papers. Some allege AI-generated prose won the Commonwealth Short Story prize this year, with judges praising its “quiet authority”. (The Commonwealth Foundation denied the claim.) LLMs have stylistic quirks. They are thought to maximise the use of long em-dashes—and the use of words like “maximise”. They like to “deep dive” (and, better yet, “delve”) into the “rich tapestry” of the world. AI writing is not about a single word or phrase, but a rich tapestry of things. Spotting AI texts can be tricky. This is in part because you need evidence beyond a few words or dashes: claiming that a text is by an LLM because it uses the word “delve” is like claiming one is by Jane Austen because it uses “imprudence”. Bots also write in slightly different ways. There is no single style of AI writing, explains Karolina Rudnicka, a linguist at the University of Gdansk in Poland, just as there is no single style of human writing. Writers have idiosyncrasies—Emily Dickinson, for instance, loved em-dashes—and bots may do, too.



But there are a few ways to identify LLM-generated text. One is to use detection algorithms that are trained to spot the texture of human or AI prose. Pangram, a leading firm, claims to have 99.98 per cent accuracy. (It has partnered with Substack, a blogging platform, on such a tool.) Detectors, however, are black-box algorithms that can give false positives. They do not give reasons for why they reach their conclusions. Related Article Opinion

Tripologist Is AI better at travel advice than me? I put it to the test Michael Gebicki The Tripologist Researchers have also tried scouring texts for suspicious words or comparing papers from before and after LLMs were made available to the public. But these approaches have drawbacks too, not least because it is hard to disentangle AI quirks from other language trends. You can discover AI’s hallmarks by comparing the writing of man and machine. To do this you need a baseline that is distinctive and familiar. The Economist turned to prose that we’re sure is human and that readers will recognise: our own. We designed a study to ask top LLMs—OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, Google’s Gemini and xAI’s Grok—to write versions of our articles without consulting the web. (As a prompt, we gave them the AI-generated summaries that we have experimentally added to some of our articles.) This gave us a corpus of human and AI creations and we compared them across 55,940 sentences and 1.2 million words. To make sure we were detecting AI quirks rather than our own, we also checked the AI texts against journalism from CNN, the New York Times and the Washington Post. Excerpts from hit novels published between 1950 and 2022 offered another test.



Our findings are surprising. AI prose is distinguishable by word and punctuation choice as well as sentence and paragraph structure. But its hallmarks are not what you might expect, partly because its writing style has changed with software updates. That does not mean that LLMs are great writers: their prose lacks lucidity and elegance and is often formulaic. So those aspiring to be impressive (human) storytellers should avoid the following peculiarities in their own prose. Loading First, consider words. The vocabulary that bots overuse has changed: they no longer “delve” and there are not as many “tapestries”. Instead they offer a significant number of polysyllables like “significant”, “increasingly” and “consequences”. They use more rare words (“interdependence”, “reindustrialisation”) and scientific lingo (“parameter”, “methodology”) than humans, and are fond of nominalisations (making nouns from verbs, such as “expansion” from “expand”). All the LLMs in our study use such words, but particularly Gemini and Claude. Much of this language could be described as what George Orwell called “pretentious diction”. He railed against writers who “dress up simple statements” with complicated words and jargon to sound clever. Such pontificating penmen, Orwell observed, also believe that “Latin or Greek words are grander than Saxon ones”. (Bots agree: more Latinate suffixes crop up in their writing than in human texts.) Then look at punctuation. Many believe LLMs stuff their prose with em-dashes, but that is not true after the most recent updates. Today only Claude uses more em-dashes than human writers, with ChatGPT using markedly fewer than any other writer in our study. Humans rejoice—and start using dashes again.



A better way to spot AI-generated writing would be to look for texts without much punctuation at all. LLMs are very Joycean about it: they use fewer commas and semicolons than humans (and hardly any parentheses). They use less punctuation in part because they write longer sentences—“and” is their most overused word—and in part because they do not quote experts. Related Article AI AI used to create new viruses in the lab Finally, study the sentence. Bots’ sentences tend to be long; paragraphs are rarely interrupted with short, punchy statements. How dull. When LLMs want to make their sentences more lively, they often reach for a rhetorical device. Their favourites include: “not X but Y”, “not only but also” and the “rule of three”. (Grouping ideas in threes makes them more engaging, as we did just then.) ChatGPT and Claude use more of these constructions per 1,000 sentences than other LLMs and humans. So if you want to spot AI writing, look for bland, pretentious prose lavished with Latinate words—at least for now. With every update, our study shows, AI writing is becoming more similar to human prose. Pangram successfully detected AI-generated copy, but may struggle in future. LLMs are trained on human writing and learn from human feedback, notes Tommie Juzek of Florida State University, picking up things people find impressive and dropping things they do not. Bots learn fast, too. Take ChatGPT: until very recently it used an em-dash in almost every sentence. When your correspondent asked an older model whether it thought AI overused the dash, it said: “Ha—great question!” Ask the bot the same thing today and it soberly says “they’re best used sparingly.” Only a ghost could shapeshift so quickly.

World.title: It’s Gang of Youths - but not how you remember them
World.content:
Concert Hall, Sydney Opera House, August 8

“Thanks for letting us play the show we want to play,” says Gang of Youths frontman David Le’aupepe as the evening draws to a close.

The show they wanted to play eschews the bluster, adrenaline, and stadium-filling affectations that have long been the Sydney-born, London-based band’s trademark. Instead, we get something more thoughtful, restrained and effortlessly confident.

Gang of Youths got to play the show they wanted to play. Jess Gleeson

It’s in the way Le’aupepe begins the performance – the group’s first in Australia in three years – sitting solo at the piano, teasing the opening chords of goal of the century.

While on record the song is a string-soaked epic with peaks and valleys and lavish production flourishes, here it is naked, fragile and breathtakingly delicate.

It sets the tone for an evening in which the band – now an eight-piece in the live setting – bypass many of their hits, and deconstruct those they do play to breathe new life into the material.

By performing the normally rousing Magnolia solo on guitar, Le’aupepe lends even more desperation to the song’s cry for help.

The Deepest Sighs, the Frankest Shadows is slowed to half time, surging with a newfound power complemented by the harmonies of singer-songwriter Gretta Ray, who provides backing vocals.

Do Not Let Your Spirit Wane starts smaller than its recorded form, the band teasing it to a powerful and majestic climax; Let Me Down Easy adds more nuance to its motorik strut, and is sexier for it.

A handful of new songs are debuted, hinting at an evolution in the outfit’s forthcoming fourth album.

Things Take Time is soulful and quietly joyous, with trumpet lines lending it a Burt Bacharach-esque lightness; in another, country-leaning song “about tarot cards” the horn adds a more desolate touch.

Peppering the set with moments of levity and humour adds to the sense that this is a group comfortable in their own skin – witness the cover of Jimmy Buffett’s A Pirate Looks at Forty, complete with onstage margaritas and dedicated to Le’aupepe’s wife, who turned 39 days earlier.

That it all looks so effortless is a trick only the truly great acts can pull off.

World.title: Hato Hone St John declares major incident as demand for ambulances spikes
World.content:
Hato Hone St John has activated its major incident response following its busiest single day on record.

The move comes after the ambulance service also saw a week of sustained high demand. That is expected to continue on Monday.

On Saturday, 2562 calls came into the ambulance service through 111 - the highest number received in a single day. A normal day would see around 1900 calls.

Hato Hone St John director of ambulance operations Doug Gallagher said it was the third time the daily record had been broken this week, with 2404 calls received on Monday, 3 August, and 2454 calls received on Thursday, 6 August.

Gallagher explained the ambulance service's concerns at a press conference on Sunday afternoon, as St John confirmed the major incident response.

"All three days were busier than any recorded during the Covid-19 pandemic or on traditionally high-volume dates such as New Year's Eve. At the peak, emergency call handlers were answering a call every 20 seconds," he said.

By 2pm on Sunday, the ambulance service had received 15,268 calls this week. It is set to beat the previous weekly record of 15,289 calls, which was set between 27 July and 2 August.

Before that, the busiest week on record had seen 14,984 calls. That record was set between 25 and 31 August in 2025.

"Saturday is not normally our busiest day, so this level of demand is highly unusual," Gallagher said.

"Our emergency ambulance staff are continuing to respond effectively, but the workload is not showing the signs of easing that we would normally expect over a weekend.

"With demand remaining high and Mondays typically bringing the greatest workload, we are preparing for further pressure."

On Saturday, 2562 calls came into the ambulance service through 111. St John / Supplied

Declaring a major incident and activating its Emergency Operations Centre was "an early and precautionary decision" to ensure it could keep giving effective care during a period of unprecedented demand, Gallagher said.

"We want to reassure people that emergency ambulance help remains available, and we are continuing to respond to those who need us.

"Our first priority is patient safety. Ambulance staff continue to prioritise people with life-threatening and time-critical conditions."

People with less urgent conditions may experience longer waits than usual. A person calling 111 may receive alternative support instead of an ambulance response if deemed appropriate, St John said in a statement to media.

"These are clinically led decisions based on the individual patient's condition and needs. They are about providing the right care, at the right time and in the right place," Gallagher added.

According to Hato Hone St John, the major incident response gives the ambulance service a clear national structure for coordinating decisions and resources at pace. The Emergency Operations Centre brings teams together to maintain a detailed national view of demand and ambulance availability.

World.title: Timor-Leste: The new tourism frontier
World.content:
For the adventurous traveller, finding somewhere genuinely undiscovered has become almost impossible. Modern travel, globalisation and social media have left few blank spaces on the map. One country, however, has so far escaped mass tourism: Timor-Leste, a peaceful nation with a complicated history, a distinctive culture and a special bond with New Zealand. Anna Thomas reports.

Timor-Leste, or East Timor, is a name most New Zealanders would recognise but few could probably locate on a map. The most direct route is by flying to Bali, then taking a two-hour flight to the capital of Dili. But while Bali attracts 16 million visitors a year, Timor-Leste receives just 26,000, even then, most of those are ex-pats or business travellers.

Change, though, is arriving quickly. Since joining ASEAN in October 2025, development in this small South East Asian nation has accelerated. New hotels and restaurants are opening, roads are being sealed, and the international airport is undergoing a US$240 million upgrade.

With Timor-Leste due to chair ASEAN in 2029, a large convention centre is under construction on Dili's waterfront and thousands of political leaders, media and visitors are expected.

Supplied/Anna Thomas

Roughly the size of Hawke's Bay, the country has a population of 1.4 million. It has a rich and complex history marked by colonisation, conflict and occupation but as 'independent' Timor-Leste, its history is still being written.

It remains the poorest country in South East Asia, with almost half its people living below the poverty line. Ironically though it is also one of the most expensive countries with the majority of its goods imported. While oil and gas reserves remain the country's main revenue earner, tourism is increasingly seen as a potential golden goose.

A Kiwi connection

Diane Clayton has been living in Timor-Leste for a year. After 10 years with Tourism New Zealand, she and husband Tristam decided they needed an adventure. She signed up with Volunteer Service Abroad with the plan to help Timor-Leste develop eco-tourism. While the well-travelled couple were given a lengthy brief before arriving, she says nothing can quite prepare you.

"It's really quite a crazy place", she laughs "especially the lack of infrastructure, the heat, and the pollution. But very quickly we were made to feel at ease because the Timorese are so friendly."

VSA worker Diane Clayton with Timor-Leste Forestry Rangers. Supplied/Diane Clayton

Clayton has been working alongside tourism operators sharing her knowledge on everything from marketing to basic customer service. She explains that very few of the locals have experienced being a tourist themselves sowhen you're advising on hospitality you're starting from scratch.

And while health and safety wasn't part of her job description, Clayton discovered first hand, it needed to become a priority.

"On day two of my job I was asked if I'd like to join a group of Australian tour operators heading to Atauro Island."

The island is roughly 36km from Dili, about 1.5 hours by a small boat, and it has one of the world's most biodiverse coral reefs. The waters around Timor-Leste also have at least 24 species of whales and dolphins living or travelling through them. Clayton says the weather wasn't ideal and from the beginning she had a bad feeling.

"Because of the wind and swells the trip was on-again off-again but the call was made to proceed. There were 14 of us in a 10 person boat with no lifejackets.

The trip over was OK but when we arrived visibility wasn't good enough for snorkelling. So we had lunch and decided to return to Dili. However, halfway across the channel, the boat just stopped. We had run out of gas."

Diane and Tristram Clayton on Atauro Island. Supplied/Diane Clayton

The crew couldn't speak English and refused to use the boat radio but luckily there was some phone coverage. "Calls were being made but because of the deteriorating weather no one wanted to bring out extra fuel. As the hours ticked by, and the seas got rougher passengers were scared and a few of them were throwing up.

Finally, after waiting four hours, help arrived." Clayton told me it was the first time she had ever feared for her life.

As a result of that incident, Clayton has been working on health a safety protocols. But like most things in the country, developing industry standards is a work in progress.

One of the many picturesque rivers around Timor-Leste. Supplied/Anna Thomas

VSA volunteers like Clayton have been making a small but important contribution in the tourism sector. Clayton's predecessor, Jonty Crane, spent a year producing tourism videos and articles that remain the country's most visible promotional material online.

Australian expat Barry Hinton, who owns 'Barry's Place' one of Atauro Island's original eco-resorts credits Crane with doing more for Timorese tourism than anyone else. Hinton arrived in 2001 to teach English, later settling on Atauro and marrying locally.

Up to 85 percent of guests at 'Barry's Place' are Australians who are drawn to the island's marine environment.

Barry Hinton is an ex-pat Australian who owns the ecolodge Barry's Place on Atauro Island. Supplied/Anna Thomas

Hinton employs 30 local staff, doesn't advertise and books entirely through WhatsApp. His main frustration is bureaucracy. "The laws are changed all the time," he says.

"They (government) want investment, they want tourism, but they don't get how difficult they've made it." Still, he stays for the lifestyle. "It's just the rawness and the beauty of a very simple life and meeting guests who want an ethical holiday."

The next generation

'Friendly' and 'resilient' are the two words most commonly used to describe Timorese. Despite the poverty, the people of Timor-Leste are always smiling.

Mateus Varela Belo de Almeida is a 24-year-old tour guide from Dili. He is sharp, enthusiastic and hungry to learn. He started work in a car rental firm and when customers kept asking for recommendations of what to do and where to go, he saw an opportunity.

He's been running his business MaunTimor Guide for three years.

Varela Belo de Almeida says because Timor-Leste is an expensive country, it's not really suited to backpackers. Most of his clients are Australians and some New Zealanders, who want to learn more about the country where many of their soldiers served first in WWII and then again from 1999 as part of a multinational force restoring peace to the newly independent country.

Mateus Varela Belo de Almeida, 24, has been guiding tourists around Timor-Leste for three years. Supplied/Mateus Varela Belo de Almeida

Varela Belo de Almeida says an ideal itinerary is about six days; a couple of days in Dili, visiting Christo Rei (a smaller version of Rio's Christ the Redeemer), Santa Cruz cemetery, markets and museums, then Baucau to see Portuguese architecture, and then up to the remote and pristine Jaco Island.

Supplied/Mateus Varela Belo de Almeida

He says getting around the island can be challenging. "The roads can be dangerous at times and you could travel for hours only to discover the guest house you booked has increased the price, given away your room or has run out of food."

A typical washed out road in Timor-Leste. Supplied/Anna Thomas

While guiding can't support him full time yet, he says the knowledge and expertise he's received through Clayton has been invaluable. "I have learnt so much in her workshops on story-telling, hospitality and customer service, and especially marketing. I'm hoping as a result business will grow."

As Clayton's one year posting comes to an end she says volunteering gives you a rare insight and access to this young nation.

She is looking forward to returning in a few years to see how the country has developed. And for those considering visiting Timor-Leste, Clayton has some advice. "Come with your eyes wide open. Have low expectations and you'll be delighted."

World.title: National promises Budget Responsibility Rules if elected
World.content:
The National Party are calling on Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori to release their plans to get New Zealand back into surplus.

The party has committed to three so-called Budget Responsibility Rules aimed at returning to surplus, cutting debt and keeping taxes low, and promise to adhere to them if re-elected as a bulwark against economic shocks.

National leader Christopher Luxon said an economy that cannot support itself was both a financial and strategic risk.

"If the Crown's own books aren't in order, the whole country stays exposed and vulnerable to major shocks here at home and abroad."

Luxon said the government had historically carried less debt than other developed countries as a buffer against crises, but that buffer had "eroded considerably."

"Rebuilding it is what allows a future government of whatever colour to meet the next earthquake, the next pandemic, the next global disruption without a fiscal crisis on top of the actual crisis it has to deal with," he said.

The Budget Responsibility Rules

Prioritising a return to surplus in 2028/29 and staying in surplus over time so the country's debt curve bends down

Getting debt down below 40 percent of GDP and keeping it there over time

Keeping taxes low by cutting Crown expenditure as a share of the economy down towards 30 percent of GDP

Finance spokesperson Nicola Willis said those rules were the "fiscal guard-rails" her party intended to follow, and it "well past time" for parties to set out their own.

"I accept the premise that says they are not yet in a position to provide a detailed fiscal plan, however, they should be well able to say whether they will commit to these three basic things that have informed the fiscal strategies of successive governments and which represents what it is to be a responsible fiscal manager," she said.

National's finance spokesperson Nicola Willis. RNZ/Samuel Rillstone

Willis said it was "striking" to her that Labour and the Greens set out their own fiscal rules leading up to the 2017 election but had not yet released theirs.

"As I stand here today I am not even aware whether they believe a surplus target is appropriate where they think debt should be or whether or not they believe that we need to reduce core crown spending in order to keep taxes low. "

"Those are very basic questions and they do form the parameters for National's campaign."

Asked if National would commit to not imposing new taxes if elected, Willis said there would be "no new taxes on working people".

Pushed again, she said the party's tax policies would be released over the course of the election.

"Listen to me very carefully, no new taxes on working people... what New Zealanders can expect is no new taxes on their work, their savings, their investments or their capital," she said.

Budget 2026 forecasted a return to a budget surplus in 2028/29 from a mix of an increased tax take, controls on government spending, capital projects and a reduction in borrowing and debt service costs.

ACT leader David Seymour. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Three years too late - ACT's Seymour

ACT leader David Seymour said National's promise to follow the rules was three years too late.

In a statement, Seymour said saving money took courage.

"Reducing spending to 30 percent of GDP sounds impressive, but [former Labour finance minister] Grant Robertson spent only 28 percent in his first two budgets before he lost all control during Covid. Today the government is spending 32.6 percent of GDP and isn't forecast to go below 30 this decade.

"Achieving 30 percent of GDP will take real courage to face down the causes of higher spending. They are rising superannuation and health costs, rising welfare costs, and the size and complexity of cabinet and government departments."

Seymour said his party had a track record of taking on hard issues, pointing to changes to pay equity and the school lunch programme.

"National wanted to spend $380 [million] on a medical school, we negotiated it down to $80 million. They wanted to spend $250 million on electric car chargers, we got it down to a repayable loan of $60 million. National wanted to pay out $375 million in tax credits for fuel, even if the price went back down.

"ACT may still save the taxpayer hundreds of millions more with the sensible suggestion that the payments end when fuel prices normalise."

He said ACT "killed" three new taxes while in government.

"Without ACT we would be seeing taxes on housing, tourism and banks that are all ultimately paid by New Zealanders and their businesses. Controlling spending is only half the equation, controlling taxes is the other half ... the taxpayer would be on the hook for billions more, but even more savings are needed," he said.

Labour finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Rules nothing new - Labour's Edmonds

Labour finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds told RNZ National's fiscal rules were nothing new.

"That's what is already in their fiscal strategy as a government. This just seems like it's putting fake pressure on the rest of the political parties to try and keep up with them."

Edmonds said Labour did have to "put the umbrella up" during the pandemic but "that's what every government does to make sure that you can buffer an economic shock".

"But their track record over the three years has made things worse. We have businesses in record liquidation, we have families who are having to make a choice between food or fuel.

"The government really needs to have a look in the mirror about what they're trying to say to New Zealand, as opposed to just constantly blaming Labour."

The party would release its fiscal strategy when it was ready.

"That's because we are announcing it in our time, not just out of fake pressure from the National Party and Nicola Willis," Edmonds said.

Green Party co-leader Chloe Swarbrick. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Rules silly and meaningless - Greens' Swarbrick

Green Party co-leader Chloe Swarbrick told RNZ the rules were silly and meaningless.

"If all it takes for you to meet your goals is to set goals or KPIs that are completely untethered from improving people's lives, then sure, well done, you're hitting your bingo card," she said.

"But people's lives aren't getting any better, and I think that makes you a pretty bloody irresponsible government."

Swarbrick said the rules could stand in the way of critical infrastructure investment.

World.title: Alert warns Ohakune residents of water outage after quake damage
World.content:
An emergency mobile alert has been sent to Ohakune residents as the central North Island town faces a water crisis.

The water supply has been turned off after the pipeline supplying the ski town's reservoir broke in last month's 5.9 earthquake near Taumarunui.

Residents and visitors are being told not to use tap water or flush toilets, and to conserve supplies.

Water tankers and portable toilets had been set up in the town, Horizons Regional Council chair Nikki Riley said.

"The reservoir has been drained, so it takes time for that reservoir to refill and then for the treatment to come through.

"But until then, the good people of Tongariro Water will be supplying water for the township."

Tap water was not expected to be restored until 5pm Monday. If restored before then, the water would need to be boiled before use, the council said.

It warned against using public toilets.

Drinking water was available at various locations around the town, it said.

Nearly 1400 people live in Ohakune but the population can double or treble during the ski season.

Drinking water

Bottled water: Ruapehu District Council office, 38 Ayr St; Thames St opposite the Powderhorn; Goldfinch St/Shannon St corner; rear car park of the Ohakune iSite; Clyde St car park; Moore St outside Top 10 Holiday Park.

Water tanker: Council office. Please reuse empty 5-litre bottles and refill them there.

World.title: Greens propose $2.4b funding to back 'critical' marae
World.content:
The Green Party is campaigning on establishing a $2.4 billion trust dedicated to marae.

Co-leader Marama Davidson said marae were critical infrastructure and needed funding certainty to continue their work responding to weather emergencies and supporting communities.

Te Rangatiratanga Trust would be owned and governed by hapū and iwi, with $2.44 billion of government investment over four years.

There would be two funds within that: the $2 billion Te Tōtara Haemata Intergenerational Fund, dedicated to long-term investment in marae and their communities; and the $400 million Te Rākau Whakarauora Restoration Fund, which would provide immediate access to funding for urgent needs.

The trust would cost about $40 million to set up and run.

Davidson said the intergenerational fund could return between $47 million and $118 million once it had matured.

"This funding recognises that marae have been critical infrastructure for a long, long time, and supports marae to do even more."

She said marae voluntarily stepped up during weather emergencies, feeding and housing locals and tourists who needed it. The investment would ensure they were appropriately funded to do so.

"But it will also support marae to do longer-term planning, climate-resilience planning, adaptation planning, housing, social services, health services," she said.

The Greens would run nationwide wānanga to establish the trust, the two funds and governance mechanisms.

Iwi Māori would design it and decide where funding would go, Davidson said.

"This is actual tino rangatiratanga for iwi," she said.

"It might take about a year with wānanga throughout the motu to sort of figure out and design exactly how the funds will be distributed."

World.title: Youth accused of murdering Napier teen Kaea Karauria to face trial in October
World.content:
A youth charged with the murder of Napier 15-year-old Kaea Karauria is due to face trial this year.

A three-week trial has been scheduled to begin in the High Court at Palmerston North on 27 October.

The 16-year-old defendant's name has been suppressed, as have other details of the case.

Kaea died in the early hours of 11 May, 2025.

He was discovered critically injured with stab wounds on Alexander Ave in Napier by police responding to reports of disorder at a birthday party nearby.

He died at the scene despite the efforts of ambulance staff to save him.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Family Court orders no contact after father’s ‘uninhibited, dysregulated’ and abusive behaviour
World.content:
WARNING: This story contains content that may be disturbing to some readers.

When a woman's ex-partner stood outside the Family Court courtroom during proceedings, staring at her through a door window, the woman gasped, curled into a foetal position and tried to move as far away from his sight as possible.

The moment followed years of volatile behaviour, false allegations and intimidation of professionals.

A judge later described the man's conduct as "uninhibited, dysregulated, and at times, frankly abusive", both inside and outside the courtroom.

With no agency willing to supervise him and a pattern of behaviour that placed his children and former partner at ongoing risk, the court has now made the rare decision that his children have no contact with him.

The decision was released in a Family Court ruling by Judge Stephen Coyle, bringing eight years of litigation to an end. The family has automatic name suppression.

The court heard the relationship ended after a family barbecue when the man argued with others before leaving with his partner and children in the car.

During the journey home, he drove at 120km/h and the mother told the court she feared for their lives.

The incident was recorded and played to the judge, who noted it was "a distressing incident to watch".

The man was heard saying, "You know what I'm f***ing capable of, I'll go for your dad's f***ing throat",** and telling everyone to shut up when asked to stop.

When they got home, the woman said he did a doughnut in the driveway and drove at speed towards the carport before abruptly stopping.

He took the woman's phone and, as she was crying, she said he licked her tears and said: "Hmmm, I love the way they taste."

The woman later applied for a temporary protection order (TPO) and an interim parenting order with supervised access, which were granted. But the TPO was not made final and was discharged a year later.

Months later, unsupervised access was granted to the father but, in 2022, he alleged his children were being sexually abused and did not return them.

The woman applied for a warrant to enforce the parenting order and the children were returned to her care.

Oranga Tamariki (OT) investigated the allegations and found no evidence of abuse, but the father continued raising his concerns with authorities.

In December 2022, the father took one of the children to an emergency department alleging she had suffered a head injury, but staff became concerned about his behaviour.

He reportedly yelled at a nurse, telling her to "f*** off", and a report of concern was made to OT.

OT visited the father days later and reported he was agitated and unable to hold a direct line of conversation. The social workers became frightened by his presentation and left.

He again refused to return the children and the mother had to file another application for a warrant, which was granted.

The same day, the man had taken the girls to a police station to report the allegations of abuse.

Oranga Tamariki (OT) investigated the allegations and found no evidence of abuse from the mother, but the father continued raising his concerns with authorities. NZME / Supplied

Unbeknownst to him, the warrant had been issued for the children to be uplifted, and police executed it at the station.

"This was not a straightforward process. [The father] was understandably upset that the warrant had been granted given his belief that the girls were at risk in their mother's care," Judge Coyle said in the decision.

"He had to be arrested by the police and removed so that [the children] could be returned to their mother's care."

After being released, he turned up to an OT office and when staff became afraid, he was removed and a trespass order was issued.

He then called 111 and claimed his children had been taken.

School concerns

According to the decision, the children's school gave evidence to the Family Court that it became concerned about the father's behaviour, particularly when he turned up to a "funky fun day" event and took photos of children and staff.

He then posted the photos online with derogatory comments and the school implemented a lockdown policy if he was sighted near the school.

The mother was granted another interim protection order, which became final when the man did not file any opposition.

She was also granted a further variation of the parenting order, reinstating supervised access for the father.

But supervised contact could not proceed because the provider terminated its contract due to his behaviour.

He then filed an application seeking day-to-day care and the discharge of the parenting order, which proceeded to a hearing.

Several delays occurred before the eight-day hearing, including the father failing to file evidence and two assigned senior lawyers withdrawing from acting for him.

Lawyer Michael Roots was eventually assigned and Judge Coyle commended his role.

"My observation was that Mr Roots showed enormous forbearance in the face of, at times, rude and belligerent attacks by [the father]."

Court behaviour

The judge found that during the cross-examination of the mother, the father used the process to psychologically abuse her.

For days, the man routinely interrupted the judge and would loudly interrupt his lawyer with questions he wanted asked of the woman.

"During the last session of the first day of the hearing I had to ask [the father] to leave the courtroom as his behaviour in court had become untenable," the decision said.

"He did so, but then stood at the door peering into the courtroom through the window and was staring directly at [the mother] and in doing so he was breaching the protection order.

"When she saw him [as the screen used did not shield her from that view] she instantly gasped, scooted in her chair as far away as she could in the witness box, curled up into the foetal position on the chair, and stated, 'He's staring, I mean he's just right there in the doorway'."

The judge described her distress as instinctive and visceral.

At the hearing, the father claimed he was the victim of family violence at the hands of the woman, but the judge ruled he had no evidence to support the allegations.

Judge Coyle said that when questioned about the barbecue incident, the man claimed his ex-partner was drunk and that he had been acting in self-defence.

"His evidence was chilling in his attempt to blame her. The video speaks for itself," the judge said.

"His language towards her was abusive and dismissive, he essentially tried to shut her down so that she had no voice or agency in her distress. It was behaviour designed to belittle, antagonise, frighten, demean and diminish [the mother].

"There is no evidence that [the mother] was drunk as asserted by [the father]. He is simply making that up in an attempt to victim-blame."

Intimidating professionals

The court also heard evidence that Family Court staff had been reduced to tears by the man's behaviour, particularly a senior Family Court practitioner.

"There are patterns in relation to [the father's] interactions with virtually every person or agency he has come into contact with which have caused people to be concerned for their physical and/or psychological safety.

"My assessment therefore is that there is an extremely high risk of future family harm to [the mother] in particular if the protection order was discharged."

The judge directed the protection order be made final and made a rare order granting sole care of the children to the mother with no contact for the father.

"His behaviour in court, at a time in which [the father] should have been on his best behaviour while the gaze of the court was on him, was uninhibited, dysregulated, and at times, frankly abusive and intimidating," Judge Coyle said.

"In order to protect [the children], there could only be supervised contact with [the father]. But there is no agency willing to supervise [his] contact with these girls.

"I therefore have determined that an order should be made that [the children] are to have no contact with [the father]."

The judge also ruled the man's behaviour amounted to litigant abuse and ordered that he not file any new proceedings against his ex-partner for three years.

World.title: Labour promises small businesses easier access to government contracts
World.content:
The Labour Party would make it easier for small businesses to get government contracts and cut down the time they spend on paperwork, if elected.

The party would set a target so 15 percent of government contracts went to small businesses and start-ups. It would also break up bigger contracts into smaller jobs so work was easier to bid for.

Labour also wants to change how government agencies share information. It is proposing a New Zealand Business Number so businesses would not have to give the same information to multiple agencies.

Finance and economy spokesperson Barbara Edmonds said in a media release that the government bought around $50 billion of goods and services annually.

"Small business owners don't want a handout, they just want a fair go," she said.

"Government is the biggest customer in the country, buying around $50 billion of goods and services annually. That means huge opportunities for local businesses, from printing and landscaping to IT and building maintenance," she said.

Revenue spokesperson Deborah Russell said paperwork and compliance costs wasted too much time and money and the party would review tax administration, including provisional tax, filing requirements and January and February deadline pile-ups.

World.title: Infantino denies 'defamatory' affair claims made in British newspaper
World.content:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino, who has endured a week of scathing criticism revolving around the now shelved private investment plan for the World Cup, has been accused by a British newspaper of paying off an alleged lover while at UEFA.

According to The Daily Telegraph, the Italian-Swiss lawyer, who served as secretary general of European football's governing body from 2009 to 2016, also previously used his influence to secure a promotion for the same UEFA employee with whom he was in an intimate relationship.

Infantino has categorically denied the allegations, according to the article which was published late on Friday.

When contacted by AFP on Saturday, a FIFA spokesperson had not responded.

According to The Telegraph, which did not cite its sources, this employee received a "a six-figure sum" upon her departure – at an unspecified time – in addition to the payment of tuition fees for a business school amounting to around 45,000 British pounds ($85,900).

Gianni Infantino (right) in 2007 when he was UEFA's deputy general secretary. (Getty Images: Etsuo Hara)

When contacted by AFP, UEFA acknowledged that "a departure payment was made to the individual in question" at that time, "coupled with the payment of fees for an MBA course at a local business school".

However, it insisted "the payment was in line with the regulations that existed for departing staff at the time", before adding that "such regulations have been tightened since 2016".

Quoted by The Telegraph, a FIFA spokesperson stated that Infantino, who has been married since 2001, "strongly denies these allegations", which were "categorically untrue".

"Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory," FIFA added.

"No employee at UEFA and FIFA has ever raised a complaint regarding Infantino's behaviour because there never was an incident where he was involved."

Infantino, who is standing for re-election next March, has been embroiled in a crisis since the announcement late last month of his controversial — and ultimately abandoned — plan to open up the World Cup to private investors.

He faces opposition in particular from UEFA, which on Thursday stood by its threat to boycott the World Cups, deeming the mere withdrawal of the controversial plan to be insufficient.

Infantino maintains substantial support

Following a crisis meeting in Morocco on Wednesday, FIFA apologised to its 211 member associations for mistakes in the handling of the proposal and said its leadership had reaffirmed its full support for Infantino.

The fallout has cast a shadow over Infantino's bid for a fourth term at the FIFA Congress in Morocco next year. No clear candidate to challenge him has yet emerged.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino (left) has faced criticism from President of the Football Association of Norway Lise Klaveness (right). (Getty Images: Jean Catuffe)

UEFA has said it no longer has confidence in Infantino, while Norwegian Football Federation President Lise Klaveness called for him to resign on Friday, saying he no longer had the institutional trust required to govern FIFA.

But Infantino continues to enjoy substantial support among FIFA's 211 members. The Confederation of African Football (CAF) unanimously backed his leadership on Thursday, while South America's CONMEBOL rejected any attempt to oust him that did not involve a vote of all FIFA members.

Mexico's football federation (FMF) also backed Infantino, despite its regional confederation CONCACAF having called for a "comprehensive reckoning" with his presidency.

"The FMF will neither recognise nor approve any process convened outside of that institutional framework," the Mexican federation said.

AFP/Reuters

World.title: Australian Beacroft smashes U20 world record to continue golden form
World.content:
Australia's Isaac Beacroft has maintained his stunning golden streak with a record-breaking victory in the 5km race walk at the world athletics under-20 championships in the US.

Beacroft's sizzling win in Eugene, Oregon, follows his Commonwealth Games gold medal just over a week ago in the 10km race walk in Glasgow.

Victory in Oregon means he now has the prestigious world U20 championships and Commonwealth Games gold-medal double.

​Beacroft also broke the world record in Oregon at the famous Hayward Field, his time of 18:40.37 smashing more than seven seconds off the previous mark.

"I'm over the moon, I couldn't be happier," the Australian said after his stunning victory on Saturday (local time).

"I knew coming in it was going to be so hard. It definitely was pretty hard, so I'm just so happy to get it done.

"It's a massive relief. I felt a fair bit of pressure going into this one, you are a Commonwealth champion, [people think] surely it's a walk in the park to do juniors.

"It's definitely not. I have raced each race to its merits, I don't know what is harder.

"I'm stoked to have won both, that's all I can say on that.''

Beacroft's world-record time meant he beat silver medallist Huajia Pu by more than three seconds, the Chinese athlete clocking 18:43.70.

Third place went to Italy's Nicolo' Vidal, more than 12 seconds behind in a time of 18:56.19.

Despite the impressive nature of his victory, Beacroft said it was difficult to come straight from Glasgow to Oregon.

"I had a day or two after my race to try and freshen up,'' he said.

"I didn't really freshen up there, I went out with the Commonwealth Games boys and girls.

"I didn't go too hard on the partying, but there was some definitely done, then it was pretty rough to travel here.

"There was a delay with the plane, but I think getting here and getting around the whole team has given me a real lift."

In another impressive result, the Australian team of Thewbelle Philp, Zara Hagan, Grace Crowe and Emilia Reed won their heat of the women's 4x100m sprint.

World.title: 'Always by my side': Argentina mourns death of Jorge Messi
World.content:
Jorge Messi, the father of soccer star Lionel Messi, has died at a hospital in the central Argentina city of Rosario. He was 68.

The Rosario-based Club Atlético Newell's Old Boys announced his death in a social media post on Saturday that said he had undergone treatment in recent months for an unspecified illness.

The post described him as "the pillar and the person who, with vision, rigour and affection, supported the career of the best player of all time, alongside his wife, Celia Cuccittini".

Lionel Messi embraces his father Jorge Messi after the World Cup final in Qatar in 2022. (Getty Images: Robert Michael)

In a statement, the South American Football Confederation (CONMEBOL) also offered its condolences "with respect and affection for Lionel".

Lionel Messi led Argentina to a runner-up finish in this year's World Cup. In the team's first match, against Algeria, he was visibly emotional after scoring the first of his three goals. He said later that he wept for "a reason unrelated to sports".

"I went through some difficult, complicated days," he said.

"I am grateful to the delegation, to all my teammates, because they were always by my side wishing me strength so that I would be OK."

Media reports at the time outraged the Messi family, which days later released a statement confirming that "Jorge is experiencing a health issue", without specifying the nature of his condition.

"A person's health and the peace of mind of their loved ones should not be the subject of speculation or irresponsible media interest," according to the statement, which also expressed "discomfort at the lack of sensitivity, respect and scruples with which some people have treated a strictly private and family matter".

A minute of silence is held in memory of Jorge Messi, Leo Messi's father, during the FVG Cup match between Udinese Calcio and Nottingham Forest in Italy. The FVG Cup is a three team tournament that also includes Barcelona. (Getty Images: Mattia Radoni/NurPhoto)

Jorge Messi was a chemical technician and worked as a steelworker. He played soccer as a midfielder and reached the youth ranks of Newell's Old Boys but had to abandon the sport to complete his mandatory military service in Argentina.

He played a fundamental role in his third son's career, serving as his agent and managing his business affairs.

He was the one who travelled with a young Messi to Barcelona in the early 2000s for the trial that would open the doors to La Masia, the club's youth academy.

Lionel Messi made his professional debut in 2005 and went on to win eight Ballon d'Or awards. He led Argentina to the 2022 World Cup title.

Lionel Messi (back) poses with his family, including dad Jorge (centre) in 2003. (Getty Images: Marcelo Boeri/El Grafico)

"My dad was always by my side," Lionel Messi said in a 2007 interview with Radio del Plata.

"Sometimes I would lock myself in my room to cry when we arrived in Barcelona, or my dad would do the same without me seeing him, or thinking I didn't see him. We pretended we were both OK, but we weren't.

"My dad even asked me what I wanted to do when we were feeling down, if I wanted to stay or go back, and I wanted to stay, and he stayed with me."

His father negotiated the contracts with Barça and later his transfers to Paris Saint-Germain and Inter Miami, while also managing the use of his famous son's image rights and his numerous investments in real estate, hotels and restaurants.

In 2013, father and son were accused by a Spanish prosecutor of trying to conceal earnings from the player's image rights. Jorge Messi paid more than 5 million euros ($8.1 million) on August 14 to cover alleged back taxes and interest.

In Rosario, a sign at the VIP Rosario restaurant, one of the Messi family's gastronomic ventures, indicated that it was closed for the day.

The president of Argentina's soccer federation, Claudio Tapia, on Saturday issued a lengthy statement in which he recognised Jorge Messi "for having raised a person of values: humble, respectful, and deeply committed to others".

The organisation ordered a moment of silence to be observed at all matches across all categories of Argentine soccer and mandated that players, referees and coaching staff wear black armbands.

World.title: NFL star uses Hall of Fame speech to announce he has dementia
World.content:
Former star NFL running back Roger Craig has revealed during his induction speech into the Pro Football Hall of Fame that he has vascular dementia.

The former San Francisco 49ers player spoke in a pre-recorded video message while he sat on stage wearing his gold jacket at Tom Benson Hall of Fame Stadium in Canton, Ohio.

Presented by former teammate Jamie Williams, he received a standing ovation from the crowd and hugs from the many Hall of Famers on stage.

Nearly eight minutes into a nine-minute speech, Craig announced his diagnosis, saying his doctors believe "it may be related, at least in part, to the concussions" he experienced during his playing career.

"The changes were gradual," Craig said.

"At first, they were easy to dismiss as normal aging. Over time, my family noticed, too."

Symptoms of vascular dementia, according to the Mayo Clinic, include confusion; trouble finding the right words; difficulty paying attention; trouble organising thoughts or actions; difficulty planning and following through with plans; slowed thinking; uncertainty about what to do next; and memory issues.

Roger Craig was a trailblazer at the running back position for the San Francisco 49ers. (Getty Images: George Rose)

"Two things could be true," Craig said.

"Football gave me opportunities beyond anything I can imagine. It helped shape the man I became.

"At the same time, we know more today about brain health than when I played. I hope sharing my story encourages people to pay attention to their health and seek help when something doesn't feel right.

"I want people to know that this diagnosis doesn't define me. I am still Roger Craig. I am still a father, still a husband, a teammate, a friend and someone who loves this game and the people who brought it to my life.

Inside a brain with suspected CTE The effect of head knocks over Gordi Kirkbank-Ellis's decades-long sporting career isn't immediately obvious. That is, until you see what's happening to his brain.

"If sharing my story helps even one family or one former player, then it's worth it. Football gave me everything: opportunity, discipline, lifelong friends and the platform to grow as a man. This honour belongs to my parents who started it all."

Selected by the 49ers in the second round of the 1983 draft as a fullback out of Nebraska, Craig become one of the most versatile players in league history.

He excelled as a runner, receiver and blocker, helping the 49ers win three of their five Super Bowls.

In 1985, Craig became the first player in NFL history to have 1,000 yards rushing and 1,000 yards receiving in a season.

Craig was selected from the seniors category and entered the Pro Football Hall of Fame Class of 2026 with Drew Brees, Larry Fitzgerald, Luke Kuechly and Adam Vinatieri.
